text: Targeted Cancer Interception Vaccines and p53 Reactivation Strategies | Speaker: Margie Lee Clapper | Tumors: colorectal cancer, lung adenocarcinoma, breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, multiple solid tumors | MOA: Clapper presented mRNA‑based vaccines targeting EGFR L858R and KRAS G12C mutations found in premalignant lung ground‑glass opacities, demonstrating CD8+ T‑cell activation and reduced tumor formation in mouse models. She also described the small‑molecule p53 reactivator REM‑491, which restores transcriptional activity of multiple hotspot p53 mutants (R175H, R273) in vitro (EC50 ~40 nM) and suppresses tumor growth in xenograft models without observable toxicity. | Findings: In a cohort of Lynch syndrome individuals, 85% maintained a positive IFN‑γ ELISpot response one year after two doses of the 209‑peptide NU209 vaccine.; Whole‑exome sequencing of 200 ground‑glass lung nodules revealed 25% harbor EGFR L858R and 40% KRAS G12C mutations.; EGFR L858R mRNA vaccine achieved >90% lipid nanoparticle encapsulation efficiency and induced robust CD8+ T‑cell responses in mice.; Mice vaccinated with EGFR L858R mRNA vaccine showed a dramatic reduction in tumor formation compared with empty nanoparticle controls.; REM‑491 induced Nox and Puma transcription in TP53‑mutant Cal‑33 cells but not in WT or p53‑null cells, confirming mutant‑specific activity.

metadata.speaker: Margie Lee Clapper
metadata.talk_title: Targeted Cancer Interception Vaccines and p53 Reactivation Strategies

text: Precision Cancer Prevention: Risk Assessment, Implementation, and Public Health Strategies | Speaker: Suzette Delaloge | Tumors: breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, lung cancer, liver cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: Delaloge outlined a public‑health‑driven precision prevention framework that integrates individual risk assessment (clinical scores, breast density, polygenic risk scores) with AI‑enhanced imaging, digital tools, and coordinated care pathways to deliver risk‑adapted screening, surveillance, and risk‑reduction interventions across multiple cancer types. | Findings: In the MIPEPS trial, 36% of 28,000 women were classified as low risk and 33% as high risk, with a 5‑year invasive breast cancer risk of 1.67% in the high‑risk group.; Turnaround time for the PEARS risk score was a median of 7 weeks, demonstrating feasibility of large‑scale academic risk profiling.; The US Wisdom trial (non‑inferiority) met its primary endpoint of Stage 2B breast cancer incidence, supporting risk‑adapted screening.; The LIBER letrozole prevention trial suffered low accrual (18% acceptance) and 75% 5‑year adherence, resulting in an underpowered study with no observed risk reduction.; The French interception pilot program achieved a 1‑point improvement in the WCRF lifestyle score in 41% of participants and high adherence to recommended screening.

metadata.speaker: Suzette Delaloge
metadata.talk_title: Precision Cancer Prevention: Risk Assessment, Implementation, and Public Health Strategies

text: Metabolic vulnerabilities of Nrf2-activated cancer cells and cysteine availability in vivo | Speaker: Gina | Tumors: lung adenocarcinoma, liver cancer, pancreatic cancer | MOA: Gina demonstrated that Nrf2 activation rewires cysteine and glutathione metabolism, creating dependencies on cystine uptake, glutamine metabolism, and NADPH production; she showed tissue-specific cysteine sourcing via transsulfuration in liver versus reliance on extracellular cystine in lung tumors, and highlighted how microenvironmental nutrient gradients shape these vulnerabilities. | Findings: Liver tumors retain transsulfuration activity, while KRAS-driven lung tumors lack cysteine synthesis and depend on extracellular cystine.; Interstitial fluid of lung tumors contains ~40 µM reduced cysteine and ~1 mM reduced glutathione, indicating a shift to cysteine uptake.; Blocking cystine uptake with GGSTOP impairs tumor growth in vivo, but technical issues limited chronic dosing.; Nrf2-active cells become glutamate‑limited and are sensitized to glutaminase inhibition (CB‑839) in standard RPMI but not in tumor‑derived sTIF media.; sTIF media, mimicking interstitial fluid, rescues cystine‑starved cells and abolishes CB‑839 sensitivity, revealing context‑dependent metabolic vulnerabilities.

metadata.speaker: Gina
metadata.talk_title: Metabolic vulnerabilities of Nrf2-activated cancer cells and cysteine availability in vivo

text: Mitochondrial protein degradation drives heme‑mediated CD8 T‑cell exhaustion | Speaker: Ping‑Chi Ho | Tumors: melanoma, lung adenocarcinoma | MOA: Ho showed that chronic antigen exposure in tumors leads to accumulation of depolarized mitochondria in CD8 T cells; blocked mitophagy forces proteasomal degradation of mitochondrial proteins, releasing heme that binds and degrades BACH2, relieving repression of BLIMP1 and driving terminal exhaustion. | Findings: MDR‑low CD8 T cells in tumors have high mitochondrial mass but low membrane potential and upregulated proteasome genes.; Proteasome inhibition (MG132) restores BACH2 and reduces BLIMP1, partially reversing exhaustion markers.; Heme released from degraded mitochondrial hemoproteins increases in exhausted T cells and correlates with exhaustion severity in vivo.; Exogenous heme treatment in vitro drives PD‑1 up‑regulation, TCF1 loss, and cytokine production decline.; BACH2 mutant resistant to heme binding preserves stemness markers even in tumor‑derived damaged‑mitochondria T cells.

metadata.speaker: Ping‑Chi Ho
metadata.talk_title: Mitochondrial protein degradation drives heme‑mediated CD8 T‑cell exhaustion

text: TIM‑4/AMPK‑TREM1 axis controls mitochondrial metabolism and immunosuppression in tumor‑associated macrophages | Speaker: Stanley Huang | Tumors: melanoma, lung carcinoma, ovarian cancer, liver cancer | MOA: Huang identified that tumor‑derived signals up‑regulate TIM4, which activates AMPK, suppresses TREM1 expression, and enhances mitochondrial complex II activity and glutamine‑derived α‑KG production in tumor‑associated macrophages; the resulting α‑KG fuels JMJD3‑mediated H3K27 demethylation, driving an immunosuppressive M2‑like phenotype. | Findings: Tumor‑associated macrophages show ~70% reduction of TREM1 protein compared with splenic macrophages.; TIM4 deficiency or blockade restores TREM1 expression, reduces mitochondrial complex II activity, and diminishes α‑KG production.; Myeloid‑specific TREM1 deletion hyperactivates mitochondrial respiration, increases immunosuppressive markers, accelerates tumor growth, and shortens mouse survival.; AMPK activation downstream of TIM4 suppresses TREM1; AMPK knockdown rescues TREM1 and lowers mitochondrial activity.; GMG3 loss in myeloid cells reduces tumor size, TAM numbers, and immunosuppressive markers while enhancing CD8 T‑cell infiltration.

metadata.speaker: Stanley Huang
metadata.talk_title: TIM‑4/AMPK‑TREM1 axis controls mitochondrial metabolism and immunosuppression in tumor‑associated macrophages

text: Cancer risk and genotype‑phenotype correlations in telomere biology disorders | Speaker: Dr. Sharon Savage | Tumors: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, AML, MDS, pulmonary fibrosis, liver disease | MOA: Germline mutations in telomere maintenance genes (e.g., TINF2, RTEL1, TERT) cause critically short or dysfunctional telomeres, leading to stem‑cell failure and a strong selective pressure for clonal hematopoiesis; specific somatic mutations (TP53 loss, MDM4 overexpression, U2AF1) further drive malignant transformation, resulting in markedly elevated risks of head‑and‑neck SCC, AML, and MDS. | Findings: Median overall survival of the entire TBD cohort was 52 years, but carriers of biallelic or X‑linked/TINF2 variants had median survival only in the 30s.; Overall cancer risk was ~3‑fold higher than the general population, rising to ~4‑fold before transplant.; Head‑and‑neck squamous cell carcinoma risk was ~50‑fold higher (median onset age 14.7 years) in TINF2 mutation carriers.; AML risk was ~50‑fold and MDS risk ~500‑fold higher than expected in age‑sex matched controls.; Clonal hematopoiesis with non‑cancer‑associated mutations (POT1, TERT promoter, PPM1D) correlated with better prognosis, whereas TP53 loss, MDM4 overexpression, or U2AF1 mutations predicted cancer development.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Sharon Savage
metadata.talk_title: Cancer risk and genotype‑phenotype correlations in telomere biology disorders
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

text: Genotype‑specific risk assessment and screening strategies for Lynch syndrome | Speaker: Dr. Faye Kastrinos | Tumors: colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer, gastric cancer, hepatobiliary cancer, pancreatic cancer, urothelial cancer | MOA: Germline pathogenic variants in mismatch‑repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) cause microsatellite instability, markedly increasing risk of colorectal, endometrial and other cancers; genotype‑specific modeling shows earlier onset for MLH1/MSH2 and later, lower‑penetrance disease for MSH6/PMS2, informing age‑adjusted colonoscopy intervals and the potential integration of non‑invasive FIT screening to reduce colonoscopy burden. | Findings: Lynch syndrome prevalence is ~1/350 in the US, with ~63 % of carriers lacking any personal or family cancer history that would trigger clinical suspicion.; MSH6 and PMS2 carriers constitute the majority of pathogenic variants in population‑based cohorts, yet they have later onset and lower absolute cancer risks compared with MLH1/MSH2.; Genotype‑specific colonoscopy recommendations (e.g., start at 25 y for MLH1/MSH2 annually, at 35 y for MSH6 every 2 y, at 40 y for PMS2 every 3 y) improve risk‑benefit balance and reduce colonoscopy burden.; Modeling shows that integrating biennial FIT with extended colonoscopy intervals (e.g., every 4 y) for PMS2 carriers maintains cancer prevention while improving quality‑adjusted life years and cost‑effectiveness.; Aspirin chemoprevention at 161 mg daily is recommended for all carriers, based on emerging evidence, despite limited data on genotype‑specific efficacy.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Faye Kastrinos
metadata.talk_title: Genotype‑specific risk assessment and screening strategies for Lynch syndrome

text: Precision modeling and targeted therapy testing in Fanconi anemia‑associated head and neck cancer | Speaker: Unnamed Head & Neck Surgeon | Tumors: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, esophageal cancer, vulvar cancer, liver cancer, breast cancer | MOA: Patient‑derived Fanconi anemia head‑and‑neck cancer xenografts retain the underlying DNA‑repair deficiency and display heterogeneous driver alterations; EGFR overexpression predicts response to cetuximab and dacomitinib, PIK3CA E545K predicts sensitivity to alpelisib (with additive effect when combined with EGFR blockade), and high BCL2/BCLXL expression confers venetoclax sensitivity, providing a precision‑medicine framework for this ultra‑rare population. | Findings: Two of three Fanconi anemia HNSCC PDX models were the most platinum‑sensitive among >30 sporadic HNSCC models tested.; Model #1 (high EGFR/HER2/HER3) showed exquisite sensitivity to cetuximab and dacomitinib, with dose‑dependent tumor regression.; Model #3 (PIK3CA E545K) was resistant to cetuximab but responded to alpelisib; the combination of alpelisib plus cetuximab produced greater tumor shrinkage than either agent alone.; Model #2 (high BCL2/BCLXL) was resistant to EGFR inhibitors but displayed marked sensitivity to the BCL2 inhibitor venetoclax, suggesting a novel therapeutic avenue.; Heterogeneity across the three PDXs underscores the need for genotype‑guided therapy selection rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all approach in Fanconi anemia‑associated HNSCC.

metadata.speaker: Unnamed Head & Neck Surgeon
metadata.talk_title: Precision modeling and targeted therapy testing in Fanconi anemia‑associated head and neck cancer
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

text: Tobacco use trends and regulatory landscape | Speaker: Suchitra Krishnan-Sarin | MOA: The speaker presented epidemiologic data on declining cigarette use, stable cigar use, and rising e‑cigarette use, highlighting the impact of FDA regulatory pathways (PMTA, MRTP) and the need for balanced risk‑benefit assessment of novel nicotine products. | Findings: U.S. cigarette prevalence is trending downward toward the Healthy People 2030 target of 5%; Cigar use rates have remained flat over recent years; E‑cigarette use has steadily increased since market entry in 2009, both in the U.S. and globally; Youth cigarette use spiked after the introduction of Juul in 2014‑2015 before declining with subsequent regulations

metadata.speaker: Suchitra Krishnan-Sarin
metadata.talk_title: Tobacco use trends and regulatory landscape

text: Lung cancer screening impact and policy gaps | Speaker: Doug Wood | Tumors: lung cancer | MOA: Low‑dose CT screening of high‑risk smokers reduces lung cancer mortality by 20% (NLST) and improves 5‑year survival dramatically; however, current policy limits uptake to ~19% of eligible individuals, suggesting that simplifying criteria and expanding eligibility could save tens of thousands of lives. | Findings: NLST demonstrated a 20% mortality reduction with low‑dose CT in high‑risk smokers; Only 19% of eligible U.S. adults are currently screened, yet this still yields ~15,000 lives saved over five years; Modeling suggests expanding criteria could increase lives saved to ~90,000 in five years; Simplifying smoking metrics (duration vs pack‑years) improves equitable identification of high‑risk individuals; Current upper age limit of 80 and 15‑year smoking cessation rule exclude many who could benefit

metadata.speaker: Doug Wood
metadata.talk_title: Lung cancer screening impact and policy gaps

text: Screening test implementation and follow‑up gaps | Speaker: Electra Paskett | Tumors: breast cancer, cervical cancer, colorectal cancer, lung cancer | MOA: The presenter highlighted gaps between screening test availability and completion of the screening process, showing low follow‑up rates for abnormal results across breast, cervical, colorectal, and lung cancer screening, especially in underserved populations, and argued for policy changes to support navigation and coverage. | Findings: U.S. screening uptake is high for breast (80%) but low for lung cancer (14%); Timely follow‑up after abnormal screens ranges from 60% (cervical) to 66% (mammography) and is lower for lung (48‑58%) and FIT/FOBT (18‑57%); Out‑of‑pocket costs for follow‑up (e.g., $800‑$1,600 for abnormal mammogram) hinder completion; Medicaid expansion improves screening rates and cancer survival in rural, high‑poverty areas; Implementation barriers, not just test availability, limit effective screening worldwide

metadata.speaker: Electra Paskett
metadata.talk_title: Screening test implementation and follow‑up gaps

text: NCI cancer prevention research pipeline and population impact | Speaker: Phil Castle | MOA: The speaker outlined NCI's structured pipeline from target discovery (CAPiT, natural products, immunoprevention) through PREVENT contracts to early‑phase trials (CPCTnet) and large population trials (NCOR), emphasizing the need for biomarkers, prevention agents, and policy support to translate discovery into population benefit. | Findings: NCI supports a continuum from target discovery (CAPiT, natural products) to PREVENT contracts bridging discovery to clinical trials; Early‑phase prevention trials are coordinated through CPCTnet and NCOR; Biomarker development is a priority for lung cancer risk stratification and broader MCED applications; Policy and funding gaps hinder long‑term prevention studies due to long timelines and limited ROI for industry

metadata.speaker: Phil Castle
metadata.talk_title: NCI cancer prevention research pipeline and population impact

text: Measuring cancer evolution with mathematical modeling | Speaker: Andrea Sottoriva | Tumors: colorectal cancer, breast cancer, leukemia, melanoma, pan-cancer | MOA: Sottoriva presented population genetics models that use bulk variant allele frequency distributions to infer clonal dynamics, mutation rates, and selection coefficients in tumors, enabling prediction of evolutionary trajectories and treatment response. | Findings: Derived analytical relationship (1/F^2) between subclonal mutation frequency and mutation rate in expanding tumor populations.; Demonstrated that positive selection shifts subclonal driver mutations to higher frequencies, distinguishable from neutral drift.; Implemented Bayesian and machine‑learning deconvolution methods to estimate mutation rates and selection coefficients from bulk sequencing data.; Extended models to spatially resolved data, showing sampling bias can obscure selection events.

metadata.speaker: Andrea Sottoriva
metadata.talk_title: Measuring cancer evolution with mathematical modeling

text: Evolutionary‑informed adaptive therapy and virtual clinical trial design | Speaker: Sandy Anderson | Tumors: prostate cancer, melanoma, basal cell carcinoma | MOA: Anderson described adaptive therapy, an on‑off dosing strategy that exploits fitness costs of resistance, using PSA dynamics to trigger treatment pauses, thereby prolonging control of resistant prostate cancer and other solid tumors. | Findings: Adaptive therapy using a 50% PSA reduction rule extended median progression‑free survival to 33 months versus 14 months with continuous dosing.; Patients received <50% of the cumulative drug dose while maintaining disease control.; Virtual trial simulations with calibrated digital twins accurately predicted the adaptive trial outcome before enrollment.; Stratifying patients by first‑cycle PSA dynamics (high/medium/low thresholds) could further improve adaptive therapy efficacy.

metadata.speaker: Sandy Anderson
metadata.talk_title: Evolutionary‑informed adaptive therapy and virtual clinical trial design

text: Metabolic quiescence and ATP synthase reversal as a vulnerability in enzalutamide‑resistant prostate cancer | Speaker: Speaker Unknown | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: The presenter identified that enzalutamide‑resistant prostate cancer cells enter a metabolically quiescent state with reversed ATP synthase activity driven by loss of ATPIF1, creating a depolarized mitochondrial membrane that can be selectively targeted with the mitochondria‑directed cation MitoQ, leading to tumor regression in vivo. | Findings: Resistant cells show reduced basal and maximal respiration across multiple substrates.; Mitochondrial membrane potential is depolarized in resistant cells due to reverse ATP synthase activity.; ATPIF1 expression is decreased in resistant cells and in patient CTCs from non‑responders.; Pharmacologic inhibition of p38 restores ATPIF1 levels and sensitizes resistant cells to enzalutamide.; MitoQ treatment selectively kills resistant cells in vitro and causes tumor regression in resistant xenograft models.

metadata.speaker: Speaker Unknown
metadata.talk_title: Metabolic quiescence and ATP synthase reversal as a vulnerability in enzalutamide‑resistant prostate cancer

text: Personalized Neoantigen Vaccines in Glioblastoma and the Impact of Tumor Intrinsic Programs | Speaker: Cathy Wu | Tumors: glioblastoma | MOA: The speaker investigated personalized peptide vaccines in glioblastoma, finding that the mesenchymal transcriptional subtype is a key predictor of response due to higher HLA class I expression and T cell infiltration. The study explored the timing of anti-PD-1 therapy, suggesting that pretreatment with pembrolizumab followed by vaccine may be superior to vaccine followed by pembrolizumab. Additionally, Temozolomide was found to improve outcomes by depleting circulating Tregs and promoting antigen-specific T cell responses. | Findings: Mesenchymal subtype in GBM is associated with higher HLA class I expression and better response to ICB monotherapy.; Dexamethasone treatment suppresses the ability of patients to mount circulating T cell responses following vaccination.; In a 40-patient trial, the cohort receiving pembrolizumab before the vaccine showed better outcomes than those receiving pembrolizumab after the vaccine.; Temozolomide-treated patients showed improved overall survival and decreased Treg upregulation following neoantigen vaccination.; Vaccine-reactive T cell clonotypes were detectable in post-treatment tumors and were predominantly CD4+ cells.

metadata.speaker: Cathy Wu
metadata.session_title: Cancer Vaccines: The Next Immunotherapy Breakthrough
metadata.talk_title: Personalized Neoantigen Vaccines in Glioblastoma and the Impact of Tumor Intrinsic Programs

text: Mechanisms by which mRNA Vaccines Augment Response to Immune Checkpoint Blockade | Speaker: Adam Griffin | Tumors: NSCLC, melanoma, osteosarcoma | MOA: The speaker proposes that mRNA vaccines, even those not targeting tumor antigens (like the COVID-19 vaccine), can sensitize tumors to ICI by triggering an MDA5-mediated surge in interferon alpha. This systemic interferon alpha activates myeloid cells (DCs and macrophages), which then prime anti-tumor T cells that infiltrate the tumor and secrete interferon gamma, leading to compensatory PD-L1 upregulation and subsequent sensitivity to PD-1 blockade. | Findings: Retrospective pan-tumor analysis showed patients receiving the COVID mRNA vaccine within 30 days prior to ICI had significantly longer survival.; In mouse models, the COVID vaccine sensitized B16-F0 and Lewis lung carcinoma to ICI via an interferon alpha-dependent mechanism.; Blocking interferon alpha completely abrogated the benefit of the COVID vaccine in mouse models.; The mRNA-LNP complex activates the MDA5 receptor, bypassing the TLR7 silencing provided by N1-methylpseudouridine.; Human data showed a 30% increase in tumor PD-L1 expression in patients vaccinated prior to biopsy.

metadata.speaker: Adam Griffin
metadata.session_title: Cancer Vaccines: The Next Immunotherapy Breakthrough
metadata.talk_title: Mechanisms by which mRNA Vaccines Augment Response to Immune Checkpoint Blockade

text: Optimizing Peptide Vaccines and Adoptive Cell Therapy through Stem-like T Cell Generation | Speaker: Robert Seder | Tumors: colorectal cancer, melanoma, GI tumors | MOA: The speaker developed a nanoparticle peptide vaccine platform using a Toll 7/8 agonist and a cathepsin-cleavable linker to improve antigen solubility and cross-priming. IV administration of this vaccine induces stem-like CD8 T cells (TCF7+) and systemic type I interferon, which remodels the TME by depleting CHIL3+ monocytes. Furthermore, using a PI3K delta inhibitor during TIL expansion preserves T cell stemness, which, when combined with vaccination, leads to superior tumor control compared to effector-like cells. | Findings: IV administration of the nanoparticle vaccine induced stem-like CD8 T cells and systemic type I interferon, whereas subcutaneous administration induced effector cells and provided no protection.; Protection from IV vaccination was completely abrogated by depleting type I interferon, which specifically reduced a CHIL3+ monocyte population in the TME.; PI3K delta inhibition during T cell expansion preserved stem-like characteristics (TCF1+, CCR7+, CD62L+), which were significantly more effective in tumor regression when combined with vaccination.; Combination of stem-like ACT and vaccination led to massive immune infiltration and shifted the tumor transcriptome toward an interferon-gamma reactive state.; Blocking either interferon gamma or the interferon alpha/beta receptor completely abrogated the protection provided by stem-like ACT + vaccine.

metadata.speaker: Robert Seder
metadata.session_title: Cancer Vaccines: The Next Immunotherapy Breakthrough
metadata.talk_title: Optimizing Peptide Vaccines and Adoptive Cell Therapy through Stem-like T Cell Generation

text: Inducing De Novo CD8 and CD4 T Cell Immunity in Pancreatic Cancer | Speaker: Vinod Balachandran | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: The speaker developed a personalized RNA vaccine (autogene cevumarán) for PDAC, targeting high-quality neoantigens. The vaccine induces de novo, long-lived CD8+ and CD4+ Th1 effector T cells. These responses correlate with delayed recurrence and improved overall survival, with CD4+ cells appearing transiently in the blood but expanding in recurrent tumors and supporting CD8+ longevity. | Findings: Personalized RNA vaccines induced neoantigen-specific T cells in 50% of unselected PDAC patients.; Vaccine-induced CD8 T cells showed exceptional longevity, with a median estimated lifespan of 7.7 years.; At 6-year follow-up, vaccine responders had significantly better overall survival (7/8 alive) compared to non-responders (2/8 alive).; 97.5% of induced CD8 and 100% of induced CD4 clones were absent in pre-vaccination tissues, proving de novo induction.; Induced CD4 T cells transition to a Th1 effector-like phenotype (granzyme+, T-bet+) and are clonally expanded in recurrent tumors.

metadata.speaker: Vinod Balachandran
metadata.session_title: Cancer Vaccines: The Next Immunotherapy Breakthrough
metadata.talk_title: Inducing De Novo CD8 and CD4 T Cell Immunity in Pancreatic Cancer

text: Advancing BCMA and Novel Targets in Multiple Myeloma CAR T Therapy | Speaker: Karina Patel | Tumors: multiple myeloma | MOA: BCMA‑directed CAR T cells (ide‑cel, cilta‑cel) engage the TNFRSF17 antigen on >95% of myeloma cells, delivering potent cytotoxicity and inducing deep MRD‑negative remissions; next‑generation CARs add dual‑epitope binding or tandem targeting of GPRC5D to overcome antigen escape and improve durability, while novel manufacturing (fast off‑rate D‑domain CARs, allogeneic CRISPR‑edited products) aim to reduce CRS/ICANS and broaden access. | Findings: Ide‑cel Phase 1 in heavily pre‑treated MM achieved 72% ORR and median PFS 11.1 months, surpassing historical expectations.; KarMMa‑3 Phase 3 showed CAR‑T median PFS 13.3 months versus 4.4 months with daratumumab‑based triplet (HR ≈ 0.33).; Cilta‑cel produced 97‑98% ORR with 33% of patients remaining disease‑free at 5 years, indicating functional cure potential.; GPRC5D‑targeted CAR T yielded 87% ORR (94% in BCMA‑naïve patients) and PFS up to 24.3 months, demonstrating efficacy after BCMA failure.; Fast‑off‑rate D‑domain CAR (Anita Cell) reported 96% ORR and 74% stringent CR with a favorable safety profile in early data.

metadata.speaker: Karina Patel
metadata.session_title: CAR-T Therapy: Transforming the Landscape of Adult and Pediatric Blood Cancers
metadata.talk_title: Advancing BCMA and Novel Targets in Multiple Myeloma CAR T Therapy

text: Emerging Multi‑Antigen CAR T Strategies in Lymphoma and Leukemia | Speaker: Matthew Frank | Tumors: large B-cell lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, follicular lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, ALL, CLL | MOA: Multi‑antigen CAR T constructs (tandem, bicistronic, trispecific) co‑express CARs against CD19, CD20, CD22 or CD79B, enabling simultaneous recognition of distinct B‑cell markers to prevent antigen loss; rapid manufacturing platforms reduce vein‑to‑infusion time, while higher upfront dosing and armored IL‑18 CARs aim to boost expansion and overcome an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. | Findings: Zantacel (CD19/CD20 tandem) achieved 73% ORR and ~50% CR in heavily pre‑treated large B‑cell lymphoma with only 4% grade 3 ICANS.; Kite‑363 bicistronic CD19/CD20 CAR showed ~90% ORR and ~80% CR in primary refractory lymphoma, with reduced neurotoxicity compared to axicel.; J&J tandem CD19/CD20 CAR reported >90% ORR and 75‑80% CR across high‑risk cohorts, with low severe ICANS rates.; Cargo CD22 CAR in post‑CD19 relapse patients yielded 70% ORR and 53% CR overall, and 100% CR in follicular lymphoma cohort, without grade 3+ CRS/ICANS.; Higher upfront CAR dose (double infusion) in high‑LDH patients produced 93% ORR and 80% CR with manageable toxicity.

metadata.speaker: Matthew Frank
metadata.session_title: CAR-T Therapy: Transforming the Landscape of Adult and Pediatric Blood Cancers
metadata.talk_title: Emerging Multi‑Antigen CAR T Strategies in Lymphoma and Leukemia

text: Advances and challenges in autologous CAR T manufacturing and scalability | Speaker: Christine Brown | Tumors: brain tumors, solid tumors, hematologic malignancies, autoimmune diseases | MOA: Brown highlighted that rapid, automated manufacturing (1-3 day processes) and point‑of‑care production can preserve T‑cell fitness and reduce cost, while maintaining the potency of autologous CAR T cells for brain and solid tumors. She described collaborations using Solaris' Cell Shuttle to enable dual‑CAR, pooled approaches and emphasized decentralized manufacturing to improve access. | Findings: City of Hope has treated 500 patients across 16 phase‑1 autologous CAR T trials.; Manufacturing capacity ranges from 55 to 85 patient‑specific products per year.; Rapid manufacturing platforms (1‑3 days) can shorten time to infusion from ~30 days to ~14 days.; Automated systems (Miltenyi Prodigy, Lonza Cocoon, Ori Biotech Airo, Solaris Cell Shuttle) reduce hands‑on labor and enable point‑of‑care production.; A pooled CAR approach targeting multiple GBM antigens is being developed with Solaris.

metadata.speaker: Christine Brown
metadata.talk_title: Advances and challenges in autologous CAR T manufacturing and scalability

text: Allogeneic CAR T cell platform: manufacturing, persistence strategies, and MRD‑guided trials | Speaker: Zachary Roberts | Tumors: large B‑cell lymphoma, renal cell carcinoma, multiple myeloma | MOA: Roberts described Allogene's allogeneic CAR T platform that uses TRAC and CD52 gene edits to eliminate TCR and render cells resistant to alemtuzumab (CD52‑targeting) lymphodepletion, enabling selective host T‑cell depletion and enhanced CAR T expansion. He introduced the CD70‑targeting “dagger” CAR that cis‑masks CD70 to prevent fratricide and leverages host allo‑reactivity for superior expansion and persistence, demonstrated in RCC trials. | Findings: Allogene's celma‑cel (CD19 CAR with TRAC and CD52 knockout) achieved a 67% ORR in relapsed/refractory LBCL, with most responses being complete.; No high‑grade CRS, ICANS, or GVHD observed across >200 treated patients.; In the ALPHA III MRD‑positive LBCL trial, 60% of celma‑cel patients cleared ctDNA versus 16.7% on observation (p<0.01).; CD70‑targeting dagger CAR (ALO329) yielded a 31% durable ORR in CD70‑high RCC with unprecedented Cmax and AUC28 expansion.; Higher lymphodepletion intensity (e.g., alemtuzumab exposure) correlated with greater CAR T expansion (AUC28) in phase 1 LBCL studies.

metadata.speaker: Zachary Roberts
metadata.talk_title: Allogeneic CAR T cell platform: manufacturing, persistence strategies, and MRD‑guided trials

text: In vivo CAR T engineering using GeneWriter RNA‑LNP platform | Speaker: Alberto Diaco | Tumors: hematologic malignancies, solid tumors | MOA: Diaco introduced Tessera's GeneWriter platform, an RNA‑based non‑LTR retrotransposon system packaged in targeted LNPs that delivers a template RNA encoding a CAR and a GeneWriter mRNA encoding the editing protein, enabling site‑random genomic integration of the CAR without viral vectors. In vitro, GeneWriters achieve 3‑25% CAR‑positive T cells; in vivo mouse studies reach ~25‑30% CAR‑positive T cells with tumor clearance and B‑cell aplasia at doses as low as 0.03 MPK. | Findings: Five GeneWriter variants yielded 3‑25% CAR expression in human T cells in vitro.; GeneWriter integration shows a near‑random genomic distribution, unlike lentiviral vectors which favor active genes.; In NSG tumor models, LNP‑delivered CD19 GeneWriter achieved ~30% CAR‑positive T cells by day 13 and complete tumor eradication.; In a humanized mouse model, CD20 GeneWriter at 0.3 MPK produced ~20% CAR‑positive T cells and rapid B‑cell depletion; lower dose (0.03 MPK) still achieved delayed but measurable CAR expression and B‑cell aplasia.; GeneWriter integration pattern suggests lower bias toward essential genes, potentially reducing insertional mutagenesis risk.

metadata.speaker: Alberto Diaco
metadata.talk_title: In vivo CAR T engineering using GeneWriter RNA‑LNP platform

text: CAR-PRISM trial of cilta-cel in high-risk smoldering multiple myeloma | Speaker: Dr. Omar Nadeem | Tumors: multiple myeloma | MOA: Cilta-cel, a BCMA-directed CAR T-cell product, is infused after lymphodepletion in high-risk smoldering myeloma patients, leading to rapid CAR T expansion, potent tumor cell killing, and universal MRD negativity without induction therapy, demonstrating a curative intent in an early disease setting. | Findings: All 20 treated patients achieved MRD negativity at a sensitivity of 10^-6 (100% MRD-negative rate).; Overall response rate was 100% with 90% achieving complete or stringent complete responses.; No dose-limiting toxicities or grade ≥3 CRS/ICANS were observed; CRS was limited to grade 1–2 in all patients.; Non-ICANS neurotoxicities occurred in 35% of patients, mostly low-grade and reversible.; Median follow-up of 15.3 months showed no disease progression; median PFS and OS not reached.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Omar Nadeem
metadata.talk_title: CAR-PRISM trial of cilta-cel in high-risk smoldering multiple myeloma

text: First-in-human dose escalation of multi-chain KIR CAR targeting mesothelin | Speaker: Dr. Janos Tanyi | Tumors: mesothelioma, ovarian cancer, cholangiocarcinoma | MOA: The multi-chain KIR CAR separates the antigen-binding SS1 scFv (targeting mesothelin) from the DAP12 intracellular signaling domain, providing an on/off switch that activates T cells only upon mesothelin engagement, reducing tonic signaling and exhaustion compared with traditional single-chain CARs. | Findings: Multi-chain KIR CAR showed minimal tonic signaling and lower exhaustion marker expression versus conventional single-chain CARs in vitro.; In mouse xenograft models, the KIR CAR achieved significant tumor regression with lower peripheral CAR T-cell persistence.; In the first-in-human dose escalation (9 patients), no dose-limiting toxicities, CRS (grade 1‑2) in 33%, and no ICANS were observed.; Disease stabilization was achieved in 55% of patients across dose levels, with one partial response at the highest dose.; CAR T-cell expansion in peripheral blood increased with dose but was not proportional, suggesting a plateau effect.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Janos Tanyi
metadata.talk_title: First-in-human dose escalation of multi-chain KIR CAR targeting mesothelin

text: FAP‑targeted 4‑1BB ligand trimer amplifies T‑cell engager in MSS colorectal cancer | Speaker: Dr. Ignacio Melero | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Civisatuximab engages CD3 on T cells and CEA on tumor cells, providing signal 1; the FAP‑targeted trimeric 4‑1BB ligand binds fibroblast activation protein in the tumor stroma, delivering conditional 4‑1BB co‑stimulation (signal 2) only where FAP is present, thereby enhancing T‑cell activation, proliferation, and antitumor efficacy in MSS colorectal cancer. | Findings: Combination yielded an overall response rate of 13% (20% at highest 4‑1BB ligand dose) in heavily pretreated MSS colorectal cancer.; Disease control rate reached 50%, exceeding historical monotherapy with civisatuximab.; CRS was mostly grade 1‑2; grade ≥3 CRS occurred in 2% of patients, indicating manageable safety.; Pharmacodynamic analyses showed increased peripheral IFN‑γ, sCD25, and IL‑6, and enhanced intratumoral CD8+ T‑cell density, especially in fibrotic stromal regions.; Higher tumor FAP and CEA expression trended with better tumor shrinkage, suggesting potential biomarkers.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Ignacio Melero
metadata.talk_title: FAP‑targeted 4‑1BB ligand trimer amplifies T‑cell engager in MSS colorectal cancer

text: Phase 1/2 mRNA‑4359 vaccine plus pembrolizumab in first‑line advanced melanoma | Speaker: Dr. Pavlina Spiliopoulou | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: Lipid‑nanoparticle mRNA‑4359 encodes PD‑L1 and IDO1; after intramuscular injection, dendritic cells translate and present these antigens, priming PD‑L1‑ and IDO1‑specific CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells that infiltrate tumors, target PD‑L1⁺/IDO1⁺ tumor and suppressor cells, and synergize with pembrolizumab to overcome checkpoint resistance. | Findings: Objective response rate of 83% (2 CR, 8 PR) with a 92% disease control rate in 12 first‑line melanoma patients.; No vaccine‑related grade ≥3 adverse events; safety profile consistent with other mRNA vaccines.; All evaluable patients showed increased PD‑L1 and IDO1‑specific T‑cell responses by ELISpot.; De novo peripheral TCR clonal expansion observed irrespective of clinical response.; Responses occurred regardless of baseline PD‑L1 expression or prior adjuvant therapy.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Pavlina Spiliopoulou
metadata.talk_title: Phase 1/2 mRNA‑4359 vaccine plus pembrolizumab in first‑line advanced melanoma

text: Immune‑stimulating ADCs with TLR7 agonist payloads and dual payload strategies | Speaker: Nathan Toomey | Tumors: breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, colorectal cancer, lung cancer | MOA: The presented work develops immune‑stimulating ADCs (ISACs) that deliver a permeable TLR7 agonist (E104) via a legumain‑cleavable linker, using Fc‑silent antibodies to reduce Fcγ‑mediated uptake and cytokine release; dual‑payload ADCs combine the TLR7 agonist with MMAF to achieve synergistic tumor growth delay in mouse models. | Findings: Fc‑silent, legumain‑cleavable TLR7‑ADC showed potent macrophage activation in co‑culture assays with minimal cytokine release compared to Fc‑active controls.; In HER2‑positive xenografts, the Fc‑silent ADC achieved tumor regression at 10 MPK Q4D×3, whereas the Fc‑active isotype control caused only modest delay and systemic cytokine release.; Trop‑2‑targeted ISAC demonstrated efficacy at 3 MPK in immune‑competent mice with no activity from isotype or naked antibody controls.; Dual‑payload ADC (MMAF + E104) produced significant tumor growth delay and regression in xenograft models, outperforming each single‑payload ADC, without observable weight loss or behavioral toxicity.; Anti‑Trop‑2 antibody responses were detected in mice after dosing, indicating immunogenicity despite Fc silencing.

metadata.speaker: Nathan Toomey
metadata.talk_title: Immune‑stimulating ADCs with TLR7 agonist payloads and dual payload strategies

text: PI3K/mTOR inhibitor payloads for ADCs targeting B‑cell and HER2 cancers | Speaker: Shixiong Wang | Tumors: B‑cell lymphoma, DLBCL, breast cancer, head and neck cancer, pancreatic cancer | MOA: Optimized pan‑PI3K/mTOR inhibitors were conjugated to antibodies (CD79B, HER2, CD71) via stable linkers to create ADCs that deliver potent intracellular kinase inhibition, achieving tumor‑stasis doses as low as 1.5 MPK in lymphoma models and demonstrating synergistic activity with venetoclax through MYC degradation in double‑hit DLBCL. | Findings: DAR10 ADCs with optimized PI3K/mTOR payloads showed sub‑nanomolar in‑vitro potency across lymphoma cell lines.; In CD79B‑targeted ADCs, a tumor‑stasis dose of ~3 MPK was identified, with regression at 5‑15 MPK, outperforming the free inhibitor (copanlisib).; Combination of the PI3K‑ADC with venetoclax in MYC‑BCL2 double‑hit lymphoma yielded superior tumor suppression and sustained efficacy versus either agent alone.; HER2‑targeted PI3K‑ADC demonstrated bystander killing in mixed HER2‑positive/negative cultures and tumor regression at 9 MPK, with more durable AKT pathway suppression than alpelisib.; Preclinical tolerability studies showed the ADCs were well‑tolerated in rats (up to 150 MPK) and monkeys (up to 100 MPK), with toxicity profiles consistent with on‑target PI3K effects.

metadata.speaker: Shixiong Wang
metadata.talk_title: PI3K/mTOR inhibitor payloads for ADCs targeting B‑cell and HER2 cancers

text: Degrader Antibody Conjugates (DAC) using SMARCA2/4 targeted protein degraders as payloads | Speaker: Koichi Ito | Tumors: prostate cancer, breast cancer, AML, multiple myeloma, solid tumors | MOA: Prelude’s DAC platform conjugates highly potent SMARCA2/4 PROTAC degraders to tumor‑specific antibodies (e.g., anti‑PSMA, anti‑mutant CALR), delivering intracellular degradation of SWI/SNF ATPase subunits, resulting in selective tumor cell killing with reduced systemic toxicity compared to the free degrader. | Findings: VHL‑based SMARCA2/4 degrader (Degrader‑04) achieved ~300 nM degradation potency; switching to cereblon (Degrader‑06) improved potency to ~40‑90 pM but reduced plasma stability.; DAC‑02 (anti‑PSMA conjugated to Degrader‑04) showed antigen‑specific internalization and SMARCA2/4 degradation in PSMA‑positive LNCaP cells, with robust tumor regression and no significant weight loss, unlike the free degrader.; Cereblon‑based Degrader‑07 achieved >200 h plasma half‑life and picomolar degradation potency, enabling more stable DACs for in‑vivo studies.; Mutant CALR‑targeted DAC demonstrated selective SMARCA2/4 degradation and anti‑proliferative activity in CALR‑mutant cells, with tumor regression in TF1 xenografts at tolerable doses.; Global proteomics confirmed on‑target degradation of SMARCA2/4 with minimal off‑target effects.

metadata.speaker: Koichi Ito
metadata.talk_title: Degrader Antibody Conjugates (DAC) using SMARCA2/4 targeted protein degraders as payloads

text: Heterobifunctional PARP-BET molecules induce PARP2 trapping and synthetic lethality | Speaker: Michael Erb | Tumors: prostate cancer, HR-deficient tumors | MOA: PSIP1 is a heterobifunctional small molecule that weakly engages PARP1/2 and BRD4 but induces a ternary complex preferentially with PARP2, leading to PARP2 chromatin trapping, inhibition of DNA repair, S‑phase arrest and synthetic lethality in HR‑deficient cells. | Findings: PSIP1 shows minimal binary engagement of PARP1/2 and BRD4 yet induces potent cytotoxicity comparable to BET inhibition.; Synthetic lethality of PSIP1 is retained in BRCA2‑deficient DLD1 cells and is abolished by stereochemical inversion of the JQ1 moiety.; FRET and co‑IP experiments confirm ternary complex formation between PARP2 and BRD4 that is lost with the inactive enantiomer.; PARP2 knockout confers resistance to PSIP1, whereas PARP1 knockout sensitizes cells, indicating PARP2‑dependent toxicity.; CRISPR screens identify SUMO pathway components (PIAS4, SEMP1) and ABCC1 as selective modifiers of PSIP1 activity.

metadata.speaker: Michael Erb
metadata.talk_title: Heterobifunctional PARP-BET molecules induce PARP2 trapping and synthetic lethality

text: Beyond degradation: induced proximity strategies entering the clinic | Speaker: William Gibson | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, non‑small cell lung cancer | MOA: Daxinrasib is a bifunctional KRAS‑G12C binder that recruits cyclophilin A to create a neo‑protein‑protein interface, enabling high‑affinity inhibition of the previously undruggable KRAS G12C mutant and producing durable tumor regressions in PDAC and NSCLC. | Findings: Phase 1/2 trial of daxinrasib in KRAS G12C PDAC (n≈40) achieved an ORR of ~50%.; In the larger RASalute‑302 cohort (n=83) the ORR was 35% in second‑line PDAC patients.; Registrational data (RASalute‑303) show a hazard ratio for overall survival of 0.40 versus standard chemotherapy.; Efficacy appears superior in earlier‑line settings and in NSCLC compared with docetaxel.

metadata.speaker: William Gibson
metadata.talk_title: Beyond degradation: induced proximity strategies entering the clinic

text: High‑throughput discovery of induced‑proximity molecules using ratiometric transcriptional activation | Speaker: Steven Banic | MOA: The platform couples degradation of a transcriptional inhibitor fused to a protein of interest with activation of a reporter gene, enabling sensitive, multiplexed detection of protein degradation or induced protein‑protein interactions across thousands of small‑molecule and target combinations. | Findings: Ratiometric transcriptional activation detects as little as 10% protein degradation, outperforming HiBiT and direct fluorescence readouts.; Multiplexed screening of 10,000 cereblon‑binding molecules against 120 targets identified selective degraders (e.g., PDE6D) and protein‑dependent toxicities.; RNA‑barcode readout amplifies a 1% fluorescence change to a 15% signal, enabling simultaneous profiling of ~200 proteins per well.

metadata.speaker: Steven Banic
metadata.talk_title: High‑throughput discovery of induced‑proximity molecules using ratiometric transcriptional activation

text: Orally bioavailable macrocyclic cyclin inhibitors for cancer | Speaker: Justin Shapiro | Tumors: small cell lung cancer, triple-negative breast cancer, mantle cell lymphoma, ER-positive breast cancer | MOA: Macrocyclic peptides bind the RXL substrate pocket on cyclin A/B or the cyclin D1–Rb interface, disrupting substrate recruitment and cyclin–CDK complex formation, leading to replication stress, mitotic catastrophe, and selective tumor cell death while sparing normal fibroblasts. | Findings: Compound three achieved double‑digit nanomolar cellular potency against SCLC lines with improved MDCK permeability.; Compound six reached single‑digit nanomolar biophysical affinity for cyclins A/B, retained selectivity over cyclin E, and showed oral bioavailability (~30% F) in mice.; Oral dosing of compound six (30–100 mg/kg PO) produced robust tumor regressions in CDX SCLC models without body‑weight loss.; The same compound demonstrated tumor regressions in patient‑derived xenograft models of triple‑negative breast cancer.; Isoform‑selective cyclin D1 inhibitor potently inhibited cyclin D1–Rb interaction, blocked proliferation of mantle‑cell lymphoma and ER‑positive breast cancer lines, and outperformed acalabrutinib in a mantle‑cell lymphoma CDX model.

metadata.speaker: Justin Shapiro
metadata.talk_title: Orally bioavailable macrocyclic cyclin inhibitors for cancer

text: Structure‑guided discovery of DHXX8 RNA‑helicase inhibitors | Speaker: Rob | Tumors: breast cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: Compound 54 binds the RNA‑binding tunnel of DHXX8, mimicking a phosphate backbone, and stabilizes the enzyme in an inactive ADP‑bound conformation, blocking RNA translocation and splicing, leading to intron retention of oncogenic transcripts and tumor cell death. | Findings: Fragment‑based screening identified a carboxylic‑acid fragment that binds the DHXX8 RNA‑binding tunnel and mimics a phosphate group.; Structure‑guided optimization yielded compound 54 with sub‑micromolar biochemical potency and cellular target engagement.; Compound 54 shows good permeability, low clearance, and >24 h exposure above cellular IC50 in PK studies.; In SUM159 xenografts, compound 54 modulated splicing of MCL1 and HSF1, with maximal effect at 6 h for MCL1.; At 30 mg/kg daily, compound 54 produced two complete tumor regressions in HT29 CDX mice, but high doses caused >10 % body‑weight loss, indicating a narrow therapeutic index.

metadata.speaker: Rob
metadata.talk_title: Structure‑guided discovery of DHXX8 RNA‑helicase inhibitors

text: Activation lethality: MAPK and WNT pathway activators as cancer therapeutics | Speaker: Amy | Tumors: melanoma, colorectal cancer, lung cancer, pan-cancer | MOA: Small molecules disrupt the ERK–p15 interaction or act as molecular glues to degrade CK1α, thereby releasing negative regulators of MAPK or WNT pathways; this hyper‑activates the pathways beyond tolerable levels in oncogene‑addicted cells, causing mitotic catastrophe or synthetic lethality, while normal cells tolerate the activation. | Findings: DTX‑067 binds the ERK‑p15 interface; SAR yielded DTX‑MAPK1 with 300‑fold biochemical and 1,000‑fold cellular potency improvement.; DTX‑MAPK1 selectively activates phospho‑ERK in MAPK‑mutant tumor cells with minimal activation in normal hepatocytes and skin.; Oral dosing of DTX‑MAPK1 (60 mg/kg daily) produced strong tumor regressions in BRAF‑mutant melanoma and colorectal models.; CK1α molecular‑glue degrader selectively degrades CK1α, activates WNT signaling, and induces tumor stasis in APC‑mutant CRC xenografts and PDX models.; MAPK activators sensitize KRAS‑inhibitor‑resistant cells and, after resistance to the activator, re‑sensitize tumors to MAPK inhibitors (cross‑sensitization).

metadata.speaker: Amy
metadata.talk_title: Activation lethality: MAPK and WNT pathway activators as cancer therapeutics

text: Covalent chemoproteomic approaches to target transcription factors and epigenetic rewiring | Speaker: Dan Nomura | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Covalent chemoproteomic probes identify hyperreactive cysteines in intrinsically disordered transcription factors (e.g., MYC C203). Stereoselective electrophiles covalently engage these sites, destabilize the protein, and trigger proteasomal degradation, while linked recruiters (e.g., MBD2 inhibitor) enable small‑molecule epigenetic rewiring (TRACER) that recruits HDAC complexes to silence locus‑specific transcription such as ER or AR‑V7. Molecular glues (e.g., ZD186) covalently attach to BCL6 and recruit BRD9, leading to MYC down‑regulation via neomorphic transcriptional complexes. | Findings: Identified >100,000 ligandable cysteine sites across the human proteome using activity‑based protein profiling.; Stereoselective MYC degrader 236 caused dose‑responsive MYC degradation with EC50 ~2 µM, rescued by proteasome inhibition, and engaged C203 with >100 off‑targets.; Optimized degrader 219A achieved sustained MYC degradation for 24 h, reduced off‑target engagement, and lowered MYC levels by >90% in VCAP cells.; TRACER heterobifunctional molecule linking an estrone agonist to an MBD2 inhibitor suppressed ER transcription >90% at low nanomolar concentrations and maintained inhibition after washout for days.; Molecular glue ZD186 recruited BRD9 to BCL6, resulting in rapid MYC down‑regulation (observed before P21 up‑regulation) and rescue of the phenotype with BRD9 inhibition or knockout.

metadata.speaker: Dan Nomura
metadata.talk_title: Covalent chemoproteomic approaches to target transcription factors and epigenetic rewiring

text: RIP‑Tag platform: tumor‑specific induced proximity targeting essential proteins | Speaker: Katherine Kaiser‑Burkher | Tumors: prostate cancer, breast cancer | MOA: RIP‑Tag molecules are heterobifunctional agents that bind a tumor‑specific protein (e.g., AR or ER) and a pan‑essential protein (BRD4). The induced ternary complex sequesters BRD4, causing loss‑of‑function of this essential transcriptional co‑activator selectively in tumor cells, leading to potent cell death independent of the oncogenic driver. Positive cooperativity (>60) between the two ligands drives tumor‑specific activity and a wide therapeutic window. | Findings: Identified >100,000 ligandable cysteine sites across the proteome, enabling covalent recruitment of novel E3 ligases.; HLD0915 formed a ternary complex with AR and BRD4 at EC50 ≈ 2 nM and inhibited VCAP cell proliferation (GI50 ≈ 3 nM).; In vivo, HLD0915 induced dose‑dependent ternary complex formation and BRD4 loss‑of‑function markers (↓cMyc, ↑HEXIM1) in tumor tissue.; Preclinical efficacy demonstrated tumor regressions in AR‑amplified, AR‑V7+, and AR‑independent prostate cancer xenografts, outperforming enzalutamide.; Phase 1 mCRPC trial (31 patients) showed PSA50 response of 70% and PSA90 of 40% across AR‑amplified, non‑amplified, AR‑mutant, and AR‑V7 sub‑cohorts.

metadata.speaker: Katherine Kaiser‑Burkher
metadata.talk_title: RIP‑Tag platform: tumor‑specific induced proximity targeting essential proteins

text: Expanding induced proximity: molecular glues, viral E3 ligases and lysosomal targeting chimeras | Speaker: Ryan Potts | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Amgen generated large DNA‑encoded libraries of low‑affinity ligands for >35 E3 ligases (≈350 chemotypes) and screened them for molecular glue activity using high‑throughput proteomics and barcode‑encoded bead assays. Hits such as a VHL‑glue induce selective degradation of caspase‑2 via ternary complex formation. Viral‑derived E6 ligase (E6AP) was repurposed (VIPER‑TAC) to degrade pan‑essential SARS‑1 selectively in HPV‑positive cells, achieving tumor‑specific killing. Lysosomal‑targeting chimeras (LIMTACs) recruit plasma‑membrane KRAS G12D to the lysosomal membrane protein Rnf152, causing relocalization and lysosomal degradation, yielding sustained MAPK pathway inhibition beyond simple kinase inhibition. | Findings: Built a >500,000‑compound molecular glue library covering 35 newly enabled E3 ligases.; Proteomics screen identified a VHL‑based glue that selectively degrades caspase‑2, confirmed as proteasome‑ and VHL‑dependent with KD ≈70 nM ternary complex.; DNA‑encoded bead assay of 25,000 VHL‑glues uncovered dGem3, which induces transcriptional changes via recruitment of the SMN complex component Gemin3; ternary complex KD ≈70 nM.; VIPER‑TAC using HPV E6/E6AP and a small‑molecule recruiter of SARS‑1 achieved selective degradation of SARS‑1 in HPV‑positive cells, leading to dose‑dependent cell killing absent in HPV‑negative controls.; LIMTAC strategy demonstrated that a bifunctional molecule can relocalize KRAS G12D from the plasma membrane to lysosomal membranes via Rnf152, resulting in KRAS degradation and sustained phospho‑ERK suppression after washout.

metadata.speaker: Ryan Potts
metadata.talk_title: Expanding induced proximity: molecular glues, viral E3 ligases and lysosomal targeting chimeras

text: Applying molecular classifications to therapy and trials in diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma | Speaker: Christopher R. Flowers | Tumors: diffuse large B-cell lymphoma | MOA: Polatuzumab vedotin delivers a cytotoxic payload to CD79B‑expressing B‑cells, enhancing the efficacy of R‑CHOP and improving PFS (HR 0.73) in frontline DLBCL, especially in ABC and high‑IPI patients. Parallel work leverages gene‑expression and whole‑exome classifiers (COO, DZ‑signature, LymphGen) to stratify patients for targeted regimens such as tafasitamab + lenalidomide + R‑CHOP or chemotherapy‑free SMART combinations, aiming to replace CHOP with biology‑driven, less toxic therapies. | Findings: Polatuzumab‑R‑CHOP improved PFS versus R‑CHOP (HR 0.73) in a global phase III POLARIX trial, establishing a new frontline standard for DLBCL.; Subgroup analysis showed the greatest PFS benefit in ABC‑type DLBCL, confirming genotype‑guided therapy.; A rapid (median 10‑day) whole‑exome/RNA‑seq pipeline accurately classifies COO, DZ‑signature, and LymphGen subtypes in both newly diagnosed and relapsed patients.; Streamlined eligibility criteria (13 essential vs 37 traditional) enabled faster trial enrollment and maintained efficacy (HR ~0.75) for tafasitamab + lenalidomide + R‑CHOP.; SETD2 haploinsufficiency is enriched in patients of African ancestry; preclinical models demonstrate synthetic lethality with SETD2 inhibition, though clinical development was paused after company acquisition.

metadata.speaker: Christopher R. Flowers
metadata.talk_title: Applying molecular classifications to therapy and trials in diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma

text: Chromatin-associated ENL condensates drive oncogenic transcription | Speaker: Dr. Liling Wang | Tumors: acute myeloid leukemia, Wilms tumor | MOA: Oncogenic mutations in the ENL YEATS domain promote formation of large, low‑dynamics chromatin condensates that concentrate transcriptional elongation machinery at HOXA loci, driving hyper‑activation of oncogenes; disruption of ENL‑histone acetyl binding or RNA‑mediated nucleation impairs condensate formation, reduces transcriptional bursting, and blocks leukemogenesis. | Findings: ENL hotspot mutations generate large, stable nuclear condensates that colocalize with active HOXA transcription sites.; Condensate formation requires both histone acetyl‑binding via the YEATS domain and RNA interaction; a 3A charge‑neutralizing mutant reduces RNA binding and condensate number by ~30‑40%.; Disruption of condensates (genetic or with a YEATS‑domain inhibitor) displaces ENL from target genes, lowers HOXA transcriptional bursting, and extends survival of mice with aggressive AML by >5 months.; Partial reduction of condensate formation (3A mutant) is sufficient to abolish tumorigenesis in vivo, indicating a threshold effect for oncogenic transcription.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Liling Wang
metadata.talk_title: Chromatin-associated ENL condensates drive oncogenic transcription

text: Targeting the menin–MLL interaction in AML: clinical advances and resistance mechanisms | Speaker: Dr. Scott Armstrong | Tumors: acute myeloid leukemia | MOA: Menin inhibitors disrupt the menin–MLL interaction, causing loss of menin and MLL fusion occupancy at HOXA/MEIS1 loci, leading to transcriptional repression of oncogenic programs; resistance arises via point mutations in the menin binding pocket or stabilizing mutations in MLL or LEDGF that restore complex binding. | Findings: Revumenib and ziftomenib achieve FDA approval for KMT2A‑rearranged and NPM1‑mutant AML, demonstrating clinical efficacy (ORR 30‑40%).; Base‑editor screens identified recurrent menin‑binding pocket mutations (e.g., M327, G331) that confer 5‑15‑fold IC50 shifts and drive resistance.; Higher dosing of menin inhibitors in PDX models prolongs survival and reduces frequency of binding‑pocket mutations, but selects for alternative resistance via MLL or LEDGF mutations.; MLL‑fusion cells acquire mutations in integrase‑binding motifs (S119L, G123V, G141S) that stabilize the MLL‑menin‑LEDGF complex, bypassing inhibitor disruption.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Scott Armstrong
metadata.talk_title: Targeting the menin–MLL interaction in AML: clinical advances and resistance mechanisms

text: Cell-intrinsic mechanisms and synthetic lethalities of chromosomal instability | Speaker: Uri Ben-David | Tumors: triple-negative breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, brain tumor, ovarian cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: Chromosomal instability creates aneuploidy‑induced stresses (DNA damage, proteotoxicity, metabolic imbalance) that generate synthetic lethal dependencies such as KIF18A, CDC20, RAF signaling, SCD1, and Aurora B; targeting these dependencies selectively kills CIN‑high tumor cells while sparing diploid normal cells. | Findings: KIF18A identified as a unique synthetic lethal vulnerability of chromosomally unstable aneuploid tumor cells across multiple independent studies.; CDC20 loss sensitizes CIN‑positive cells to spindle assembly checkpoint inhibition.; Aneuploid cells exhibit basal DNA damage and chronic MAPK (RAF) activation; sub‑lethal RAF inhibition resensitizes them to DNA‑damaging chemotherapy.; Proteasome inhibition is more effective in highly aneuploid tumors when patients are retrospectively stratified by aneuploidy score.; Loss of chromosome 17p (mono‑allelic TP53 loss) creates dependence on SCD1 for fatty‑acid synthesis in brain‑metastatic breast cancer, and SCD1 inhibitors show potent in vitro, ex‑vivo, and in vivo activity.

metadata.speaker: Uri Ben-David
metadata.talk_title: Cell-intrinsic mechanisms and synthetic lethalities of chromosomal instability

text: Cell‑extrinsic immune rewiring by chronic STING activation in chromosomal instability | Speaker: Ashley Loughney | Tumors: triple-negative breast cancer, lung cancer (metastasis model), mouse mammary tumor models | MOA: Chronic chromosome missegregation generates micronuclei that rupture, activating cGAS‑STING; persistent STING signaling shifts from interferon production to an ER‑stress program that promotes metastasis via immune‑suppressive remodeling, while specific STING domains mediate interferon versus ER‑stress outputs. | Findings: Chronic STING activation in CIN‑high cells abolishes the interferon response and induces a pro‑metastatic ER‑stress transcriptional program.; STING‑dependent metastasis requires an intact immune system; immune‑deficient mice lose the effect.; Stat‑seq saturation mutagenesis mapped distinct loss‑of‑function domains for interferon signaling (cGAMP‑binding and C‑terminal tail) and for ER‑stress signaling (N‑terminal region).; Specific STING variants (e.g., K337) are enriched in lung metastases, indicating gain‑of‑function for metastatic fitness.; STING agonist DMXAA failed in humans because a single amino‑acid difference (position 229) prevents binding; the platform correctly predicted this species‑specific resistance.

metadata.speaker: Ashley Loughney
metadata.talk_title: Cell‑extrinsic immune rewiring by chronic STING activation in chromosomal instability

text: Translating chromosomal instability vulnerabilities: KIF18A inhibitors and cGAS‑STING modulation | Speaker: Velastra Therapeutics CSO | Tumors: high-grade serous ovarian cancer, lung adenocarcinoma (LKB1‑mutant), triple‑negative breast cancer, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma | MOA: KIF18A inhibition exploits a synthetic lethal interaction with RB‑pathway loss in CIN‑high tumors, while chronic cGAS‑STING signaling in aneuploid cancers desensitizes interferon output; transient cGAS inhibition restores STING protein levels and re‑sensitizes tumors to STING agonists, enabling acute interferon‑driven anti‑tumor immunity. | Findings: KIF18A inhibitors (VLS‑1488, savolnisib) show clinical activity only in p16‑positive (RB‑deficient) tumors, with partial responses in all p16‑positive cases except one mixed‑histology outlier.; p16 IHC serves as a robust predictive biomarker for KIF18A inhibitor response across multiple tumor types and dose levels.; RB loss drives MAD2 overexpression, creating the synthetic lethal context required for KIF18A inhibitor efficacy.; In chromosomally unstable tumors, chronic cGAS‑STING activation suppresses type‑I interferon via STING degradation and ER‑stress induction, rendering STING agonists ineffective.; Pharmacologic cGAS inhibition (RU521) or genetic cGAS knockout restores STING levels, re‑activates interferon signaling, and markedly enhances response to STING agonists in mouse models.

metadata.speaker: Velastra Therapeutics CSO
metadata.talk_title: Translating chromosomal instability vulnerabilities: KIF18A inhibitors and cGAS‑STING modulation
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

text: Claudin 18.2 antibody therapy clinical data and translational insights | Speaker: Kohei Setara | Tumors: gastric cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, ovarian cancer | MOA: Zorvotaximab is an IgG1 monoclonal antibody that binds the extracellular loop 1 of claudin‑18.2 and mediates tumor cell killing primarily through ADCC and CDC; cerpituximab adds ADCP activity and can modulate the tumor microenvironment by increasing NK and macrophage infiltration and chemokine release, thereby enhancing T‑cell recruitment. | Findings: Zorvotaximab monotherapy achieved <10% ORR but 30‑40% disease stabilization in claudin‑18.2 positive gastric cancer.; Randomized FASTO phase 2 showed improved PFS when Zorvotaximab was combined with fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy.; Global phase 3 trials demonstrated an overall survival benefit leading to regulatory approval of the Zorvotaximab‑chemo combination.; Cerpituximab monotherapy induced ADCP and increased tumor‑infiltrating NK cells, macrophages, and chemokines (CXCL9/10) in gastric cancer biopsies.; In pancreatic cancer, cerpituximab plus chemotherapy failed to improve OS despite 28% ORR, suggesting that subcellular localization and KRAS mutation status affect efficacy.

metadata.speaker: Kohei Setara
metadata.talk_title: Claudin 18.2 antibody therapy clinical data and translational insights

text: Translational rationale for claudin‑targeted ADCs and bispecific T‑cell engagers | Speaker: Sameh El‑Gammal | Tumors: gastric cancer, breast cancer, multiple myeloma | MOA: Claudin‑18.2 ADCs deliver high‑potency cytotoxic payloads (e.g., topoisomerase inhibitors) directly to antigen‑positive tumor cells, while bispecific T‑cell engagers (2+1 format) recruit CD3‑positive T cells to form immune synapses independent of HLA, enabling cytotoxicity even at moderate antigen density and providing bystander killing of neighboring claudin‑negative cells. | Findings: ASP2138 ADC induced potent killing across gastric cancer cell lines with varying claudin‑18.2 density, though higher expression correlated with greater potency.; Claudin‑18.2 bispecific TCE showed cytotoxicity in vitro even at low antigen levels and mediated bystander killing in mixed claudin‑positive/negative organoid cultures.; Pre‑clinical data suggest that lower CD3 affinity bispecifics can retain efficacy while potentially reducing cytokine release syndrome risk.; Clinical data from an Astellas claudin‑18.2 ADC (phase 3) demonstrate activity comparable to HER2‑targeted ADCs, supporting the therapeutic window in gastric cancer.; Heterogeneous claudin expression (≈87% of gastric tumors) underscores the need for strategies such as dual‑antigen targeting or bystander effects to overcome antigen loss.

metadata.speaker: Sameh El‑Gammal
metadata.talk_title: Translational rationale for claudin‑targeted ADCs and bispecific T‑cell engagers

text: Claudin‑18.2 CAR‑T cell therapy in gastric and pancreatic cancer | Speaker: Lin Shen | Tumors: gastric cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Claudin‑18.2 CAR‑T cells are engineered to recognize the extracellular loop of claudin‑18.2, leading to antigen‑specific T‑cell activation, cytokine release, and tumor cell lysis; persistence is limited by rapid exhaustion, prompting strategies such as naive T‑cell enrichment, novel lymphodepletion, and repeat infusions to improve durability. | Findings: Monotherapy claudin‑18.2 CAR‑T achieved a 55% ORR and ≥19% disease control rate in gastric cancer.; Sequential treatment (chemo → PD‑1 → CAR‑T) yielded an 80% ORR and 15‑month median PFS, suggesting benefit of tumor debulking before CAR‑T.; Randomized trial showed a four‑fold higher response rate and a two‑fold OS improvement versus standard therapy, reducing mortality risk by 63%.; High claudin‑18.2 expression, absence of liver/bone metastases, and a TZMK⁺/TPX⁺ immune‑rich microenvironment predicted long‑term responders.; Grade ≥3 gastric mucosal injury occurred in ~10% of patients but was manageable with PPIs and fasting; pulmonary toxicity was rare and linked to CRS.

metadata.speaker: Lin Shen
metadata.talk_title: Claudin‑18.2 CAR‑T cell therapy in gastric and pancreatic cancer

text: EHR-based phenotyping of cancer cachexia and identification of anatomical subtypes | Speaker: Ed Reznik | Tumors: melanoma, pancreatic cancer, colon adenocarcinoma, kidney cancer, pan-cancer | MOA: Reznik's group defined cachexia windows using longitudinal weight loss criteria in EHR data, aligned these windows with serologic, imaging, and genomic measurements, and identified three CT-based anatomical subtypes (A, B, C) distinguished by organ volume changes and systemic inflammation, with TP53 mutations emerging as a genomic risk factor when modeled as a time-to-event. | Findings: Implemented a 5% weight loss over 6‑month EHR algorithm to define cachexia windows in >60,000 cancer patients.; Found ~30% prevalence of cachexia episodes in melanoma and high prevalence in pancreatic cancer.; Identified three CT‑based cachexia subtypes: Type A (fat loss + spleen/liver enlargement), Type B (fat loss + organ atrophy and radiodensity increase), Type C (mixed).; Type A subtype associated with worst overall survival across diseases.; TP53 mutation is the most significant genomic correlate of cachexia risk when modeled as a time‑to‑event, validated in an independent cohort.

metadata.speaker: Ed Reznik
metadata.talk_title: EHR-based phenotyping of cancer cachexia and identification of anatomical subtypes

text: Observational study of cachexia phenotypes using patient-reported outcomes and biomarkers | Speaker: Richard Dunn | Tumors: lung cancer, pancreatic cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: Dunn presented the design and early baseline findings of two prospective observational cohorts (Lotus and UNCOVER) that longitudinally collect patient-reported outcomes, body composition imaging, and blood/tumor biomarkers to identify cachexia phenotypes; preliminary symptom clustering revealed high‑symptom and low‑symptom groups, with the high‑symptom group showing elevated GDF15, IL‑6, and IL‑8 and worse early disease progression. | Findings: Enrolled ~1,000 patients in Lotus (U Rochester) and ~800 in UNCOVER (Kaiser) to prospectively phenotype cachexia.; Baseline: >50% of patients already have ≥5% weight loss; pancreatic cancer patients show highest prevalence.; Symptom clustering identified three groups: low symptom burden (similar to weight‑stable), high symptom burden (fatigue, anorexia, emotional distress), and intermediate.; High symptom burden cluster associated with higher serum GDF15, IL‑6, and IL‑8 levels.; Patients in high symptom burden cluster had lower physical activity, higher appetite stimulant use, and higher 3‑month disease progression rates.

metadata.speaker: Richard Dunn
metadata.talk_title: Observational study of cachexia phenotypes using patient-reported outcomes and biomarkers

text: Prostaglandin E2–driven cachexia and immunotherapy resistance in lung cancer models | Speaker: Dr. Gonsalves | Tumors: lung adenocarcinoma | MOA: Gonsalves demonstrated that elevated prostaglandin E2 production by tumor‑associated neutrophils and tumor cells drives cachexia and impairs anti‑PD‑L1 efficacy; CRISPR‑mediated knockdown of PTGES or PTGS2 reduces PGE2, delays weight loss in KRAS/LKB1 mouse models and C26 allografts, linking PGE2 to both wasting and immunotherapy resistance, with dysbiotic lung microbiota further amplifying neutrophil activation. | Findings: In KRAS/LKB1 (KL) lung cancer mice, ~80% develop cachexia with up to 20% weight loss; non‑cachectic littermates retain weight despite similar tumor burden.; Cachectic mice show higher tumor and serum IL‑6 family cytokines and enrichment of arginase‑positive macrophages and prostaglandin‑producing neutrophils.; Prostaglandin E2 levels are markedly increased in cachectic mouse tumors and in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid of cachectic lung cancer patients.; CRISPR knockdown of PTGES in KL tumors suppresses PGE2 and significantly delays cachexia onset.; CRISPR knockout of PTGS2 in C26 cachectic cells eliminates tumor PGE2 and protects mice from weight loss.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Gonsalves
metadata.talk_title: Prostaglandin E2–driven cachexia and immunotherapy resistance in lung cancer models

text: Methodological considerations for incorporating real-world data into clinical trial design | Speaker: Rebecca Hubbard | MOA: Hubbard presented a framework for hybrid control trial designs that augment internal control arms with external real-world data, comparing analysis strategies (full pooling, static borrowing, propensity score weighting) via simulations to assess bias, type I error, and power, highlighting propensity weighting as a method that controls bias while improving efficiency. | Findings: Full pooling of external control data introduces substantial bias in treatment effect estimates.; Static borrowing reduces bias but still shows inflated type I error under strong confounding.; Propensity score weighting eliminates bias and restores type I error to nominal levels while providing a power boost.; Dynamic borrowing yields estimates close to trial-only results with minimal efficiency gain.

metadata.speaker: Rebecca Hubbard
metadata.talk_title: Methodological considerations for incorporating real-world data into clinical trial design

text: Real-world data curation from EHRs and applications to clinical trials | Speaker: Neil Meropol | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer, multiple myeloma, pancreatic adenocarcinoma | MOA: Meropol described methods for extracting structured variables from EHRs using human abstraction, machine learning, and large language models, presented quality assessment frameworks, and illustrated applications such as external control arm construction for the RESOLVE pancreatic trial and outcome analyses in NSCLC and bladder cancer. | Findings: LLM-extracted progression dates showed high reliability compared to human abstraction across multiple tumor types.; External control arms built from multiple real-world data sources closely matched the RESOLVE trial control arm after propensity score adjustment.; In bladder cancer, patients receiving cisplatin off-label had better outcomes than those who did not.; In early-stage NSCLC, neoadjuvant immunotherapy improved distant metastasis-free survival, but additional adjuvant therapy did not show further benefit.

metadata.speaker: Neil Meropol
metadata.talk_title: Real-world data curation from EHRs and applications to clinical trials

text: Prospective real-world data registry embedded in an ECOG-ACRIN phase III trial | Speaker: Peter O'Dwyer | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer | MOA: O'Dwyer outlined the design and early feasibility results of a prospective real-world data registry (PRECOG 1702) run in parallel with the ECOG-ACRIN phase III trial EA5182, demonstrating high data completeness (>85%) and rapid accrual, and discussed operational challenges such as site CRA engagement, IRB barriers, and EHR documentation gaps. | Findings: Prospective real-world registry achieved >85% capture of predefined key variables after minimal data cleaning.; Accrual reached target of 25 patients/month after an initial slow start, now active at 40 institutions.; CRAs are critical for data collection; engagement and regular communication improve site performance.; Regulatory challenges include IRB exemptions for patient-reported outcomes and social determinants of health.

metadata.speaker: Peter O'Dwyer
metadata.talk_title: Prospective real-world data registry embedded in an ECOG-ACRIN phase III trial

text: PACER method reveals TCL1A as a driver of clonal hematopoiesis and leukemia | Speaker: Siddharth Jaiswal | MOA: Jaiswal introduced the PACER (passenger approximated clonal expansion rate) method to infer clone age from passenger mutations, identified TCL1A promoter SNP rs2887399 as a regulator of clonal fitness, and demonstrated that ectopic TCL1A expression drives HSC expansion and myeloid leukemia in transgenic mice, establishing TCL1A as a causal driver of CHIP. | Findings: PACER can quantify clonal expansion rates from bulk WGS data using passenger mutation counts.; Driver mutation identity accounts for most variance in clone fitness; splicing factor mutations (U2AF1, SRSF2, SF3B1) and JAK2 show highest fitness.; Smoking is the only measured environmental factor positively correlated with clonal expansion rate in humans.; GWAS identified rs2887399 in the TCL1A promoter; the T allele slows expansion of multiple CHIP drivers.; TCL1A is normally silent in HSCs; driver mutations de‑repress TCL1A, leading to HSC fitness advantage.

metadata.speaker: Siddharth Jaiswal
metadata.talk_title: PACER method reveals TCL1A as a driver of clonal hematopoiesis and leukemia

text: Phylogenetic and methylation mapping of somatic evolution in blood | Speaker: Jyoti Nangalia | Tumors: myeloid malignancy, breast cancer | MOA: Nangalia described a combined whole‑genome and whole‑methylome sequencing pipeline for single‑cell colonies, enabling reconstruction of somatic mutation phylogenies and assignment of CpG methylation changes to specific ancestral branches, revealing massive early‑life epiallelic remodeling and that driver mutations both shape and are shaped by these epigenetic landscapes, with some epigenetic changes acting as oncogenic drivers themselves. | Findings: Developed an automated low‑input pipeline to obtain both WGS and whole‑genome methylomes from ~2 ng DNA per colony.; Mapped ~5,000 CpG‑segment epialleles that change early in embryogenesis (≈10–15 somatic mutations) with ~10,000‑fold higher rate than later life.; Identified ~4,000–5,000 early‑life CpG segments (mostly promoters) that acquire stable methylation states, many showing allele‑specific patterns beyond X‑inactivation.; Demonstrated that CHIP driver mutations (e.g., DNMT3A, TET2, 1q+, DNMT3A Y66F) are associated with increased numbers of epimutations per branch.; Showed that epigenetic silencing of one BRCA1 allele can occur pre‑gastrulation, creating a mosaic that predisposes to BRCA‑like breast cancer.

metadata.speaker: Jyoti Nangalia
metadata.talk_title: Phylogenetic and methylation mapping of somatic evolution in blood

text: Inflammatory and metabolic consequences of CHIP and therapeutic implications | Speaker: Ben Ebert | Tumors: myeloid malignancy, cardiovascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, liver disease, lung cancer | MOA: Ebert showed that loss of TET2 in hematopoietic cells reprograms lipid metabolism, leading to accumulation of triglycerides, diacylglycerols and cholesterol esters, which drives heightened IL‑1β‑mediated inflammation in atherosclerosis, COPD, NASH and other age‑related diseases; genetic screens identified ACLY and OGT as key mediators, and pharmacologic inhibition of lipid pathways normalizes the inflammatory phenotype. | Findings: CHIP carriers have increased risk of atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, heart failure, arrhythmias, liver disease, kidney disease, COPD, osteoporosis and lung cancer.; TET2 loss leads to lipid droplet accumulation in neutrophils/macrophages, driving IL‑1β‑dependent inflammation.; In vivo CRISPR screen in Tet2‑deficient mice identified ACLY and OGT as essential for the inflammatory phenotype; knockout of these genes restores wild‑type inflammation levels.; TET2 directly binds OGT; loss of TET2 liberates OGT, causing aberrant protein O‑GlcNAcylation and metabolic dysregulation.; A simple risk score incorporating genotype, clone size, RDW, MCV, cytopenias and age stratifies CHIP individuals into low, intermediate and high risk for myeloid malignancy and overall mortality.

metadata.speaker: Ben Ebert
metadata.talk_title: Inflammatory and metabolic consequences of CHIP and therapeutic implications

text: What Do We Do Now That We've Machine Learned Everything? | Speaker: Jeffrey Leake | MOA: Leake outlined the current landscape of AI applications across oncology drug development, emphasizing the distinction between supervised and generative models, the regulatory uncertainty surrounding generative AI, and the need for robust benchmarks, representation, and guardrails to ensure safe, responsible deployment. | Findings: AI is now embedded in >1,500 FDA regulatory submissions over the past decade, with oncology accounting for ~27% of AI‑containing submissions.; The FDA received 307 AI‑related oncology submissions in 2024 alone, reflecting rapid growth.; Four major impact areas for AI in oncology were identified: care/operations, drug discovery, drug development, and consumer health.; Generative AI models present greater regulatory challenges than supervised models due to broader use cases and lack of clear pathways.; Benchmarking, representation across diverse populations, and external validation were highlighted as critical gaps to address.

metadata.speaker: Jeffrey Leake
metadata.talk_title: What Do We Do Now That We've Machine Learned Everything?
