text: Chemical‑genetic convergence of UM171 and KBDBD4 cancer insertions | Speaker: Brian Liao | Tumors: medulloblastoma | MOA: UM171 binds the HDAC active site and creates a groove in the KBDBD4 kelch domain, acting as a molecular glue that recruits HDAC1/2‑CoREST for ubiquitination; cancer‑derived 2B2C loop insertions in KBDBD4 mimic UM171 by inserting residues into the HDAC pocket, producing neodegradation of CoREST (genetic glue). | Findings: Cryo‑EM shows UM171 occupies HDAC active site and contacts KBDBD4 2B2C loop.; Cancer insertions (+2 aa) in KBDBD4 2B2C loop drive CoREST degradation without UM171.; Deep mutational scanning of 5,000 KBDBD4 variants identified insertions as the most potent neodegraders.; Structural superposition reveals UM171 arms recapitulate side‑chains of PR and TTYML insertions.; Activation‑lethality phenotype correlates with co‑REST degradation; mutants in lower‑right quadrant of DMS plot are both degradative and cytotoxic.

metadata.speaker: Brian Liao
metadata.talk_title: Chemical‑genetic convergence of UM171 and KBDBD4 cancer insertions

text: TRIM21 molecular glues targeting the nuclear pore complex in pancreatic cancer | Speaker: Steven Corsello | Tumors: pancreatic adenocarcinoma, head and neck cancer | MOA: The small‑molecule PRLX binds the PRY/SPRY domain of TRIM21, enabling recruitment of TRIM21 to the autoproteolytic domain of NUP98; this induces ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of multiple nucleoporins, collapsing nuclear‑cytoplasmic transport, reducing short‑half‑life oncoproteins (MCL1, MYC) and triggering intrinsic apoptosis in TRIM21‑high pancreatic cancer cells. | Findings: TRIM21 expression is a strong predictive biomarker for PRLX sensitivity across >4,000 compounds screened.; CRISPR KO of TRIM21 completely rescues cells from PRLX‑induced death; overexpression confers sensitivity.; PRLX directly binds TRIM21 PRY/SPRY domain (crystal structure) and recruits TRIM21 to NUP98 APD, leading to NPC ubiquitination and degradation.; Degradation of NPC components reduces cytoplasmic MCL1 and MYC, causing rapid caspase activation.; In KRAS‑mutant pancreatic xenografts, oral JWZ8103 induces tumor regressions with favorable pharmacokinetics.

metadata.speaker: Steven Corsello
metadata.talk_title: TRIM21 molecular glues targeting the nuclear pore complex in pancreatic cancer

text: Cereblon‑based molecular glue degraders of ZBTB11 to overcome KRAS inhibitor resistance | Speaker: Fleur Ferguson | Tumors: pancreatic adenocarcinoma | MOA: A cereblon‑binding IMiD scaffold is linked to a ZBTB11‑binding moiety, forming a ternary complex that recruits cereblon to ZBTB11, leading to ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation; loss of ZBTB11 reverses the KRAS‑resistance metabolic program by down‑regulating mitochondrial biogenesis and ribosome genes, restoring sensitivity to KRAS inhibitors without affecting neuronal OXPHOS. | Findings: JWJ‑0136 degrades ZBTB11 with Dmax ~80 % in resistant cells, dependent on cereblon and proteasome.; Degradation is abolished by a K866A ZBTB11 mutant, confirming on‑target ternary complex formation.; ZBTB11 loss normalizes mitochondrial biogenesis and reduces basal/maximal OCR in resistant cells.; Combination of JWJ‑0136 with KRAS inhibitors restores drug sensitivity across multiple KRAS‑mutant resistant lines and organoids.; Neuronal assays show no significant impact on mitochondrial health or viability, indicating a favorable therapeutic window.

metadata.speaker: Fleur Ferguson
metadata.talk_title: Cereblon‑based molecular glue degraders of ZBTB11 to overcome KRAS inhibitor resistance

text: Mechanisms of Myeloid-Mediated Resistance to Anti-PD-1 Therapy | Speaker: Tom Gajewski | Tumors: melanoma, head and neck cancer, gastric cancer | MOA: The speaker proposes that 'cold' tumors are dominated by suppressive M2-like macrophages that prevent T cell function. He identifies PKC delta and GPNMB as key negative regulators of the antitumor response; loss of these targets shifts macrophage phenotype from suppressive to inflammatory, thereby enhancing spontaneous tumor control and anti-PD-1 efficacy. | Findings: FMT from responder patients into germ-free mice restored anti-PD-L1 efficacy, a phenotype retained generationally in offspring.; Single-cell RNA-seq of FMT mice showed that responder microbiota induced an inflammatory macrophage gene signature and flipped granulocytes away from an MDSC-like phenotype.; Conditional deletion of PKC delta in hematopoietic cells led to spontaneous tumor control and markedly improved anti-PD-1 efficacy.; GPNMB is dominantly expressed in SPP1+ macrophages; its knockout resulted in substantial spontaneous tumor control in B16-SIY and orthotopic breast cancer models.; GPNMB-mediated suppression is driven by tissue-resident macrophages rather than bone marrow-derived cells, as Lysozyme M-Cre deletion showed a phenotype while Vav1-Cre did not.

metadata.speaker: Tom Gajewski
metadata.session_title: Harnessing the Power of the Immune System: Turning Cold Tumors Hot
metadata.talk_title: Mechanisms of Myeloid-Mediated Resistance to Anti-PD-1 Therapy

text: Genetic Screens and Heterotypic Clusters for Overcoming Immunotherapy Resistance | Speaker: Daniel Pieper | Tumors: melanoma, colon cancer, NSCLC, sarcoma, endometrial cancer | MOA: The speaker used genome-wide CRISPR screens to identify TRAF2 and RNF31 as survival-arm TNF pathway components that, when inactivated, sensitize tumor cells to T cell killing. Additionally, he developed a pipeline to isolate T cell-tumor heterotypic clusters, which are enriched for tumor-reactive, clonally expanded T cells with superior killing capacity. | Findings: Inactivation of TRAF2 or RNF31 tips the balance from pro-survival to pro-death, leading to tumor regression in immune-proficient mouse models.; DEP5 knockout in primary T cells boosts global translation and proliferation, leading to significant tumor control in adoptive transfer models.; CD8 T cell clusters comprise ~1.4% of all cells in melanoma lymph node metastases, with ~12% of total CD8 T cells residing in clusters.; T cells isolated from clusters show a 9-fold increase in melanoma killing capacity in vitro across 11 patients.; MGT2 was identified as a top hit in proximity labeling and cluster screens; its knockout in T cells enhances tumor killing in vitro and in vivo.

metadata.speaker: Daniel Pieper
metadata.session_title: Harnessing the Power of the Immune System: Turning Cold Tumors Hot
metadata.talk_title: Genetic Screens and Heterotypic Clusters for Overcoming Immunotherapy Resistance

text: Myeloid-Mediated Immune Suppression in Prostate Cancer and Bone Metastasis | Speaker: Larry Fong | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: The speaker identifies two distinct myeloid-mediated resistance mechanisms in prostate cancer: SPP1-high TAMs in primary/soft tissue tumors that suppress via the CD73-adenosine pathway, and IL-1beta-high mature neutrophils in bone metastases that suppress via CXCR2-mediated recruitment and IL-1beta signaling. | Findings: Sipuleucel-T induces T cells that are 'excluded' at the invasive margin, limiting clinical efficacy.; SPP1-high TAMs produce adenosine via CD73; blocking the A2A receptor with zafirlukast combined with anti-PD-1 showed clinical responses in 20% of CRPC patients.; Bone metastases are uniquely enriched for IL-1beta-high mature neutrophils, which are functionally immunosuppressive in vitro and in vivo.; Inhibition of CXCR1/2 or IL-1beta receptor rescued the efficacy of combination checkpoint inhibition in bone metastasis mouse models.

metadata.speaker: Larry Fong
metadata.session_title: Harnessing the Power of the Immune System: Turning Cold Tumors Hot
metadata.talk_title: Myeloid-Mediated Immune Suppression in Prostate Cancer and Bone Metastasis

text: Functional genomic and drug screening approaches for precision medicine in pediatric acute leukemia | Speaker: Dr. Pickman | Tumors: acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia | MOA: Functional genomic CRISPR screens identified SHMT1/2 of the one‑carbon folate pathway as essential for T‑ALL growth, and JAK1/2 as dependencies in GLIS2‑rearranged AML. Small‑molecule inhibition (RZ2994, ruxolitinib) and an FLT1‑targeted ADC (STRO‑02) demonstrated tumor burden reduction in mouse models, while compassionate‑use STRO‑02 achieved >40% MRD‑negative complete remissions in pediatric AML patients. | Findings: CRISPR screens revealed SHMT1/2 as selective vulnerabilities in T‑ALL, validated by RZ2994 treatment that reduced bone‑marrow and spleen disease in mice.; GLIS2‑rearranged AML models depend on JAK1/2; ruxolitinib inhibited leukemia growth and modestly prolonged mouse survival.; Resistance to JAK inhibition was mediated by loss of RASA2, which activated MAPK signaling and conferred ruxolitinib resistance in CRISPR screens.; FLT1 is highly expressed in GLIS2 AML; the FLT1‑ADC STRO‑02 eradicated leukemia in mouse xenografts and induced MRD‑negative CR in >40% of 40 pediatric patients on compassionate use.; FLT1‑CAR‑T cells are being developed as a follow‑up strategy for FLT1‑positive AML and osteosarcoma.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Pickman
metadata.talk_title: Functional genomic and drug screening approaches for precision medicine in pediatric acute leukemia

text: BTK inhibitor resistance in CLL and therapeutic sequencing strategies | Speaker: Jen Woyach | Tumors: chronic lymphocytic leukemia | MOA: Covalent BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib) bind C481 and are highly effective in CLL, but resistance arises via BTK C481S, T474I, L528W, and PLCγ2 activating mutations. Non‑covalent BTK inhibitor pirtobrutinib retains activity against C481S but selects for alternative BTK mutations (T474I, L528W). BTK degraders (Bexarotenoag, BGB16673) overcome many kinase‑domain mutations, achieving median PFS ~22 months in heavily pre‑treated CLL, though A428D emerges as a potential universal resistance mutation. | Findings: Covalent BTK inhibitors achieve median frontline PFS of 8.9 years (ibrutinib) and 62–75.8% PFS at 5–6 years (acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib).; BTK C481S and PLCγ2 hotspot mutations are present in 81% of lymphocytosis‑type relapses after covalent BTK inhibitors.; Non‑covalent BTK inhibitor pirtobrutinib yields >80% ORR with median PFS 19.6 months in relapsed CLL, but selects for BTK T474I and L528W mutations.; BTK degraders (Bexarotenoag, BGB16673) produce median PFS of 22.1 months and 65.9% PFS at 16 months respectively in patients resistant to both covalent and non‑covalent BTK inhibitors.; A428D BTK mutation emerges after degrader therapy and may confer cross‑resistance to all current BTK inhibitors and degraders.

metadata.speaker: Jen Woyach
metadata.talk_title: BTK inhibitor resistance in CLL and therapeutic sequencing strategies

text: High‑throughput approaches to identify new targets and sequencing strategies in multiple myeloma | Speaker: Faith Davis | Tumors: multiple myeloma | MOA: RAS‑mutant myeloma cells exhibit elevated macropinocytosis, a nutrient‑scavenging pathway. A small monobody conjugated to a MMAE payload is preferentially internalized via macropinocytosis in KRAS/NRAS‑mutant cells, delivering cytotoxic drug selectively and reducing tumor growth in mouse xenografts without affecting wild‑type myeloma. | Findings: KRAS/NRAS‑mutant myeloma cells display markedly increased macropinocytosis compared with wild‑type cells.; A nanobody‑MMAE conjugate is selectively internalized by RAS‑mutant myeloma via macropinocytosis, leading to tumor shrinkage in mouse models.; No significant off‑target toxicity was observed in wild‑type myeloma or normal tissues in preclinical studies.; The approach is potentially applicable to other RAS‑driven cancers (pancreatic, colorectal, lung).

metadata.speaker: Faith Davis
metadata.talk_title: High‑throughput approaches to identify new targets and sequencing strategies in multiple myeloma

text: Single-Dose HPV Vaccination Efficacy and Immunogenicity | Speaker: Amy Kramer | Tumors: cervical cancer | MOA: A single dose of prophylactic HPV L1 virus‑like particle vaccine induces durable neutralizing antibodies that are four‑fold lower than three‑dose levels yet provide comparable protection against incident HPV 16/18 infection, demonstrating non‑inferiority to the standard two‑dose schedule in large randomized trials. | Findings: One‑dose HPV vaccination showed durable antibody levels up to 11 years post‑vaccination with only a four‑fold reduction versus three‑dose levels.; ESCUDO randomized trial (≈20,000 girls) met co‑primary non‑inferiority endpoints for both Cervarix and Gardasil 9, demonstrating >80% efficacy for one‑dose versus two‑dose schedules.; Global HPV vaccine uptake in 2020 was only 20% overall and ~9% in low‑resource settings, but one‑dose schedules are now adopted in ~90 countries, raising one‑dose coverage to 63%.; Meta‑analyses of single‑dose trials (Kenya, Tanzania, India) confirm high efficacy against virologic and histologic endpoints across vaccine platforms.

metadata.speaker: Amy Kramer
metadata.session_title: HPV Vaccination and Self-Sampling for Cervical Cancer Prevention and Early Detection Globally and in Underserved Settings
metadata.talk_title: Single-Dose HPV Vaccination Efficacy and Immunogenicity

text: Results from the NCI SHIP Trial: Self‑Collected HPV Testing Accuracy | Speaker: NCI SHIP Trial Presenter | Tumors: cervical cancer | MOA: Self‑collected vaginal HPV samples processed with the FDA‑approved Onclarity assay demonstrate >92% positive percent agreement with clinician‑collected samples and high sensitivity for CIN 2/3 detection, supporting regulatory approval of home‑based HPV testing. | Findings: The SHIP trial enrolled 2,088 participants across 24 US sites, with 495 completing the SO1 protocol.; Self‑collected vaginal samples achieved 89.2% sensitivity for CIN 3+ (vs 96.9% for clinician samples) and 83.7% for CIN 2+ (vs 90.7%).; Positive percent agreement between self‑collection and clinician collection was 92% for overall high‑risk HPV, 94% for HPV‑16, and ~89% for other types.; The FDA granted the first pre‑market approval for a self‑collection HPV assay (BD/Waters Onclarity) based on these data.; The trial population was diverse (23.6% Hispanic, 37.6% Black) and included 42% previously vaccinated, supporting generalizability to underserved groups.

metadata.speaker: NCI SHIP Trial Presenter
metadata.session_title: HPV Vaccination and Self-Sampling for Cervical Cancer Prevention and Early Detection Globally and in Underserved Settings
metadata.talk_title: Results from the NCI SHIP Trial: Self‑Collected HPV Testing Accuracy

text: Implementation of HPV Self‑Sampling in Safety‑Net Settings | Speaker: Jane Montealegre | Tumors: cervical cancer | MOA: Deploying mailed or clinic‑based HPV self‑collection kits, combined with patient navigation, markedly increases screening participation among underserved women, demonstrating that implementation strategy—not assay choice—is the primary driver of reach. | Findings: Mailed self‑collection kits in the PRESTESS trial doubled screening participation (47% vs 21% usual care) among under‑screened safety‑net patients.; Adding patient navigation to mailed kits further improved uptake (41% vs 21%).; Meta‑analyses show self‑sampling yields 2‑2.5‑fold higher participation compared with clinician‑collected screening in underserved populations.; Implementation context (mail, door‑to‑door, clinic integration) drives effectiveness more than the specific HPV assay used.; Cost‑effectiveness analyses indicate self‑sampling is highly sensitive to implementation design, with navigation and high return rates essential for value.

metadata.speaker: Jane Montealegre
metadata.session_title: HPV Vaccination and Self-Sampling for Cervical Cancer Prevention and Early Detection Globally and in Underserved Settings
metadata.talk_title: Implementation of HPV Self‑Sampling in Safety‑Net Settings

text: Organoid-guided randomized trial of gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel versus FOLFIRINOX in pancreatic cancer | Speaker: David Tuveson | Tumors: pancreatic cancer | MOA: Patient‑derived pancreatic organoids are cultured from core biopsies, pharmacotyped with gemcitabine, nab‑paclitaxel, and FOLFIRINOX components, and the ex vivo drug sensitivity correlates with patient outcomes; a transcriptional signature derived from sensitive organoids can predict response without the need for culture, enabling functional precision oncology. | Findings: Organoid establishment success was ~50% across 186 biopsies, with failure associated with markedly longer patient survival.; Ex vivo gemcitabine/nab‑paclitaxel sensitivity in PDOs predicted better clinical outcomes compared with FOLFIRINOX in the randomized trial.; A transcriptional oxaliplatin‑response signature derived from hypersensitive organoids stratified patients receiving FOLFIRINOX and correlated with overall survival.; Pan‑RAS inhibitor showed heterogeneous activity across KRAS‑mutant and wild‑type organoids, highlighting the need for functional testing beyond genotype.; High‑content microscopy reduced assay turnaround to <30 days while maintaining strong correlation with traditional ATP‑based readouts.

metadata.speaker: David Tuveson
metadata.talk_title: Organoid-guided randomized trial of gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel versus FOLFIRINOX in pancreatic cancer

text: Functional ex vivo testing and cell‑state‑guided therapy in AML | Speaker: Jeffrey Tyner | Tumors: AML | MOA: High‑throughput ex vivo drug screens of primary AML blasts reveal that differentiation state, rather than mutation alone, dictates sensitivity; stem‑like blasts are venetoclax‑sensitive, while monocytic blasts resist venetoclax but are vulnerable to CDK4/6 inhibition, enabling rational venetoclax + palbociclib combinations. | Findings: Cell state signatures (stem‑like vs monocytic) explain response to >70% of 120 tested drugs.; Venetoclax is highly effective against stem‑like AML but ineffective against monocytic AML.; Panobinostat shows the opposite pattern, being active in differentiated AML.; Venetoclax + palbociclib demonstrates superior ex vivo activity and synergy, especially in RAS‑mutant or monocytic‑like samples.; The pharma‑type composite ex vivo signature predicts clinical response to venetoclax + HMA with near‑perfect accuracy in newly diagnosed AML.

metadata.speaker: Jeffrey Tyner
metadata.talk_title: Functional ex vivo testing and cell‑state‑guided therapy in AML

text: Functional Precision Oncology: ChemoID‑guided therapy improves outcomes in recurrent glioblastoma and platinum‑resistant ovarian cancer | Speaker: Pier Paolo Claudio | Tumors: glioblastoma, ovarian cancer | MOA: ChemoID isolates bulk tumor cells and patient‑derived cancer stem cells, tests a panel of chemotherapies and combinations ex vivo, and reports percent cell kill for each compartment; selecting agents that achieve ≥50% kill in both compartments guides therapy, leading to significant OS and ORR improvements in randomized glioblastoma and ovarian cancer trials. | Findings: ChemoID‑guided therapy extended median OS by 4.5 months in recurrent glioblastoma (12 vs 7.5 months).; In ovarian cancer, objective response rate increased from 5% to 55% with ChemoID guidance.; Median PFS improved from 3 months to 11 months in the ChemoID arm for ovarian cancer.; A ≥50% cell‑kill threshold in both bulk and cancer stem cell compartments predicted clinical response.; The assay achieved CLIA/CAP accreditation and received FDA breakthrough device designation for brain tumors.

metadata.speaker: Pier Paolo Claudio
metadata.talk_title: Functional Precision Oncology: ChemoID‑guided therapy improves outcomes in recurrent glioblastoma and platinum‑resistant ovarian cancer

text: Continuum framework for inherited cancer risk and reduced penetrance BRCA variants | Speaker: Tuva Pal | Tumors: breast cancer, ovarian cancer, prostate cancer, uterine sarcoma | MOA: Dr. Pal presented clinical case series illustrating that certain BRCA1/2 variants classified as pathogenic in ClinVar are actually reduced penetrance (hypomorphic) alleles, leading to variable cancer phenotypes across families and highlighting the need for a continuum risk framework. | Findings: Identified 16 consensus reduced penetrance BRCA1/2 variants across Myriad and Ambry labs, with multiple families carrying the same variant but showing divergent cancer histories.; Described a family with an 84‑year‑old metastatic breast cancer patient and two unaffected BRCA2‑positive daughters, illustrating late‑onset disease despite pathogenic classification.; Showed a 61‑year‑old woman with both ER‑positive and triple‑negative breast cancers carrying a BRCA2 VUS that was classified as pathogenic by six labs and VUS by two, underscoring discordant interpretations.; Highlighted that ClinVar entries often label such variants as pathogenic but note hypomorphic potential in buried comments, leading to counseling challenges.; Emphasized that reduced penetrance variants can still warrant standard risk‑reducing interventions (e.g., breast MRI) while allowing shared decision‑making for prophylactic surgery.

metadata.speaker: Tuva Pal
metadata.talk_title: Continuum framework for inherited cancer risk and reduced penetrance BRCA variants

text: Functional analysis framework for reduced penetrance pathogenic variants | Speaker: Alvaro Monteiro | Tumors: breast cancer, ovarian cancer, colorectal cancer, pancreatic cancer | MOA: Dr. Monteiro described a high‑throughput multiplexed assay (MAVE) pipeline that quantifies protein activity for BRCA1/2 variants, using a VARcall mixture model to translate activity scores into pathogenicity probabilities and to identify intermediate‑activity hypomorphic alleles as candidate reduced penetrance pathogenic variants. | Findings: Developed a VARcall two‑component mixture model that separates neutral from pathogenic activity distributions and flags intermediate‑activity variants as potential reduced penetrance pathogenic variants.; Demonstrated that known hypomorphic BRCA1 variants (e.g., R1699W, V1736A) fall in the intermediate activity zone and correlate with atypical family segregation patterns.; Showed that large‑scale functional screens (e.g., from Shendure and Couch labs) can identify a subset of missense variants with activity scores between clearly benign and clearly pathogenic, providing a pool of candidate reduced penetrance variants.; Proposed a calibration strategy where a few functionally validated reduced penetrance variants are used to set activity thresholds for genome‑wide classification.

metadata.speaker: Alvaro Monteiro
metadata.talk_title: Functional analysis framework for reduced penetrance pathogenic variants

text: Clinical management challenges for reduced penetrance pathogenic variants in hereditary cancer syndromes | Speaker: Bryson Catona | Tumors: colorectal cancer, gastric cancer, duodenal cancer, endometrial cancer, uterine cancer | MOA: Dr. Catona reviewed phenotype‑directed management for reduced penetrance APC variants in attenuated FAP and gene‑specific surveillance strategies for reduced penetrance MSH6 variants in Lynch syndrome, highlighting the need for variant‑specific risk calibration and flexible screening intervals. | Findings: Attenuated FAP caused by 5' APC variants can be managed using polyp burden (Spiegelman score) to dictate duodenal and colorectal surveillance intervals, avoiding premature colectomy.; A specific MSH6 missense variant present in ~4% of MSH6 carriers showed no statistically increased risk for colorectal, ovarian, or uterine cancer compared with population risk, suggesting a reduced penetrance phenotype.; Proposed extending colonoscopy intervals to the maximum guideline‑allowed three years for carriers of the low‑risk MSH6 variant and deferring prophylactic hysterectomy to age 50 or possibly omitting it.; Emphasized that gene‑specific guidelines (e.g., earlier colonoscopy for MLH1/MSH2 vs. later for PMS2) remain essential, but variant‑specific data are needed to refine recommendations.

metadata.speaker: Bryson Catona
metadata.talk_title: Clinical management challenges for reduced penetrance pathogenic variants in hereditary cancer syndromes

text: Immunotherapy-induced extracellular matrix remodeling and BMP1-targeted ADC | Speaker: Yuval Shaked | Tumors: triple-negative breast cancer, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, lung carcinoma | MOA: Anti-PD-1 therapy activates CD8 T cells that secrete BMP1, which activates LOX and remodels the extracellular matrix, creating a physical and immunosuppressive barrier that limits T cell infiltration; inhibition of BMP1 with a small‑molecule or BMP1‑ADC restores ECM permissiveness and enhances anti‑tumor immunity. | Findings: Anti‑PD‑1 treatment induces dense collagen I/III deposition in 4T1 and Lewis lung tumors via CD8 T‑cell‑derived BMP1.; SCID mice lacking T cells do not show ECM remodeling after anti‑PD‑1, which is rescued by adoptive transfer of T cells.; BMP1 expression is up‑regulated in CD8 T cells and plasma after anti‑PD‑1 in mice and in head‑and‑neck SCC patients.; Combination of anti‑PD‑1 with the BMP1 inhibitor UK‑383367 restores tumor sensitivity and reduces ECM density.; A BMP1‑ADC (antibody‑drug conjugate delivering the BMP1 inhibitor) retards tumor growth in multiple models.

metadata.speaker: Yuval Shaked
metadata.talk_title: Immunotherapy-induced extracellular matrix remodeling and BMP1-targeted ADC
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

text: Aging‑driven arginase‑1 mediated NK cell suppression promotes metastatic colonization | Speaker: Mitchell Fain | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: Aging increases ARG1 expression in lung and liver myeloid cells and fibroblasts, depleting arginine and suppressing NK cell proliferation and cytotoxicity; pharmacologic inhibition of ARG1 restores NK cell numbers and function, reducing age‑associated metastatic outgrowth of melanoma. | Findings: Aged lung and liver exhibit markedly higher ARG1 expression in CD45+ myeloid cells and fibroblasts.; Recombinant ARG1 administration to young mice reactivates dormant melanoma cells and increases liver colonization.; ARG1 treatment selectively reduces NK cell infiltration and activation in metastatic sites.; ARG1 inhibition with CB‑1158 in aged mice significantly decreases liver metastasis and restores NK cell frequency and activation markers (decreased PD‑1, increased DNAM‑1).; ARG1 high expression in TCGA melanoma patients correlates with poorer overall survival and is enriched in patients >55 years.

metadata.speaker: Mitchell Fain
metadata.talk_title: Aging‑driven arginase‑1 mediated NK cell suppression promotes metastatic colonization

text: Multimodal Treatment Strategies and Spatial Niche in Gastric Cancer Peritoneal Metastasis | Speaker: Sun Young Ra | Tumors: gastric cancer | MOA: Spatial transcriptomics of matched primary and peritoneal gastric cancer lesions revealed a fibroblast‑rich, dense extracellular matrix niche that physically shields tumor cells from immune effector cells and limits drug delivery. FGFR2 amplification and collagen/ECM‑related pathways are up‑regulated in peritoneal deposits, while immune‑checkpoint activation is reduced, suggesting that CAF‑mediated barrier formation drives immune evasion and therapeutic resistance in gastric cancer peritoneal metastasis. | Findings: Peritoneal metastasis occurred in 70.8% of stage IV gastric cancer patients (n=3,200) and was associated with markedly poorer overall survival compared with lymph‑node‑only disease.; HER2‑negative gastric cancers showed a higher peritoneal metastasis rate (≈75%) than HER2‑positive cases (≈50%).; FGFR2 amplification was significantly enriched in peritoneal metastasis tissues versus primary tumors, suggesting a potential therapeutic target.; Spatial profiling identified four CAF subtypes (remodeling, immune‑controlling, mesothelial, stress‑related) with remodeling and immune‑controlling CAFs markedly increased in peritoneal lesions.; Peritoneal lesions exhibited higher fibroblast, endothelial, macrophage, and T‑cell infiltration but reduced T‑cell activation and granzyme expression, indicating an immunosuppressive microenvironment.

metadata.speaker: Sun Young Ra
metadata.talk_title: Multimodal Treatment Strategies and Spatial Niche in Gastric Cancer Peritoneal Metastasis

text: Molecular Heterogeneity in Colorectal Peritoneal Metastasis | Speaker: Raghav Sundar | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Colorectal peritoneal metastases are highly enriched for the mesenchymal CMS4 subtype, characterized by TGF‑β activation, stromal infiltration, and EMT. Multi‑omic profiling shows that CMS4 tumors retain the same driver mutations as primaries but undergo transcriptional reprogramming and distinct microenvironmental remodeling, leading to resistance to standard HIPEC agents. Targeting stromal components such as moesin or PAI‑1 may overcome this resistance. | Findings: CMS4 is significantly over‑represented in colorectal peritoneal metastases compared with primary tumors and liver metastases.; Within CMS4, three molecular subgroups (RAS‑mutated mucinous, inflamed, and others) exhibit distinct RAS/TP53 mutation patterns and microenvironment compositions.; Genomic landscapes (TP53, APC, KRAS) are largely conserved between primary and peritoneal lesions, indicating polyclonal seeding rather than subclonal divergence.; CMS4 peritoneal metastases display poor prognosis (HR 0.56 vs non‑CMS4) and are less responsive to oxaliplatin‑based HIPEC, but show greater sensitivity to mitomycin C in vitro.; Targeting stromal proteins moesin or PAI‑1 with monoclonal antibodies reduced tumor burden in preclinical peritoneal models, suggesting a novel therapeutic avenue.

metadata.speaker: Raghav Sundar
metadata.talk_title: Molecular Heterogeneity in Colorectal Peritoneal Metastasis

text: Mutational Signatures and Cellular Phenotypes in Ovarian Peritoneal Metastasis | Speaker: Ignacio Garcia | Tumors: ovarian cancer | MOA: Whole‑genome signatures separate HR‑deficient (BRCA1/2‑like) from HR‑proficient ovarian tumors. HR‑deficient peritoneal metastases display heightened interferon/JAK‑STAT signaling, increased antigen presentation, and frequent clonal loss of HLA (6p LOH), leading to T‑cell dysfunction. Genome doubling is universal, generating ongoing chromosome missegregation and micronuclei; however, genome‑doubled cells down‑regulate cGAS‑STING signaling to tolerate instability, shaping immune evasion in the peritoneal niche. | Findings: ≈50% of high‑grade serous ovarian cancers are HR‑deficient, identifiable by tandem‑duplication (BRCA1‑like) or interstitial deletion (BRCA2‑like) signatures.; HR‑deficient tumors up‑regulate type‑I interferon and JAK‑STAT pathways and show higher expression of antigen‑presentation machinery compared with HR‑proficient (FBI) tumors.; Clonal 6p LOH (HLA loss) is enriched in BRCA1‑like HRD‑DUP tumors and correlates with increased T‑cell dysfunction.; All tumors contain genome‑doubled cells; genome doubling drives extensive cell‑specific aneuploidies and micronucleus formation.; cGAS‑positive micronuclei are abundant in diploid cells but inversely correlated with cGAS‑STING signaling in genome‑doubled cells, suggesting adaptive suppression of innate immunity.

metadata.speaker: Ignacio Garcia
metadata.talk_title: Mutational Signatures and Cellular Phenotypes in Ovarian Peritoneal Metastasis

text: Modeling immune metabolism and cancer using spatial metabolomics and organoid systems | Speaker: Dr Owen Sansom | Tumors: colorectal cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, melanoma | MOA: SANSOM demonstrated that spatially resolved DESI metabolomics can map tumor metabolic phenotypes, revealing glutamine depletion and SLC7A5 upregulation in APC KRAS colorectal tumors, and that genetic deletion of SLC7A5 suppresses tumor growth and alters MAPK/mTOR signaling, highlighting metabolic dependencies that can be targeted with KRAS inhibitors or rapamycin. | Findings: DESI imaging identified glutamine depletion and high SLC7A5 expression in APC KRAS colorectal tumor epithelium versus normal tissue.; Genetic deletion of SLC7A5 in APC KRAS mouse models caused accumulation of glutamine, glutamate, and alanine and resulted in the strongest tumor suppression observed in colorectal cancer models.; SLC7A5 loss reduced phospho‑S6 signaling, sensitizing tumors to rapamycin and MAPK inhibition.; KRAS G12D inhibitor treatment eliminated phospho‑ERK signaling but did not eradicate tumors; however, it rapidly altered neutrophil, lymphocyte, and monocyte counts and remodeled macrophage and CAF spatial organization.; In pancreatic KPC mice, SLC7A5 deletion slowed tumor genesis, shifted tumors toward a more homogeneous squamous subtype, and increased immune infiltration.

metadata.speaker: Dr Owen Sansom
metadata.talk_title: Modeling immune metabolism and cancer using spatial metabolomics and organoid systems

text: Citrate carrier SLC25A1 drives T cell exhaustion and can be targeted to improve immunotherapy | Speaker: Dr Greg Delgoff | Tumors: melanoma, NSCLC, colorectal cancer | MOA: Delgoff showed that chronic TCR stimulation and hypoxia upregulate the mitochondrial citrate carrier SLC25A1, shunting citrate to the cytosol where it fuels de novo lipogenesis and protein acetylation, driving lipid droplet accumulation and hyperacetylation that enforce terminal T cell exhaustion; CRISPR knockout of SLC25A1 restores mitochondrial respiration, reduces lipid droplets, enhances polyfunctionality, and improves tumor control, synergizing with PD‑1 blockade. | Findings: Chronic TCR stimulation plus hypoxia uniquely upregulates SLC25A1 in terminally exhausted CD8+ T cells.; SLC25A1 mediates export of mitochondrial citrate, leading to cytosolic acetyl‑CoA accumulation, lipid droplet formation, and widespread protein acetylation.; CRISPR knockout of SLC25A1 increases mitochondrial respiratory capacity, glycolysis, and reduces lipid droplet burden in exhausted T cells.; SLC25A1‑deficient T cells exhibit lower PD‑1, TIM‑3, and CD39 expression, retain IL‑2 production, and display superior polyfunctionality in tumors.; Adoptive transfer of SLC25A1‑KO T cells yields greater tumor regression and synergizes with anti‑PD‑1 therapy in mouse models.

metadata.speaker: Dr Greg Delgoff
metadata.talk_title: Citrate carrier SLC25A1 drives T cell exhaustion and can be targeted to improve immunotherapy

text: Reprogramming NK cell metabolism for enhanced adoptive cell therapy | Speaker: Dr Madar | Tumors: AML, renal cell carcinoma, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, triple‑negative breast cancer | MOA: Madar described multiple metabolic engineering strategies for NK cell ACT, including CRISPR knockout of the cytokine‑inducible checkpoint CIS and TGF‑β receptor II to boost mTOR and glycolytic pathways, and overexpression of the adenoviral E4ORF1 protein to activate PI3K/AKT/mTOR and increase citrate‑derived biosynthesis, resulting in enhanced mitochondrial mass, oxidative phosphorylation, and cytotoxicity across solid and hematologic tumor models. | Findings: NK cells cultured in lipid‑rich APEL media acquire higher mitochondrial mass, elongated morphology, and increased spare respiratory capacity versus standard media.; CIS knockout NK cells display upregulated mTOR signaling, glycolysis, and improved survival in aggressive Raji lymphoma mouse models.; TGFBR2‑KO CD70 CAR NK cells demonstrate superior anti‑AML activity in preclinical models and have entered a Phase 1/2 trial (NCT‑pending).; E4ORF1 overexpression in NK cells enhances glycolysis, OXPHOS, fatty‑acid oxidation, and glutaminolysis, leading to robust killing of multiple solid tumor lines even under nutrient starvation.; AMPK activity is required for the E4ORF1‑mediated metabolic boost; inhibition of AMPK abrogates the enhanced cytotoxic phenotype.

metadata.speaker: Dr Madar
metadata.talk_title: Reprogramming NK cell metabolism for enhanced adoptive cell therapy

text: STK-12 IL-2 agonist plus pembrolizumab and chemotherapy in PD-L1 negative NSCLC | Speaker: Salman Punekar | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: STK-12 is a recombinant IL-2 partial agonist that selectively expands antigen-experienced CD8+ T cells while sparing NK and Treg cells, enhancing IFNγ and IP-10 production and clonal TCR expansion, thereby improving response rates when combined with pembrolizumab and chemotherapy in PD-L1 negative NSCLC. | Findings: Overall response rate of 50% and disease control rate of 97% in a high‑risk PD‑L1 negative NSCLC cohort (n=39).; In STK11/KEAP1/SMARCA4 altered subgroup, ORR increased to 61% with 100% disease control.; STK‑12 induced robust expansion of 4‑1BB+ CD8 T cells and >10‑fold clonal expansion of pre‑existing TCR clones.; Minimal classic IL‑2 toxicities observed; most common AE was reversible maculopapular rash in ~50% of patients.

metadata.speaker: Salman Punekar
metadata.talk_title: STK-12 IL-2 agonist plus pembrolizumab and chemotherapy in PD-L1 negative NSCLC

text: Tertiary lymphoid structures predict response to durvalumab, trastuzumab, pertuzumab in HER2‑enriched early breast cancer | Speaker: Meilin Li | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Durvalumab combined with HER2‑targeted antibodies induces formation of tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) composed of Tfh‑like CD4+ cells, mature dendritic cells, and proliferating B cells; these TLS niches correlate with enhanced CD8+ T‑cell infiltration and higher pathologic complete response in HER2‑enriched breast cancer. | Findings: TLS‑associated immune module (Tfh‑like CD4+, LAMB3+ mature DCs, cycling B cells) is enriched in pretreatment tumors of patients achieving PCR.; Spatial analysis shows co‑localization of these cell types within 20‑µm niches, defining TLS structures.; Higher TLS niche fraction predicts PCR (p<0.01) and correlates with increased intratumoral CD8+ T cells post‑treatment.; CellChat indicates CD4+ Tfh cells activate B cells via IL‑2, CD40, and ICAM pathways within TLS.

metadata.speaker: Meilin Li
metadata.talk_title: Tertiary lymphoid structures predict response to durvalumab, trastuzumab, pertuzumab in HER2‑enriched early breast cancer

text: Inhibiting nonsense‑mediated decay (SMG1) to enhance antitumor immunity | Speaker: Hongchang Fu | Tumors: colorectal cancer, lung cancer | MOA: SMG1 inhibition blocks nonsense‑mediated decay, stabilizing frameshift‑derived PTC transcripts that encode highly immunogenic neoantigens; these are presented on MHC‑I, leading to CD8+ T‑cell activation and tumor control, synergizing with anti‑PD‑1 therapy. | Findings: SMG1 inhibition increased PD‑1+ CD8 T‑cell activation in ex vivo tumor fragments without affecting adjacent normal tissue.; In Lewis lung carcinoma, SMG1 inhibitor monotherapy matched anti‑PD‑1 efficacy; combination yielded superior tumor control.; Immunopeptidomics identified six neoantigen peptides up‑regulated only after NMD inhibition; four were immunogenic in vitro.; MHC‑I blockade abolished T‑cell activation induced by SMG1 inhibition, confirming antigen‑dependent mechanism.

metadata.speaker: Hongchang Fu
metadata.talk_title: Inhibiting nonsense‑mediated decay (SMG1) to enhance antitumor immunity

text: High‑fiber dietary intervention improves immunotherapy outcomes in melanoma | Speaker: Kerry Daniel MacDougall | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: A high‑fiber, whole‑food diet reshapes the gut microbiome toward response‑associated taxa, lowers secondary/primary bile acid ratios, reduces immunosuppressive classical monocytes, and enhances intratumoral CD8+ T‑cell and cytotoxic lymphocyte infiltration, thereby improving checkpoint inhibitor efficacy in melanoma. | Findings: High‑fiber diet did not alter overall alpha/beta diversity but increased patient‑specific enrichment of known response‑associated taxa.; Serum bile acid profiling showed a significant decrease in secondary/primary bile acid ratio in the high‑fiber arm.; Classical monocyte immunosuppressive cluster decreased over time only in high‑fiber patients.; Digital spatial profiling revealed greater CD8+ T‑cell and cytotoxic lymphocyte density post‑intervention in responders receiving high‑fiber diet.

metadata.speaker: Kerry Daniel MacDougall
metadata.talk_title: High‑fiber dietary intervention improves immunotherapy outcomes in melanoma

text: IL‑17‑producing TH17 cells drive neurotoxicity in immune‑related adverse events of the CNS | Speaker: Jingyao Zhang | MOA: A POLR6‑positive CD4+ PD‑1+ TH17‑like cell subset expands in the CSF of ICI‑treated patients, secreting IL‑17 and other inflammatory mediators that drive neuroinflammation; blockade of IL‑17A mitigates PET‑detected inflammation and improves neurologic outcomes. | Findings: Identified a disease‑specific POLR6+ CD4+ PD‑1+ TH17‑like cell cluster producing IL‑17, MCP1, CCL11, granzyme B, etc.; Higher POLR6+ cell burden correlated with greater PET‑measured neuroinflammation and worse cognitive scores.; Clonal T‑cell expansions persisted up to 12 months, indicating ongoing antigen‑driven response, with NMDA‑R1 as a dominant neuroantigen.; Retrospective anti‑IL‑17A treatment was associated with reduced neuroinflammation and improved neurologic function without affecting cancer outcomes.

metadata.speaker: Jingyao Zhang
metadata.talk_title: IL‑17‑producing TH17 cells drive neurotoxicity in immune‑related adverse events of the CNS

text: NAT10‑MYC loop drives autophagy‑dependent MHC‑I downregulation and immunotherapy resistance in MSS colorectal cancer | Speaker: Junyoung Wang | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: NAT10 acetylates RNA (ac4C) stabilizing autophagy genes (ATG3, ATG5, Beclin‑1), leading to increased autophagic flux that degrades MHC‑I molecules; a MYC‑NAT10 positive feedback loop sustains this program, causing immune evasion in MSS CRC, which can be reversed by NAT10 inhibition to restore MHC‑I and sensitize tumors to anti‑PD‑1 therapy. | Findings: NAT10 is overexpressed in MSS CRC and predicts worse overall survival.; NAT10 knockout increases CD8+ T‑cell infiltration and tumor regression in mice.; Combination of NAT10 inhibition with anti‑PD‑1 yields complete tumor regression in 80% of mice.; MYC transcriptionally up‑regulates NAT10; NAT10‑mediated ac4C stabilizes MYC mRNA, forming a feed‑forward loop.

metadata.speaker: Junyoung Wang
metadata.talk_title: NAT10‑MYC loop drives autophagy‑dependent MHC‑I downregulation and immunotherapy resistance in MSS colorectal cancer

text: Versican proteolysis restores tumor matrix signaling to reverse checkpoint resistance | Speaker: Daniel Lagal | Tumors: colorectal cancer, lung cancer, pancreatic cancer | MOA: Proteolytic cleavage of versican generates bioactive fragments that promote formation of immunotriads (CD4+ Tfh‑like cells, CD8+ T cells, dendritic cells) within the tumor stroma, enhancing CD8+ T‑cell infiltration and synergizing with checkpoint blockade to overcome immune exclusion. | Findings: Versican overexpression in MC38 tumors induced immunotriad formation and cured >70% of mice with anti‑PD‑1 alone.; In VCAN‑high LSC tumors, versican plus dual checkpoint blockade (PD‑1 + CTLA‑4) was required for tumor control.; Exogenous versican delivered via LNP mRNA or recombinant protein showed monotherapy activity in VCAN‑low models and synergized with ICB.; Efficacy depended on cDC1 dendritic cells and CD8+ T cells; depletion abrogated therapeutic benefit.

metadata.speaker: Daniel Lagal
metadata.talk_title: Versican proteolysis restores tumor matrix signaling to reverse checkpoint resistance

text: Implementation planning for lung cancer screening in HIV care settings | Speaker: Jessica Islam | Tumors: lung cancer, HIV-associated cancers | MOA: Dr. Islam described a pre-implementation research package (R01) that uses multilevel epidemiologic, causal inference, and qualitative methods to characterize LDCT lung cancer screening uptake, barriers, and patient decision-making among people with HIV, with the goal of informing tailored implementation strategies. | Findings: Among ~7,000 HIV+ lung cancer patients, 75% were diagnosed at metastatic stage.; People with HIV had a 15% increased risk of metastatic lung cancer diagnosis compared to non‑HIV patients.; Socioeconomic factors (ZIP‑code education, income, care location) predicted higher probability of metastatic diagnosis.; The R01 aims to (1) describe LDCT screening patterns, (2) estimate direct/indirect effects of social determinants, and (3) explore patient decision‑making via qualitative interviews.

metadata.speaker: Jessica Islam
metadata.talk_title: Implementation planning for lung cancer screening in HIV care settings

text: Participatory approaches to prioritize colorectal cancer screening for patients with diabetes in FQHCs | Speaker: Dina Leo O'Malley | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Dr. O'Malley used implementation mapping with a multi‑stakeholder planning group to identify barriers and select four prioritized strategies (champion identification, low‑literacy educational materials, quality monitoring systems, and implementation meetings) to improve colorectal cancer screening among diabetic patients in safety‑net clinics. | Findings: Implementation planning group generated 36 potential strategies, refined to top five themes (patient education/communication, clinical flow).; Top four selected strategies: identify/prep champions; develop low‑literacy educational materials; organize quality monitoring (UDS metrics); conduct implementation meetings.; Pilot clinic A achieved 77% screening among diabetic patients (higher among uncontrolled diabetes), using champion‑driven Cologuard outreach.; Pilot clinic B, with lower baseline screening (28%), improved to 60% using adapted postcards, QR‑code videos, and staff training.; Uncontrolled diabetes patients comprised the largest unscreened subgroup in both clinics.

metadata.speaker: Dina Leo O'Malley
metadata.talk_title: Participatory approaches to prioritize colorectal cancer screening for patients with diabetes in FQHCs

text: Sustaining and scaling HPV vaccination implementation in safety‑net settings | Speaker: Jennifer Tsui | Tumors: cervical cancer, HPV‑related cancers | MOA: Dr. Tsui presented a multi‑year R37/R01 project that implemented audit‑and‑feedback, provider communication training (Announcement Approach), and co‑designed staff workflow tools to increase HPV vaccine initiation, demonstrated sustained provider practices and identified contextual factors for scaling to other FQHC systems. | Findings: After 12‑month implementation, HPV vaccine initiation increased significantly at three pilot clinics, driven by higher uptake at ages 9‑10.; 18‑month follow‑up showed sustained provider discussion of vaccination at age 9 (88% of staff) and increased confidence addressing parental hesitancy (69%).; CSAT scores indicated staff found the strategies easy to use, integrable into workflow, and clinically meaningful (median 5‑7/7).; Turnover of clinic staff remained a major barrier to sustainment; half of staff changed within 24 months.; Scale‑out to AltaMed, Chinatown Service Center, and Riverside San Bernardino IHS required adaptation of training modality (in‑person, virtual, hybrid) and cultural tailoring of materials.

metadata.speaker: Jennifer Tsui
metadata.talk_title: Sustaining and scaling HPV vaccination implementation in safety‑net settings

text: The Role of pks+ E. coli in Intestinal Stem Cell Plasticity and Early Onset of Colorectal Cancer | Speaker: Karuna Ganesh | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: pks+ E. coli produces colibactin, a genotoxin that creates AT-rich DNA lesions (SBS88) and mutates APC splice sites in young patients; colibactin also binds AT-rich motifs, displacing CDX2 and repressing differentiation programs, thereby promoting a shift of epithelial cells toward an LGR5+ intestinal stem cell state, enhancing regenerative capacity and tumor initiation in the young colon. | Findings: Developed a targeted-exome assay to detect the colibactin SBS88 signature in >80,000 clinical tumors, finding enrichment in colorectal, esophageal, bladder, and head/neck cancers.; Colibactin signature-positive tumors occur in significantly younger patients and are more often located in the rectosigmoid region.; Identified a specific APC splice-site mutation occurring in the AT-rich colibactin context, enriched in young-onset colorectal cancers, suggesting colibactin-driven initiation.; Inverted-polarity organoid model exposed to pks+ E. coli recapitulated colibactin mutational signatures and induced upregulation of LGR5 and ASCL2 stem cell markers.; pks+ E. coli exposure increased functional stem cell capacity (organoid formation) and proliferation compared to Δpks controls.

metadata.speaker: Karuna Ganesh
metadata.talk_title: The Role of pks+ E. coli in Intestinal Stem Cell Plasticity and Early Onset of Colorectal Cancer

text: Towards New Cancer Medicines with Degraders of Chromatin | Speaker: Danette Daniels | MOA: Danette presented a framework that quantifies degrader kinetics by measuring degradation rate versus Dmax, defining an inflection point (the "rate cliff") that predicts complete target loss across multiple chromatin regulators; fast degraders with high rate efficiency translate to robust in vivo pharmacodynamics independent of DC50. | Findings: A universal rate‑versus‑Dmax relationship was observed across diverse degraders (BRD9, EP300, CBP) regardless of target or cell line.; The rate inflection point (0.7–1.8) predicts ≥85–90% Dmax; compounds below this "cliff" show target recovery.; AUC of rate‑versus‑concentration curves distinguishes compounds with identical DC50 but up to five‑fold differences in maximal degradation rate.; Faster degraders exhibit higher ubiquitination levels and form more stable ternary complexes with slower koff rates measured by SPR.; In vivo PK/PD mapping of CBP degraders demonstrates that dosing at Cmax and trough samples the maximal degradation rate, leading to robust target loss in mouse models.

metadata.speaker: Danette Daniels
metadata.talk_title: Towards New Cancer Medicines with Degraders of Chromatin

text: Designing Effective Degrader Therapeutics: What Early Clinical Experience Has Taught Us | Speaker: Gwen Hansen | Tumors: chronic lymphocytic leukemia | MOA: Bexipridil is a BTK degrader that induces proteasomal removal of BTK, achieving sub‑stoichiometric target clearance; this eliminates residual kinase activity and overcomes a broad spectrum of BTK resistance mutations, providing deeper and more durable responses than BTK inhibitors. | Findings: 83% overall response rate in a heavily pre‑treated CLL population, including patients who progressed on the approved BTK inhibitor pirtobrutinib.; Median duration of response reached 20 months, exceeding the ~12‑month DOR reported for the best current inhibitor.; Degrader retained activity against all known BTK resistance mutations, whereas inhibitors showed gaps in coverage.; Higher dose (600 mg) improved progression‑free survival without increasing adverse‑event frequency, indicating a wide therapeutic index.; Comprehensive proteomics showed BTK as one of the top‑down‑regulated proteins with minimal off‑target degradation.

metadata.speaker: Gwen Hansen
metadata.talk_title: Designing Effective Degrader Therapeutics: What Early Clinical Experience Has Taught Us

text: First‑in‑Class Dual AR/ARV7 Molecular Glue Degraders | Speaker: Sherry Ao | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: Compounds 15 and 64 act as molecular glues that bind the N‑terminal domain of AR/ARV7 and recruit a Cullin‑RING ligase complex (DDB1‑containing) to induce proteasomal degradation of both isoforms, thereby suppressing AR‑driven transcription and overcoming enzalutamide resistance. | Findings: High‑throughput screen of 170,000 compounds identified 13 hits; lead chemotype 7907 degraded both AR and ARV7 via proteasome.; Medicinal chemistry optimization yielded analogs 15 and 64 with sub‑micromolar EC50s and rapid (≤4 h) degradation of both proteins.; Compound 15 suppressed AR‑driven transcription in 22RV1 cells, outperforming enzalutamide and ARV110 in RNA‑seq AR‑score analysis.; In vivo, oral dosing of compounds 15 and 64 markedly inhibited growth of ARV7‑positive 22RV1 xenografts, achieving greater tumor regression than enzalutamide or ARV110.; Mechanistic studies mapped activity to the AR N‑terminal TAL1 and AF1 subdomains; degradation required Cullin‑RING ligase activity (blocked by MLN4924) and was partially reversed by DDB1 knockout.

metadata.speaker: Sherry Ao
metadata.talk_title: First‑in‑Class Dual AR/ARV7 Molecular Glue Degraders

text: Role of Sex and Ancestry in Inflammaging, Lymphomagenesis and Its Precision Therapy | Speaker: Ari Melnick | Tumors: diffuse large B-cell lymphoma | MOA: Sex- and ancestry-specific mutations (SPEN, Notch2, ATM, MGA, SETD2) reprogram B-cell differentiation toward aged, auto-reactive AIBCs, driving aggressive DLBCL phenotypes; female BN2 DLBCLs exhibit X-chromosome instability and heightened TLR7 signaling, rendering them sensitive to IRAK inhibition, while African ancestry DLBCLs display senescence-associated secretory phenotypes linked to SETD2 loss, suggesting precision therapeutic windows. | Findings: SPEN truncation co-occurs with Notch2 truncation in BN2 DLBCLs and predicts inferior survival in a 4,500-patient cohort.; Female BN2 DLBCL mice develop X‑chromosome hypomethylation, increased TLR7 expression, and are more sensitive to IRAK inhibitors than males.; African ancestry DLBCLs harbor frequent ATM, MGA, and SETD2 mutations (>50%) and show elevated senescence (GLB1) and exhausted CD4 T‑cell infiltrates.; SETD2‑heterozygous DLBCL cells are hypersensitive to a clinical SETD2 inhibitor, offering a potential ancestry‑specific therapy.; IRAK inhibition reduces tumor growth in female BN2 DLBCL xenografts, supporting a sex‑specific precision therapy approach.

metadata.speaker: Ari Melnick
metadata.talk_title: Role of Sex and Ancestry in Inflammaging, Lymphomagenesis and Its Precision Therapy

text: Age-Associated Molecular Landscapes and Therapeutic Responses in Breast Cancer | Speaker: Sandra McAllister | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Aging reprograms breast cancer transcriptomes: older ER‑positive tumors show reduced immune and metabolic pathways, while older triple‑negative tumors acquire an inflamed, EMT‑driven phenotype; age‑selected subclones (e.g., barcode 25) become resistant to paclitaxel, but are sensitized to HDAC inhibition combined with checkpoint blockade, revealing age‑specific therapeutic vulnerabilities. | Findings: Older breast cancer patients exhibit distinct molecular landscapes: ER+ tumors lose immune/metabolic activity, while TNBCs gain an inflamed EMT phenotype.; In mouse models, aged mice show slower NET1 tumor growth but reduced response to paclitaxel + anti‑PD‑L1, despite higher CD8 infiltration and Treg expansion.; Barcode 25 subclone is enriched by age and paclitaxel, displays intrinsic paclitaxel resistance, and can be eliminated by HDAC inhibition.; Panobinostat combined with anti‑PD‑L1 dramatically extends survival in aged mice, whereas the same combination is less effective in young mice without chemotherapy.

metadata.speaker: Sandra McAllister
metadata.talk_title: Age-Associated Molecular Landscapes and Therapeutic Responses in Breast Cancer

text: Targeting GDF15‑Mediated Immunosuppression to Overcome Age‑Driven Immunotherapy Resistance in Pancreatic Cancer | Speaker: Daniel Zabransky | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Aging elevates systemic and tumor‑derived GDF15, which suppresses CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration and impairs vaccine‑induced neoantigen responses in PDAC; neutralizing GDF15 restores T‑cell priming and synergizes with KRAS peptide vaccination and checkpoint blockade to achieve tumor regression in aged mouse models. | Findings: Aged mice develop larger orthotopic KPC tumors and exhibit markedly reduced CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration compared with young mice.; Circulating GDF15 is low in young mice but rises sharply in aged mice and further increases after tumor implantation.; Genetic or antibody‑mediated GDF15 neutralization halves tumor size in aged mice and restores CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration; effect is lost after T‑cell depletion.; GDF15 neutralization enhances KRAS mutant peptide vaccine‑induced IFN‑γ T‑cell responses in aged mice.; In a PDAC GVAX trial, high tumor GDF15 expression correlates with ~2‑fold worse overall survival, independent of age.

metadata.speaker: Daniel Zabransky
metadata.talk_title: Targeting GDF15‑Mediated Immunosuppression to Overcome Age‑Driven Immunotherapy Resistance in Pancreatic Cancer

text: Evasion of Hepatic ILC1 Immunosurveillance Drives Breast Cancer Liver Metastasis | Speaker: Peng Li | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Hepatic ILC1s mediate immune surveillance of breast cancer liver metastasis via TRAIL-DR5 signaling; loss of DR5 or depletion of ILC1s enhances liver tumor burden, while GLP-1 agonist restores ILC1 numbers and reduces metastasis. | Findings: High-fat diet mice develop increased breast cancer liver metastasis compared to control diet.; RAG2 gamma knockout mice show increased liver and lung tumor burden, implicating innate lymphocytes in surveillance.; Selective depletion of conventional NK cells increases lung but not liver metastasis, indicating liver ILC1s are essential for hepatic surveillance.; ILC1s mediate tumor killing via TRAIL binding to DR5 on cancer cells; DR5 loss increases liver metastasis.; GLP-1 receptor agonist restores hepatic ILC1 numbers in steatotic mice and reduces liver tumor burden.

metadata.speaker: Peng Li
metadata.talk_title: Evasion of Hepatic ILC1 Immunosurveillance Drives Breast Cancer Liver Metastasis

text: Neutrophil Extracellular Trap Inhibition Mitigates Tumor Necrosis and Metastasis in Colorectal Cancer | Speaker: Sepideh Gholamin | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: NETs accumulate in necrotic regions of colorectal tumors, driving hypoxia, EMT, and metastasis; pharmacologic (disulfiram) or genetic (PAD4 KO) inhibition of NET formation reduces necrosis, EMT signaling, and liver metastases, and enhances chemotherapy efficacy. | Findings: PAD4 knockout mice show decreased tumor necrosis and fewer liver metastases compared to wild-type.; Disulfiram treatment reduces NETs, necrosis, and liver metastasis burden in AKPS organoid mice.; NET inhibition combined with FOLFOX chemotherapy further decreases liver metastasis compared to chemotherapy alone.; Necrotic tumor regions exhibit higher EMT markers (vimentin, SNAI1) and inflammatory pathways.; Mice with NET inhibition display increased neutrophil activation markers (citH3) reduction.

metadata.speaker: Sepideh Gholamin
metadata.talk_title: Neutrophil Extracellular Trap Inhibition Mitigates Tumor Necrosis and Metastasis in Colorectal Cancer

text: Metabolic Reuse of Tumor-Derived Signals Coordinates Dendritic Cell Function | Speaker: Mariam Belabed | Tumors: lung adenocarcinoma | MOA: Tumor-derived polyamines enhance dendritic cell uptake via RAC1 activation, while tumor-derived cholesterol fuels dendritic cell maturation through NPC1-mediated transport and lipid nanodomain formation; AXL deletion amplifies cholesterol accumulation, boosting maturation and antitumor immunity. | Findings: ODC1-deficient tumor debris is less efficiently taken up by dendritic cells in vitro and in vivo.; Blocking polyamine transport (AMTX) impairs dendritic cell uptake of tumor debris.; Polyamine deficiency reduces RAC1 expression and activation in dendritic cells.; Inhibition of NPC1 or statin treatment diminishes CCR7 and other maturation markers on dendritic cells.; AXL knockout dendritic cells accumulate more cholesterol, lipid nanodomains, and display heightened maturation and improved tumor control.

metadata.speaker: Mariam Belabed
metadata.talk_title: Metabolic Reuse of Tumor-Derived Signals Coordinates Dendritic Cell Function

text: Spatial Rewiring of IL-1β Network Limits Therapeutic Efficiency in Advanced Non‑Squamous Carcinoma | Speaker: Bo Zhu | Tumors: non‑small cell lung cancer | MOA: Anti‑IL1β therapy is effective when administered at pre‑cancer stages by disconnecting IL1β‑IL1R1 signaling in epithelial cells; in advanced disease the network shifts to fibroblast‑centric signaling, limiting efficacy despite increased IL1β levels. | Findings: IL1β pathway activity rises from normal to pre‑cancer to invasive adenocarcinoma in both human and mouse samples.; Anti‑IL1β antibody suppresses tumor growth when given at pre‑cancer stage but not at advanced stage in two mouse models.; Anti‑IL1β treatment paradoxically increases IL1β plasma levels in mice and humans.; Spatial analysis shows pre‑cancer blockade reduces IL1R1‑positive epithelial cells within the IL1β network, whereas advanced stage blockade reduces IL1R1‑positive fibroblasts.; Location‑aware cell‑cell interaction analysis reveals that IL1β‑IL1R1 contacts are disrupted in pre‑cancer but persist in advanced disease.

metadata.speaker: Bo Zhu
metadata.talk_title: Spatial Rewiring of IL-1β Network Limits Therapeutic Efficiency in Advanced Non‑Squamous Carcinoma

text: Gut Commensal Dysbiosis Modulates Lung Microenvironment to Promote Breast Tumor Metastasis via Mast Cell‑Dependent Axis | Speaker: Mika Poblete | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Gut dysbiosis elevates mast cell activation in the lung, leading to IL‑6 secretion that activates STAT3 in fibroblasts and endothelial cells, promoting ECM stiffening, angiogenesis, and M2 macrophage polarization, thereby creating a permissive niche for breast cancer lung metastasis. | Findings: Antibiotic‑induced gut dysbiosis accelerates death of mice after tail‑vein breast cancer cell injection.; Lung mast cell density inversely correlates with survival in dysbiotic mice.; Ketotifen (mast cell stabilizer) improves survival of dysbiotic mice, implicating mast cells in metastasis promotion.; Single‑cell RNA‑seq reveals dysbiotic lung mast cells upregulate IL‑6 and degranulation genes.; Fibroblasts and endothelial cells in dysbiotic lungs show STAT3‑driven fibrotic and angiogenic transcriptional programs.

metadata.speaker: Mika Poblete
metadata.talk_title: Gut Commensal Dysbiosis Modulates Lung Microenvironment to Promote Breast Tumor Metastasis via Mast Cell‑Dependent Axis

text: Mild Interferon‑γ Signaling Regulates Immune Suppression and Fibrotic TME in Pancreatic Cancer Liver Metastasis | Speaker: Takeshi Tanaka | Tumors: pancreatic cancer | MOA: Mild IFN‑γ signaling through IFNγR2 on macrophages sustains antigen‑presentation (CD80/CD86/MHC‑II) and limits immunosuppressive markers (ARG1, CD206, SPP1); loss of this signaling drives SPP1‑high macrophages, fibrosis, and T‑cell dysfunction in pancreatic cancer liver metastasis. | Findings: Systemic IFN‑γ neutralization increases tumor number and burden in liver metastasis model.; Myeloid‑specific IFNγR2 KO mice exhibit larger tumor burden and higher TAM numbers.; KO TAMs show decreased CD80/CD86/MHC‑II and increased ARG1/CD206/SPP1 expression.; T‑cell proliferation (Ki67) and cytokine production (IFN‑γ, TNF‑α) are reduced in KO mice.; Bulk RNA‑seq reveals down‑regulation of IFN‑γ response and up‑regulation of fibrosis pathways in KO tumors.

metadata.speaker: Takeshi Tanaka
metadata.talk_title: Mild Interferon‑γ Signaling Regulates Immune Suppression and Fibrotic TME in Pancreatic Cancer Liver Metastasis

text: Targeting Chronic Inflammation in Cancer and Fibrosis with Engineered uPAR‑CAR T Cells | Speaker: Ze Xiong | Tumors: ovarian cancer, lung adenocarcinoma, squamous lung cancer, pancreatic cancer | MOA: uPAR‑CAR T cells recognize and eliminate uPAR‑positive tumor cells, cancer‑associated fibroblasts, and immunosuppressive myeloid cells, thereby dismantling fibrotic stroma, enhancing T‑cell infiltration, and preventing antigen escape. | Findings: uPAR is co‑expressed on tumor cells, CAFs, and myeloid suppressor cells in >10 solid tumor types.; Single dose of uPAR‑CAR T yields durable tumor regression and protects against rechallenge in multiple xenograft models.; Cisplatin treatment up‑regulates uPAR on ovarian cancer cells, sensitizing them to uPAR‑CAR T killing.; uPAR‑CAR T reduces collagen deposition and fibrosis, leading to increased CAR T cell infiltration.; In humanized mice, uPAR‑CAR T shows antitumor activity without significant depletion of myeloid or granulocyte compartments.

metadata.speaker: Ze Xiong
metadata.talk_title: Targeting Chronic Inflammation in Cancer and Fibrosis with Engineered uPAR‑CAR T Cells

text: Novel Spatiotemporal Approaches for Built Environment Physical Disorder Measurement | Speaker: Jesse Placek | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Placek described a workflow that audits Google Street View images to quantify neighborhood physical disorder, creates a composite disinvestment score with high inter‑rater reliability, fits a spatial semivariogram and applies kriging to interpolate exposure values for individual cohort members, and links these exposures to breast cancer survival outcomes, revealing that higher disinvestment predicts shorter survival for stage 2/3 disease. | Findings: Audited 23,000 street‑view locations with standardized protocol achieving high kappa agreement, demonstrating reliable measurement of physical disorder.; Internal consistency analysis (Cronbach's alpha) justified collapsing multiple disorder items into a single composite disinvestment score.; Spatial kriging based on the fitted semivariogram provided continuous disinvestment estimates for cohort participants lacking exact address‑level data.; In the breast cancer cohort, each unit increase in the disinvestment score was associated with reduced survival time for stage 2 and stage 3 patients in accelerated failure‑time models.; The methodology enables rapid, reproducible, and scalable exposure assessment for built‑environment research across large urban areas.

metadata.speaker: Jesse Placek
metadata.session_title: Innovations in Translating Social and Structural Determinants of Health Across Population, Community, and Basic Cancer Research
metadata.talk_title: Novel Spatiotemporal Approaches for Built Environment Physical Disorder Measurement

text: Integrating Social Determinants of Health with Cancer Registry Data to Identify Geographic Drivers of Lung and Prostate Cancer | Speaker: Shannon Lynch | Tumors: lung cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer | MOA: Lynch integrated publicly available SSDOH datasets (census, EPA, zoning, etc.) with state cancer registry records, used SaTScan to detect census‑tract clusters of excess lung cancer incidence, and applied multivariable logistic regression to identify smoking, air pollution, traffic density, and old housing as independent drivers; similar neighborhood‑wide association studies linked specific SSDOH variables (e.g., public‑transport use, housing quality) to aggressive prostate cancer, demonstrating that macro‑level social and environmental exposures can be quantified and associated with cancer incidence and outcomes. | Findings: Identified multiple census‑tract clusters in Pennsylvania with significantly higher lung cancer incidence after age, sex, and race adjustment.; In multivariate models, smoking prevalence, ambient air‑pollution levels, traffic density, and proportion of old housing (asbestos proxy) were each significantly associated with cluster status (p<0.05).; Philadelphia‑specific analysis revealed high‑mortality neighborhoods with greater tobacco outlet density and elevated environmental exposures.; Neighborhood‑wide association study of >14,000 Census variables pinpointed five SSDOH factors (e.g., public‑transport use, housing disinvestment) linked to aggressive prostate cancer in Black men and 17 factors in White men.; Combining three top SSDOH variables into an exposure score markedly improved prostate cancer risk prediction beyond PSA alone (probability ≈30% vs 8% for high vs low exposure scores).

metadata.speaker: Shannon Lynch
metadata.session_title: Innovations in Translating Social and Structural Determinants of Health Across Population, Community, and Basic Cancer Research
metadata.talk_title: Integrating Social Determinants of Health with Cancer Registry Data to Identify Geographic Drivers of Lung and Prostate Cancer

text: Preclinical development of EFTX G12V, a first‑in‑class EGFR‑directed KRAS G12V selective siRNA | Speaker: Dr. Sandlin | Tumors: lung cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: EFTX G12V is an EGFR‑targeted, chemically modified siRNA that selectively silences KRAS G12V while sparing wild‑type KRAS, achieving high tumor delivery, sustained KRAS knockdown, downstream ERK inhibition, and tumor regression in KRAS G12V‑driven lung and colon models, including immunocompetent settings with CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration. | Findings: EGFR‑directed siRNA achieved ~90% tumor cell uptake after 2 h in xenograft mice.; Selective KRAS G12V silencing at RNA and protein levels with no effect on wild‑type KRAS.; Single‑agent EFTX G12V induced significant tumor growth control and complete responses in KRAS G12V lung (H727) and colon models.; Sustained tumor tissue accumulation and KRAS protein knockdown observed up to 96 h after dosing.; Immunocompetent MPK195 model showed comparable anti‑tumor efficacy and robust CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Sandlin
metadata.talk_title: Preclinical development of EFTX G12V, a first‑in‑class EGFR‑directed KRAS G12V selective siRNA

text: Targeting ORC1A to sensitize KRAS‑mutant colorectal cancer to KRAS inhibitors | Speaker: Dr. Zhaoqing Liu | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: ORC1A inhibition by olaparib synergizes with KRAS G12C inhibitors by suppressing MCL1 stability via GSK3β activation, leading to proteasomal degradation of MCL1 and caspase‑dependent apoptosis in KRAS‑mutant colorectal cancer models. | Findings: ORC1A is up‑regulated in KRAS‑mutant CRC and induced after KRAS inhibitor treatment.; Combining olaparib with KRAS inhibitors reduces KRAS inhibitor IC50 by ~10‑fold in SLIC14‑63 cells.; Synergy is driven by marked down‑regulation of MCL1 via GSK3β‑mediated proteasomal degradation.; MCL1 knockdown or pharmacologic inhibition phenocopies ORC1A inhibition, confirming MCL1 as functional driver.; Dual inhibition leads to robust tumor regression in KRAS G12C CRC PDX models without overt toxicity.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Zhaoqing Liu
metadata.talk_title: Targeting ORC1A to sensitize KRAS‑mutant colorectal cancer to KRAS inhibitors

text: The Kinase Library: a motif‑based platform to infer kinase activity from phosphoproteomics | Speaker: Tom Yaron‑Barrier | MOA: The Kinase Library uses combinatorial peptide motifs to define kinase substrate specificity across the human kinome; by scoring phosphosite sequences from quantitative phosphoproteomics, it infers kinase activity changes in any perturbation, enabling mechanistic insights and biomarker discovery without prior interaction data. | Findings: Motif‑based scoring accurately identified BRAF/ERK activity dynamics after BRAF inhibitor treatment in melanoma cells.; DNA‑damage kinases (ATM/ATR) were temporally resolved after UV exposure, matching known kinetics.; The platform can predict upstream kinases for >95% of phosphosites, vastly expanding annotation beyond PhosphoSitePlus.; Open‑source Python package and web interface released for community use.

metadata.speaker: Tom Yaron‑Barrier
metadata.talk_title: The Kinase Library: a motif‑based platform to infer kinase activity from phosphoproteomics

text: CHRNA3‑B4 targeted CAR‑T cells for neuroblastoma and neuroendocrine tumors | Speaker: Patrick Sauer | Tumors: neuroblastoma, retinoblastoma, small cell lung cancer | MOA: DISCO binders recognize the heteropentameric CHRNA3‑CHRNB4 complex on neuroblastoma cells; engineered second‑generation CD28‑CAR T cells bearing these binders selectively activate and kill double‑positive tumor cells, leading to tumor regression and survival benefit in neuroblastoma and retinoblastoma models. | Findings: ImmunoTar pipeline identified CHRNA3/B4 as a neuroblastoma‑specific surface complex.; DISCO binders specifically bind cells co‑expressing CHRNA3 and CHRNB4, not single‑positive or negative cells.; DISCO CAR T cells mediate potent in‑vitro killing of CHRNA3/B4‑positive neuroblastoma lines.; Single and double‑dose DISCO CAR T treatment induced tumor regression and prolonged survival in neuroblastoma PDX models.; Intravitreal DISCO CAR T delivery eradicated retinoblastoma tumors in mice, preserving ocular integrity.

metadata.speaker: Patrick Sauer
metadata.talk_title: CHRNA3‑B4 targeted CAR‑T cells for neuroblastoma and neuroendocrine tumors

text: REST‑driven Notch activation confers chemoresistance and immunotherapy sensitivity in small‑cell lung cancer | Speaker: Jackson Fatheree | Tumors: small cell lung cancer | MOA: REST overexpression suppresses neuroendocrine differentiation, activates Notch signaling, and up‑regulates MHC‑I antigen presentation, leading to chemoresistance but heightened sensitivity to PD‑1 blockade via increased CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration. | Findings: CRISPRa screen identified REST as a top chemoresistance hit in SCLC PDX.; REST overexpression in PDX abrogates cisplatin/topotecan‑induced tumor regression.; REST drives Notch activation (↑ NICD1/3, Hes1) which mediates resistance; gamma‑secretase inhibition restores chemosensitivity.; REST‑high tumors display increased MHC‑I, CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration, and respond to anti‑PD‑1 therapy.; Single‑cell analysis revealed a REST‑associated tumor cell cluster enriched for Notch signaling and CX3CL1 expression.

metadata.speaker: Jackson Fatheree
metadata.talk_title: REST‑driven Notch activation confers chemoresistance and immunotherapy sensitivity in small‑cell lung cancer

text: Age‑associated ferroptosis vulnerability in melanoma via WNT5A‑driven phenotype switching | Speaker: Marilo Ramos Recha | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: Aged dermal fibroblasts secrete factors that induce melanoma phenotype switching (↓MITF, ↑WNT5A), leading to down‑regulation of GPX4 and other ferroptosis defenses; this creates a lipid‑peroxidation‑rich environment that renders aged melanoma cells hypersensitive to ferroptosis inducers such as IKE or RSL3. | Findings: Aged skin fibroblast conditioned media sensitizes melanoma cells to GPX4 inhibition.; WNT5A expression inversely correlates with MITF and directly with GPX4 down‑regulation.; Aged mice (24 mo) exhibit higher tumor lipid peroxidation and respond to IKE with tumor growth suppression.; Lipid‑peroxidation inhibitor rescues IKE efficacy, confirming ferroptosis as the mechanism.; WNT5A spatially co‑localizes with 4‑HNE in both mouse and human melanoma samples.

metadata.speaker: Marilo Ramos Recha
metadata.talk_title: Age‑associated ferroptosis vulnerability in melanoma via WNT5A‑driven phenotype switching

text: Theranostics and Precision Imaging for Prostate Cancer | Speaker: Martin Pomper | Tumors: prostate cancer, pancreatic cancer | MOA: Pomper described small-molecule PSMA-targeted radioligands labeled with fluorine-18 for PET imaging and with beta or alpha-emitting radionuclides for therapy; internalization of the ligand provides prolonged tumor residence and DNA damage via emitted particles, enabling both precise diagnosis and targeted radiotherapy. | Findings: Fluorine-18 labeled PSMA small molecule provides high-contrast PET images of tiny prostate lesions, including bone marrow metastases.; PSMA-617 radioligand therapy yields PSA 50% declines superior to cabazitaxel with milder side effects.; Alpha-emitting astatine-labeled PSMA agents enable intracellular targeting and potential precision dosimetry.; FAP-targeted radiopharmaceutical detected pancreatic cancer lesions missed by CT/MR, suggesting utility for hard-to-image tumors.

metadata.speaker: Martin Pomper
metadata.talk_title: Theranostics and Precision Imaging for Prostate Cancer

text: The Revolution of Antibody Drug Conjugates From Early Concept to Next Generation | Speaker: Raffaele Colombo | Tumors: breast cancer, ovarian cancer, colorectal cancer, pancreatic cancer | MOA: Colombo presented next‑generation ADCs that balance payload potency, linker stability, and antibody affinity; examples include a moderate‑potency Top1 payload conjugated to a high‑internalizing FRα antibody (ZW291) and a pan‑RAS inhibitor payload designed for ADC delivery, achieving tumor‑specific drug exposure and bystander killing while minimizing normal‑tissue toxicity. | Findings: ZW291 achieved >50% ORR in FRα‑positive patients despite using a non‑maximally potent Top1 payload.; Dual‑binding (avidity) approach enabled selective killing of cells with >10,000 receptors/cell, improving therapeutic window.; Pan‑RAS ADC showed tumor regression at 1 mg/kg in CDX models with sustained target inhibition for 14 days, while sparing normal tissue.; Linker stability critically influences ADC PK: moderate‑stable linkers can still yield long half‑life (e.g., T‑DXd), whereas unstable linkers produce rapid payload release (e.g., sacituzumab govitecan).; Bispecific ADCs (e.g., EGFR/HER3) demonstrate activity independent of single‑target expression, suggesting broader applicability.

metadata.speaker: Raffaele Colombo
metadata.talk_title: The Revolution of Antibody Drug Conjugates From Early Concept to Next Generation

text: Protein Engineering Driving T‑Cell Engager Innovation | Speaker: Angela Coxon | Tumors: small cell lung cancer, prostate cancer, pancreatic cancer, colorectal cancer, gastric cancer | MOA: Coxon described engineered bispecific T‑cell engagers that bind CD3 and tumor antigens (DLL3, STIP1, CDH3/Mesothelin) with a silent Fc for half‑life extension; avidity‑based dual binding (zalyuritamic) and logic‑gated dual‑targeting (AMG 305) improve selectivity and therapeutic window, while combination with PD‑L1 blockade or IL‑2 muteins aims to overcome the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. | Findings: Talatamab achieved median OS 13.6 mo vs 8.3 mo chemotherapy in SCLC (Phase 3).; Frontline talatamab + atezolizumab increased median OS to 25.3 mo, maintaining manageable safety.; Zalyuritamic’s bivalent STIP1 binding yields activity only on cells with >10 k receptors/cell, sparing normal tissue.; AMG 305 shows potent killing of CDH3/mesothelin double‑positive cells with minimal toxicity in preclinical models.

metadata.speaker: Angela Coxon
metadata.talk_title: Protein Engineering Driving T‑Cell Engager Innovation

text: TIL Therapy of Solid Cancers: Features and Clinical Activity | Speaker: John Hannan | Tumors: melanoma, endometrial cancer, penile cancer | MOA: Hannan detailed autologous tumor‑infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy: surgical tumor harvest, ex‑vivo expansion with high‑dose IL‑2, lymphodepleting chemotherapy, and reinfusion; single‑cell and TCR dropout analyses identified CD25‑high, tumor‑reactive CD8 “Goldilocks” cells as key predictors of clinical response. | Findings: TIL therapy improved PFS and ORR versus ipilimumab in PD‑1‑refractory melanoma (HR significant).; Responders harbored abundant CD25+ tumor‑reactive CD8 TILs with IL‑2/STAT5 signaling signatures.; Dropout screens revealed responders recognized more neoantigens and tumor‑associated antigens, while non‑responders showed viral antigen bystander activity.; In real‑world data (n≈100), anti‑PD‑1 pretreated patients achieved 45% ORR, comparable to trial results; prior ipilimumab+nivolumab patients had lower ORR (30%).

metadata.speaker: John Hannan
metadata.talk_title: TIL Therapy of Solid Cancers: Features and Clinical Activity
