metadata.talk_title: Dual Vbeta6/Vbeta10 T‑cell agonist IPN‑1203

text: Safety and efficacy of elacrasib (D-3S001) in KRAS G12C mutant NSCLC | Speaker: Byung Chul Cho | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: Elacrasib is a CNS‑penetrant, GDP‑bound KRAS G12C covalent inhibitor that achieves sustained target engagement, depleting active KRAS even under growth‑factor stimulation, leading to tumor shrinkage and durable responses in both G12C‑inhibitor‑naïve and refractory NSCLC. | Findings: Elacrasib achieved an overall ORR of 58.8% in KRAS G12C NSCLC (phase I/II).; In G12C‑inhibitor‑naïve patients, ORR was 53.6% with a median PFS of 9.4 months.; In G12C‑inhibitor‑refractory patients, ORR was 32.3% with a median PFS of 8.1 months.; Patients with KRAS amplification (n=5) showed an ORR of 60%.; Rapid and deep ctDNA KRAS G12C allele fraction clearance correlated with radiologic response.

metadata.speaker: Byung Chul Cho
metadata.talk_title: Safety and efficacy of elacrasib (D-3S001) in KRAS G12C mutant NSCLC

text: Contextualizing KRAS G12C inhibitor landscape and future directions | Speaker: Sacher | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: The speaker reviewed the mechanisms of KRAS G12C off‑inhibitors (covalent binding to GDP‑bound KRAS) and emerging on‑state tri‑complex inhibitors, discussing potency, resistance mechanisms, and toxicity profiles. | Findings: Sotorasib demonstrated a 28.1% ORR in CodeBreaK‑200 but did not improve OS.; Divorasib showed a 53.4% ORR and median PFS of 13.1 months in early‑phase data.; Autoimmune hepatitis is a class‑specific toxicity, especially after prior PD‑1 therapy.

metadata.speaker: Sacher
metadata.talk_title: Contextualizing KRAS G12C inhibitor landscape and future directions

text: Preliminary safety and activity of zoldonrasib (RMC‑9805) in KRAS G12D NSCLC | Speaker: Jonathan Rees | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: Zoldonrasib is an oral mutant‑selective covalent inhibitor that forms a cyclophilin A‑mediated tri‑complex with the GTP‑bound KRAS G12D, sterically blocking RAF binding and shutting down downstream MAPK signaling, leading to tumor regressions. | Findings: Confirmed ORR of 52% in KRAS G12D NSCLC patients previously treated with IO and platinum.; Disease control rate reached 93% with median time to response of 1.4 months.; Median PFS was 11.1 months; 12‑month OS rate 73% with median follow‑up 13.1 months.; High ctDNA clearance: 87% >50% reduction, 73% complete clearance.

metadata.speaker: Jonathan Rees
metadata.talk_title: Preliminary safety and activity of zoldonrasib (RMC‑9805) in KRAS G12D NSCLC

text: Discussion of KRAS G12C and G12D inhibitor landscape | Speaker: Daniel Tan | Tumors: NSCLC, colorectal cancer, pancreatic cancer | MOA: The discussant highlighted molecular heterogeneity of KRAS G12D across tumor types, the impact of co‑mutations and smoking status on immunogenicity, and the rationale for combining KRAS G12D inhibitors with immunotherapy or other targeted agents. | Findings: KRAS G12D NSCLC is enriched in never‑smokers and shows lower PD‑L1 expression.; Co‑mutations (STK11, KEAP1) may influence response to KRAS inhibitors.; Preclinical models suggest KRAS G12D inhibition can increase T‑cell infiltration and synergize with checkpoint blockade.

metadata.speaker: Daniel Tan
metadata.talk_title: Discussion of KRAS G12C and G12D inhibitor landscape

text: Phase I trial of WEE1 inhibitor zetaracib + PKMYT1 inhibitor lonresorib in CCNE1/FBXW7/PPP2R1A altered tumors | Speaker: Timothy Yap | Tumors: ovarian cancer, colorectal cancer, pancreas, breast, esophageal, others | MOA: Zetaracib inhibits WEE1, preventing CDK1 Y15 phosphorylation, while lonresorib blocks PKMYT1‑mediated CDK1 T14 phosphorylation; concurrent loss of both checkpoints forces replication‑stressed tumor cells into premature mitosis, causing mitotic catastrophe. | Findings: Overall response rate of 37.5% in heavily pre‑treated ovarian cancer, rising to 50% at RP2D.; Disease control rate of 68.5% across all tumor types.; High ctDNA molecular response (47% overall, 67% in ovarian cohort).; Combination was well tolerated with mainly grade 1‑2 nausea, fatigue, anemia.

metadata.speaker: Timothy Yap
metadata.talk_title: Phase I trial of WEE1 inhibitor zetaracib + PKMYT1 inhibitor lonresorib in CCNE1/FBXW7/PPP2R1A altered tumors

text: Discussion of synthetic lethal and replication stress strategies | Speaker: Kathleen Moore | MOA: The discussant contextualized the WEE1/PKMYT1 combination within broader synthetic lethal approaches targeting replication stress, emphasizing biomarker challenges and the need for tolerable regimens. | Findings: Emphasized importance of RB loss detection (IHC) for cyclin AB inhibitor selection.; Highlighted that low‑grade toxicities may be more clinically relevant than grade 3/4 events.

metadata.speaker: Kathleen Moore
metadata.talk_title: Discussion of synthetic lethal and replication stress strategies

text: Phase I evaluation of CID‑078, a cyclin A/B RxL inhibitor, in advanced solid tumors | Speaker: Afshin Delati | MOA: CID‑078 is a macrocyclic oral agent that binds the RxL motif on cyclin A and B, blocking cyclin‑E2F and cyclin‑MYT1 interactions, causing unchecked CDK activity, DNA damage accumulation, spindle checkpoint activation and mitotic catastrophe in RB‑deficient tumors. | Findings: Linear PK from 40‑960 mg BID with ~3 h half‑life and no accumulation.; Grade 3 ALT elevations were rare (2 patients) and reversible.; Confirmed tumor responses observed in RB‑loss osteosarcoma and neuroendocrine tumor.

metadata.speaker: Afshin Delati
metadata.talk_title: Phase I evaluation of CID‑078, a cyclin A/B RxL inhibitor, in advanced solid tumors

text: Cyclin AB inhibition: the next mile in cell cycle therapy | Speaker: Allyson Schram | MOA: The discussant reviewed the mechanistic rationale for targeting the cyclin A/B RxL interface, emphasizing synthetic lethality in RB‑deficient, E2F‑high tumors and the need for biomarker‑driven patient selection. | Findings: CID‑078 blocks cyclin‑A/E2F and cyclin‑B/MYT1 interactions, leading to mitotic catastrophe.; RB loss can be detected by IHC, offering a practical selection method.

metadata.speaker: Allyson Schram
metadata.talk_title: Cyclin AB inhibition: the next mile in cell cycle therapy

text: Neural representation learning for pan‑cancer HRD prediction and platinum response | Speaker: Jason Pitt | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Pitt presented HR‑Difuse, a multi‑view neural representation learning framework that encodes SBS, indel, SV, and copy‑number features from whole‑genome sequencing, fuses them via self‑attention, and uses contrastive learning to predict homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) and platinum response, outperforming HRDetect and random‑forest‑based Cord across pan‑cancer cohorts. | Findings: HR‑Difuse achieved higher AUROC and AUPRC than HRDetect and Cord for HRD prediction in TCGA and PEACOG datasets.; The model retained predictive power for somatic HRD events lacking high microhomology‑mediated deletions, where existing tools performed poorly.; Transfer‑learning fine‑tuning of the HRD model on platinum‑response labels yielded an F1 score of ~0.75, surpassing baseline HR‑Difuse and other classifiers.; Contrastive learning of latent encodings improved cross‑view feature integration compared with pure NMF‑based signatures.

metadata.speaker: Jason Pitt
metadata.talk_title: Neural representation learning for pan‑cancer HRD prediction and platinum response

text: Dimensional structural chromosome instability and the JAVEL mass‑balance method | Speaker: Marcin Imielinski | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Imielinski described JAVEL, a mass‑balance‑principle algorithm that jointly infers copy‑number segments and rearrangement junctions from whole‑genome sequencing, leveraging stoichiometric constraints to produce coherent structural chromosome instability profiles across cancer types. | Findings: JAVEL integrates copy‑number and structural‑variant data into a unified representation based on segment neighbor balance.; The method enables detection of complex events such as chromothripsis, chromoplexy, and retrotransposition with improved resolution over separate CNV or SV callers.; Application to TCGA whole‑genome data reveals pervasive multi‑scale chromosomal instability signatures across tumor types.

metadata.speaker: Marcin Imielinski
metadata.talk_title: Dimensional structural chromosome instability and the JAVEL mass‑balance method

text: Graph-based genome analysis reveals structural chromosomal instability patterns | Speaker: Martin | Tumors: glioblastoma, acral melanoma, breast cancer, prostate cancer, colorectal cancer, pan-cancer | MOA: The presenter introduced JAVEL, a graph‑based copy‑number and breakpoint detection tool, and demonstrated how genome graphs can be mined for structural chromosomal instability (SIN) patterns such as chromoplexy, chromothripsis, ecDNA, BFB cycles and a novel class called Typhonis. Specific graph motifs correlate with DNA repair deficiencies (e.g., BRCA1 loss) and with oncogene amplification contexts (e.g., HER2 HSR vs ecDNA). | Findings: JAVEL outperforms prior methods in breakpoint precision and recall on TCGA genomes.; Identified a new structural scar highly specific for BRCA1 deficiency, present in >90% of BRCA1‑deficient tumors and rare elsewhere.; Discovered Typhonis, a distinct HSR amplification pattern affecting ~3% of cancers and enriched for MYC, CCND1, ERBB2 amplifications.; Found that glioblastoma is dominated by ecDNA amplifications of EGFR/PDGFRA, whereas most other cancers show HSR‑type amplifications.; HSR HER2 amplifications predict lower likelihood of resistance to HER2‑targeted ADCs compared with ecDNA‑based HER2 amplifications.

metadata.speaker: Martin
metadata.talk_title: Graph-based genome analysis reveals structural chromosomal instability patterns

text: Comprehensive analysis of >8,000 TCGA whole‑genome sequences reveals new coding, non‑coding and structural drivers | Speaker: Gadi | Tumors: skin melanoma, lung adenocarcinoma, lung squamous cell carcinoma, colorectal cancer, breast cancer, prostate cancer, ovarian cancer, sarcoma, glioblastoma, kidney cancer, liver cancer, head and neck cancer, pan-cancer | MOA: Using dual cloud pipelines, the team generated a high‑quality variant call set from >8,000 TCGA whole‑genome samples, uncovering sequencing artifacts (vapor‑trail T>G/A>C), correcting coverage gaps, and identifying novel coding and non‑coding driver mutations, structural variation drivers, and HRD signatures across cancer types. | Findings: Identified a novel NovaSeq‑specific sequencing artifact (T>G/A>C “vapor trail”) and created a filter that removed up to 15% of false SNVs in affected tumor types.; PCR‑free whole‑genome data recovered >90% of missed TERT promoter mutations and uncovered new hotspots in GC‑rich regions of VHL, ARID1A and other tumor suppressors.; Detected 200 million SNVs, 1.7 million DNVs, 56 million indels and 1.3 million SVs across the cohort.; Discovered new non‑coding drivers (e.g., recurrent promoter indels in albumin, surfactant genes, P63, GATA3, XBP1, ESR1 regulatory region amplifications).; SVelfi analysis revealed known SV drivers (TMPRSS2‑ERG) and novel recurrent SVs such as SLC30A4 translocations driving ETV1 overexpression in prostate cancer.

metadata.speaker: Gadi
metadata.talk_title: Comprehensive analysis of >8,000 TCGA whole‑genome sequences reveals new coding, non‑coding and structural drivers

text: Spatial metabolomics of pancreas and breast cancer reveals cell-type specific lipid and nutrient utilization | Speaker: Josh Rabinowitz | Tumors: breast cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Using MALDI imaging mass spectrometry, Rabinowitz mapped lipid species that demarcate epithelial cancer cells versus fibroblasts and immune cells, and showed spatial depletion of glucose and enrichment of ATP/ADP in cancer and immune compartments, highlighting metabolic heterogeneity and suggesting ketogenic diet–induced glucose restriction could stress tumor cells while supporting T cell ketone utilization. | Findings: Distinct phosphatidylethanolamine lipids (PE 18:1/18:1 vs PE with saturated/omega‑6 tail) specifically mark breast cancer epithelium versus fibroblasts.; Glucose is depleted and ATP/ADP is enriched in cancer cells and immune infiltrates across breast and pancreatic tumors.; Lactate tracing in mouse tumors shows universal lactate utilization across tumor cell types, contradicting prior reports of Treg‑specific lactate use.; CD8+ T cells preferentially utilize 3‑hydroxybutyrate, suggesting ketogenic diet may boost antitumor immunity.; A small phase I/II trial of a supervised ketogenic diet combined with standard chemotherapy in metastatic pancreatic cancer showed ~3‑month improvement in progression‑free and overall survival.

metadata.speaker: Josh Rabinowitz
metadata.talk_title: Spatial metabolomics of pancreas and breast cancer reveals cell-type specific lipid and nutrient utilization

text: Mitochondrial NADK2 supports proline synthesis, protein lipoylation, and mitochondrial translation | Speaker: Gerta Hoxha | Tumors: lung cancer | MOA: NADK2 generates mitochondrial NADPH, which fuels proline biosynthesis and mitochondrial fatty‑acid synthesis; the latter supplies acyl‑carrier protein lipoylation required for PDH and other dehydrogenase complexes, supporting TCA flux, oxidative phosphorylation, and mitochondrial translation, thereby promoting tumor cell proliferation. | Findings: NADK2 loss impairs lung cancer cell proliferation in vitro and tumor growth in vivo.; Supplementation with non‑essential amino acids, especially proline, fully rescues proliferation of NADK2‑deficient cells.; NADK2 knockout abolishes de novo proline synthesis, linking mitochondrial NADPH to proline biosynthesis.; Mitochondrial NADK2 is required for protein lipoylation of PDH, OGDH, GCS, and BCKDH complexes; kinase‑dead NADK2 fails to restore lipoylation.; Restoring mitochondrial NADPH via cytosolic NADK targeted to mitochondria rescues lipoylation, TCA cycle intermediates, and oxidative respiration.

metadata.speaker: Gerta Hoxha
metadata.talk_title: Mitochondrial NADK2 supports proline synthesis, protein lipoylation, and mitochondrial translation

text: Methodological advances reveal tissue‑specific nutrient environments and folate‑limited nucleotide metabolism in cancer | Speaker: Matt Vander Heiden | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia | MOA: Vander Heiden’s group quantified tissue‑specific nutrient milieus, revealing that folate scarcity in plasma‑like media limits de novo nucleotide synthesis in B‑ALL, making cells dependent on salvage; dietary folate titration directly modulates leukemia growth, linking systemic nutrient availability to replication stress and tumor progression. | Findings: Each mouse tissue exhibits a distinct nutrient composition; blood differs markedly from standard culture media.; Bone‑marrow plasma from ALL patients and mice is low in folates (~30 nM), limiting de novo nucleotide synthesis.; B‑ALL cells grown in mouse plasma‑like media become dependent on nucleotide salvage; removal of exogenous nucleotides impairs growth.; Folates are the primary driver of this phenotype; raising folate levels to physiological (~30 nM) restores proliferation even without salvage.; In vivo folate manipulation in mice alters B‑ALL tumor burden, confirming folate limitation as a growth constraint.

metadata.speaker: Matt Vander Heiden
metadata.talk_title: Methodological advances reveal tissue‑specific nutrient environments and folate‑limited nucleotide metabolism in cancer

text: Extracellular Vesicles and Particles, Their Biogenesis and Function | Speaker: Ghislaine | Tumors: melanoma, breast cancer, renal cell carcinoma | MOA: AF6 activation drives the formation of tumor microvesicles (TMVs) by recruiting Exportin‑5, pre‑microRNAs and MT1‑MMP to actin‑myosin contractile sites via a VAMP3‑CD9 complex, resulting in protease‑laden vesicles that promote matrix degradation, invasion and intercellular transfer of oncogenic RNAs and DNA. | Findings: AF6‑activated tumor cells shed large microvesicles (TMVs) enriched for AF6, VAMP3, CD9 and MT1‑MMP.; TMVs display proteolytic activity on gelatin matrices and promote endothelial tube formation with distinct phenotypes (elongated vs sprouting) depending on tumor origin.; AF6 activation increases pre‑microRNA loading into TMVs via an Exportin‑5‑GRP1 scaffold that preferentially binds GTP‑AF6.; Knockdown of GRP1 reduces pre‑microRNA content in TMVs, demonstrating its scaffolding role.; TMV‑delivered miR‑21 suppresses SMAD7 in recipient fibroblasts; this effect is reversed by miR‑21 or GRP1 knockdown.

metadata.speaker: Ghislaine
metadata.talk_title: Extracellular Vesicles and Particles, Their Biogenesis and Function

text: Biology and Translation of Large Oncosomes as Cancer Biomarkers | Speaker: Dolores Di Visio | Tumors: prostate cancer, breast cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, pancreatic cancer, melanoma | MOA: Large oncosomes released by highly aggressive cancer cells carry abundant mitochondrial RNA/proteins, kinases and DNA, which upon uptake by bone‑marrow stromal cells trigger interferon‑driven inflammatory programs, neutrophil recruitment and myeloid‑derived suppressor cell expansion, thereby fostering metastatic niche formation via STING‑dependent signaling. | Findings: Mice injected with large oncosomes after primary tumor resection develop significantly more bone metastases than those receiving small EVs.; Large oncosomes induce a strong interferon‑stimulated gene signature in bone‑marrow MSCs, driving neutrophil chemotaxis and MDSC‑like polarization (arginase‑1, IL‑10 up‑regulation).; STING inhibition abolishes large‑oncosome‑mediated NF‑κB/IFN reporter activation and blocks induction of IRF3/7 in vivo.; Large oncosomes are enriched for mitochondrial transcripts and proteins; this signature is conserved across cancer types and patient plasma.; Proteomic profiling identified a set of bona‑fide large‑oncosome surface markers (e.g., VDAC1, RP2) enabling magnetic‑bead capture from plasma.

metadata.speaker: Dolores Di Visio
metadata.talk_title: Biology and Translation of Large Oncosomes as Cancer Biomarkers

text: Activated T‑Cell Extracellular Vesicles Deliver DNA to Reprogram Immunity and Tumors | Speaker: Dr. Unknown | Tumors: pancreatic cancer, glioblastoma, triple‑negative breast cancer | MOA: Activated T‑cell extracellular vesicles (ATEVs) are enriched for extracellular DNA and granzyme B; LFA‑1 mediates their uptake by lymph‑node dendritic cells and tumor cells, where DNA reaches the nucleus, triggers antigen‑presentation gene transcription, and reprograms the tumor microenvironment toward an immune‑active state, synergizing with anti‑PD‑1 therapy to suppress tumor growth. | Findings: Activated T‑cell EVs contain ~80 % surface DNA and 20 % lumen DNA, markedly higher than non‑activated EVs.; LFA‑1 on ATEVs drives preferential uptake by dendritic cells in lymph nodes and by tumor cells in pancreatic and GBM models.; DNA‑depleted ATEVs (DNase‑treated) fail to induce antigen‑presentation gene signatures in recipient lymph‑node cells.; Single‑cell RNA‑seq shows up‑regulation of MHC‑I/II, TAP1/2 and other antigen‑processing genes only after DNA‑competent ATEV exposure.; Combination of ATEVs with anti‑PD‑1 completely arrests tumor growth in KPC pancreatic and GBM mouse models for >30 days, whereas either agent alone is less effective.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Unknown
metadata.talk_title: Activated T‑Cell Extracellular Vesicles Deliver DNA to Reprogram Immunity and Tumors

text: Integrin αvβ6-targeted theranostic peptide and lutetium therapy in pancreatic and other cancers | Speaker: Julie Sutcliffe | Tumors: pancreatic cancer, breast cancer, colon cancer, lung cancer, ovarian carcinoma, neuroblastoma | MOA: The αvβ6‑targeting peptide (A20FMDV2) is radiolabeled with F‑18 for PET imaging and later re‑engineered with a DOTA chelator and albumin‑binding moiety to create a Ga‑68 diagnostic and Lu‑177 therapeutic pair that binds with nanomolar affinity, is rapidly internalized, and delivers tumor‑specific radiation while being cleared renally. | Findings: Developed a first‑in‑human αvβ6 theranostic pair (Ga‑68 diagnostic / Lu‑177 therapeutic) after a decade of peptide optimization.; Phase I dose escalation reached 200 mCi with no dose‑limiting toxicities and acceptable renal clearance.; Imaging detected lesions missed by standard FDG‑PET, including small brain metastases, demonstrating high tumor‑to‑background contrast.; A single Lu‑177 dose produced a 40% SUV reduction and CA19‑9 decline in a heavily pre‑treated pancreatic cancer patient without tumor growth over 90 days.; The agent showed consistent tumor retention over days on SPECT, delivering 15–40 Gy per lesion at the top dose.

metadata.speaker: Julie Sutcliffe
metadata.talk_title: Integrin αvβ6-targeted theranostic peptide and lutetium therapy in pancreatic and other cancers

text: DLL3-targeted radiopharmaceuticals: antibodies, imaging, and therapeutic opportunities | Speaker: Jason Lewis | Tumors: small cell lung cancer, neuroendocrine prostate cancer, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, neuroblastoma | MOA: A high‑affinity anti‑DLL3 antibody (SC16) is labeled with Zr‑89 for PET imaging and Lu‑177 for therapy; the antibody binds low‑abundance DLL3 with high tumor‑to‑normal contrast, is internalized, and delivers β‑radiation to DLL3‑expressing neuroendocrine lesions, enabling both lesion detection and tumor control. | Findings: DLL3 PET imaging identified neuroendocrine prostate cancer lesions missed by PSMA or FDG PET.; Preclinical actinium‑225 DLL3 peptide showed dose‑dependent tumor regression in DLL3‑positive xenografts.; Antibody‑based DLL3 imaging demonstrated high specificity with minimal off‑target liver uptake when co‑administered with cold antibody to block Fc sinks.; DLL3 expression is homogeneous across tumor cells in neuroendocrine cancers, making it an attractive homogeneous target.

metadata.speaker: Jason Lewis
metadata.talk_title: DLL3-targeted radiopharmaceuticals: antibodies, imaging, and therapeutic opportunities

text: Next‑generation radioligand therapy: target selection, isotope engineering, and combination strategies | Speaker: Marcus (Novartis) | Tumors: non‑small cell lung cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, breast cancer, neuroendocrine tumors, multiple solid tumors | MOA: Novartis is engineering radioligands by pairing novel targets (e.g., FAP, DLL3) with optimized isotopes (Lu‑177, Ac‑225, Y‑90) and high‑affinity vectors (antibodies, macrocyclic peptides) to exploit cross‑fire effects, improve tumor homogeneity, and enable combination with DNA‑damage response inhibitors or immunotherapy. | Findings: Demonstrated homogeneous FAP expression in PDAC and breast cancer models, enabling cross‑fire radiation from Lu‑177‑labeled FXX‑489.; Actinium‑225 DLL3 peptide (ETN‑029) regressed DLL3‑positive SHP77 xenografts in a dose‑dependent manner.; Preclinical data show that DNA‑PK inhibition synergizes with Lu‑177‑based radioligands across multiple tumor types.; Cross‑fire from β‑emitters can overcome intra‑tumoral heterogeneity, while α‑emitters provide high‑potency for radiosensitive lesions.

metadata.speaker: Marcus (Novartis)
metadata.talk_title: Next‑generation radioligand therapy: target selection, isotope engineering, and combination strategies

text: NK cell heterogeneity, NKG2A blockade and NK cell engager therapeutics | Speaker: Eric | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer, acute myeloid leukemia, multiple myeloma, pancreatic cancer, ovarian cancer | MOA: The presenter defined three conserved NK cell subsets (NK1, NK2, NK3) across species, identified tumor‑associated NK3 cells (CD39+, NKG2A+, CD103+) in NSCLC that correlate with better survival, showed that anti‑NKG2A antibody (Monalizumab) can unleash their activity, and described tri‑ and tetra‑specific NK cell engagers that combine tumor antigen binding, NKp46 activation, and cytokine payloads (IL‑2 or IFN‑α) to enhance NK cytotoxicity in preclinical AML, MM, and solid tumor models. | Findings: NK3 subset expands in NSCLC tumors and its high frequency predicts improved overall survival and better response to anti‑PD‑1 therapy.; Monalizumab (anti‑NKG2A) increases granzyme A/B expression in autologous tumor fragments, indicating functional rescue of exhausted NK cells.; Tri‑specific NK cell engagers targeting CD123 (AML) and BCMA (MM) achieved complete remissions in early‑phase AML patients, earning FDA fast‑track designation.; Tetra‑specific engagers incorporating IL‑2 or IFN‑α showed superior tumor control in MC38‑hCD20 and Raji xenograft models compared with bispecific formats.; IL‑2‑armed NK engagers induced proliferation of memory‑like NK cells in vitro, generating a CD39‑positive, cytokine‑induced memory phenotype.

metadata.speaker: Eric
metadata.talk_title: NK cell heterogeneity, NKG2A blockade and NK cell engager therapeutics

text: Memory‑like NK cell adoptive therapy in AML and solid tumors | Speaker: Rizwan Homi | Tumors: acute myeloid leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, head and neck cancer, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, mesothelioma | MOA: Memory‑like NK cells are generated by overnight activation with IL‑12, IL‑15, and IL‑18, acquiring enhanced IFN‑γ production and prolonged in vivo persistence; when infused post‑transplant or after lymphodepletion, they mediate anti‑leukemic activity and, when engineered with CARs (e.g., mesothelin, CD70) and TGF‑β‑responsive IL‑12/IL‑18 payloads, they overcome tumor‑derived suppression and achieve tumor regression in solid tumor mouse models. | Findings: Memory‑like NK cells persisted up to 200 days in some post‑transplant AML patients, far exceeding the typical 10‑12 day lifespan of conventional NK cells.; Four of eight AML patients achieved MRD‑negative complete remission after a single infusion of memory‑like NK cells.; In heavily pre‑treated head and neck cancer patients, 7 of 10 achieved disease control, including one dramatic partial response lasting ~12 months.; CAR‑NK cells armed with a TGF‑β‑responsive IL‑12/IL‑18 circuit cured >90% of mice in aggressive pancreatic and kidney cancer models without systemic toxicity.; Combining engineered tumor‑targeting bacteria expressing IL‑12 and adenosine deaminase with CAR‑NK cells doubled survival in pancreatic cancer mouse models.

metadata.speaker: Rizwan Homi
metadata.talk_title: Memory‑like NK cell adoptive therapy in AML and solid tumors

text: Logic‑gate engineered allogeneic NK cells for AML | Speaker: Tim Lu | Tumors: acute myeloid leukemia | MOA: SENTI‑202 uses allogeneic NK cells engineered with dual activating CARs targeting CD33 and FLT3 to kill AML blasts and leukemic stem cells, combined with an inhibitory CAR against endomucin (EMCN) to protect healthy hematopoietic stem cells, and an IL‑15 transgene to enhance NK persistence, resulting in MRD‑negative remissions with minimal off‑target toxicity. | Findings: Overall response rate of ~50% in heavily pre‑treated relapsed/refractory AML patients.; CR/CRh achieved in 30‑40% of patients with median CR duration of 7.6 months.; High MRD‑negative conversion rates observed across responders.; NK‑cell related adverse events were limited to Grade 1‑2 pyrexia; cytokine release syndrome was minimal compared with CAR‑T therapies.; Platelet and neutrophil counts recovered rapidly after lymphodepletion, indicating limited bone‑marrow toxicity.

metadata.speaker: Tim Lu
metadata.talk_title: Logic‑gate engineered allogeneic NK cells for AML

text: Biomarker‑based non‑endoscopic detection and surveillance of Barrett's esophagus | Speaker: Sandy Markowitz | Tumors: esophageal adenocarcinoma | MOA: EsaCheck uses a swallowable textured balloon to collect distal esophageal cells, while EsaGuard detects methylated VIM and CCNA1 DNA; together they achieve high‑sensitivity non‑endoscopic Barrett's detection. The BAD algorithm combines aneuploidy with six driver chromosome alterations to identify high‑grade dysplasia or cancer, and methylated CCNA1 serves as a minimal residual disease marker after ablation. | Findings: EsaCheck/EsaGuard achieved 90% sensitivity and 92% specificity for non‑dysplastic Barrett's in a pilot of 120 high‑risk asymptomatic subjects.; In four clinical cohorts, Barrett's detection sensitivity ranged 80‑90% and cancer detection was ~100% (one miss).; BAD Very Bad score detected 96% of cancers and 68% of high‑grade dysplasias while flagging only 7% of non‑dysplastic lesions.; Methylated CCNA1 positivity post‑ablation conferred a 25‑fold increased risk of recurrence (13/27 vs 1/53).; EsaCheck received FDA 510(k) clearance; EsaGuard earned FDA breakthrough device designation and guideline inclusion.

metadata.speaker: Sandy Markowitz
metadata.talk_title: Biomarker‑based non‑endoscopic detection and surveillance of Barrett's esophagus

text: AI foundation models for personalized cancer imaging and adaptive trial design | Speaker: Adam Yala | MOA: Pillar Zero is a vision‑language foundation model pre‑trained on massive DICOM volumes and radiology reports, enabling higher accuracy across hundreds of imaging findings; Mirai demonstrates that image‑only deep learning can outperform traditional risk calculators, and the BRIDGE trial framework reuses overlapping high‑risk patient subsets across successive AI model generations to accelerate adaptive clinical trials. | Findings: Pillar Zero achieves 82‑90% average accuracy across >100 radiology findings, outperforming major commercial vision models.; Image‑only Mirai model surpasses Tyrer‑Cuzick questionnaire for 5‑year breast cancer risk prediction.; CT‑based AI outperforms smoking‑history questionnaires for lung cancer risk.; BRIDGE statistical framework shows >90% overlap of top 5% high‑risk patients across successive AI model versions, enabling adaptive trial reuse.

metadata.speaker: Adam Yala
metadata.talk_title: AI foundation models for personalized cancer imaging and adaptive trial design

text: Germline DAM2 R404W variant promotes glioma tumorigenesis in mouse models | Speaker: Tiffany Choi | Tumors: glioblastoma, glioma | MOA: The germline DAM2 R404W variant enhances glial progenitor proliferation and skews differentiation toward a glial fate, expanding a pro‑tumorigenic niche that promotes glioma growth in vitro and in orthotopic mouse models. | Findings: Overexpression of DAM2 R404W in patient‑derived GBM stem‑like cells increased tumor sphere size relative to wild‑type and GFP controls.; Orthotopic xenografts of R404W‑overexpressing cells showed larger bioluminescent tumor burden and higher Ki‑67 proliferation than controls.; DAM2 R404W knock‑in mice displayed increased Sox9⁺/BrdU⁺ glial progenitors and decreased double‑cortin⁺ neuronal progenitors in the subventricular zone.; In vitro cultured neural stem cells from R404W mice recapitulated the increased glial progenitor phenotype, indicating a cell‑intrinsic effect.; Low‑grade glioma models generated via rCas9‑tVA with PDGF‑β showed higher proliferation (OLIG2⁺) and histologic features of malignant transformation in R404W mice.

metadata.speaker: Tiffany Choi
metadata.talk_title: Germline DAM2 R404W variant promotes glioma tumorigenesis in mouse models

text: Age‑dependent mammary tumorigenesis driven by mutant PIK3CA H1047R in mice | Speaker: Thangaraj Warren Mohan | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Lentiviral delivery of the hotspot PIK3CA H1047R mutation into mammary ducts of aged mice expands basal epithelial cells, accelerates tumor onset, and yields widespread epithelial proliferation, while aged microenvironments increase the proportion of PIK3CA‑positive cells at the basal‑luminal interface, linking age‑associated niche changes to mutant PI3K‑driven tumorigenesis. | Findings: Aged (22 mo) mice injected with lentiviral PIK3CA H1047R develop palpable tumors earlier and with higher incidence than young (2 mo) mice.; Mid‑aged mice show non‑palpable micro‑lesions with high Ki‑67, indicating early oncogenic activation.; Whole‑mount analysis reveals focal lesions in young mice versus diffuse ductal proliferation in aged mice.; Tumor growth rate is slower in aged mice despite earlier onset, mirroring clinical observations of less aggressive tumors in older patients.; ERα expression is higher in tumor‑adjacent glands, suggesting hormonal priming in the aged niche.

metadata.speaker: Thangaraj Warren Mohan
metadata.talk_title: Age‑dependent mammary tumorigenesis driven by mutant PIK3CA H1047R in mice

text: Genotype‑specific PI3K inhibition and CAF‑mediated organoid engraftment in bladder cancer | Speaker: Philip Abosh | Tumors: bladder cancer | MOA: CRISPR‑engineered bladder organoids harboring PIK3CA H1047R are sensitized to alpelisib in vitro; in vivo, engraftment in immunocompetent mice requires co‑injection with cancer‑associated fibroblasts, which secrete IL‑6, while organoids produce GM‑CSF, establishing a cytokine crosstalk that modulates immune suppression and tumor growth. | Findings: PIK3CA H1047R bladder organoids show increased sensitivity to alpelisib and pirtobrutinib (piptilicide) compared with WT organoids in vitro.; Both hotspot and WT organoids are resistant to growth in immunocompetent mice unless co‑implanted with CAFs.; Co‑implantation with CAFs enables tumor formation in flank; alpelisib treatment reduces tumor size and Ki‑67 proliferation in both genotypes.; Co‑culture reveals CAF‑derived IL‑6 and organoid‑derived GM‑CSF; GM‑CSF knockout does not consistently affect tumor formation.

metadata.speaker: Philip Abosh
metadata.talk_title: Genotype‑specific PI3K inhibition and CAF‑mediated organoid engraftment in bladder cancer

text: Multi‑omic patient‑derived organoid platform for predicting NSCLC immunotherapy response | Speaker: Anna Pasto | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer | MOA: Integrated spatial transcriptomics, bulk RNA‑seq of NSCLC organoids, and co‑culture with allogeneic activated immune cells reveal that organoids from clinically non‑responding patients exhibit higher CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration with an exhausted phenotype, despite greater immune cell penetration, linking organoid immune interactions to patient outcomes. | Findings: Organoids recapitulate tumor‑type specific transcriptomic signatures (adenocarcinoma vs squamous) observed in spatial profiling.; Responder patients (no event at 2 yr) show enrichment of inflammatory pathways in organoids, whereas non‑responders do not.; Co‑culture with pre‑activated allogeneic immune cells shows significantly higher CD45⁺ infiltration in non‑responder organoids.; Infiltrating CD8⁺ T cells in non‑responder organoids display an exhausted phenotype (e.g., PD‑1⁺, TIM‑3⁺) both at baseline and after cisplatin exposure.; PD‑L1 CPS and mutation status did not predict organoid responder classification.

metadata.speaker: Anna Pasto
metadata.talk_title: Multi‑omic patient‑derived organoid platform for predicting NSCLC immunotherapy response

text: 3D nanobioreactor imaging of APOBEC3C‑driven splicing alterations in aged human HSPCs | Speaker: Emma Clarkin | MOA: APOBEC3C overexpression in aged human HSPCs induces C‑to‑T editing of splicing regulatory elements, promoting exon skipping as visualized by a GFP‑reporter in a 3D nanobioreactor, thereby linking inflammaging‑driven APOBEC activity to splicing dysregulation and potential pre‑cancerous phenotypes. | Findings: Aged bone marrow CD34⁺ cells transduced with APOBEC3C show a ~10‑fold increase in GFP‑reporter exon‑skipping versus cord blood controls.; RNA‑seq of aged APOBEC3C‑overexpressing HSPCs reveals up‑regulation of spliceosome genes (SRSSFs, SF3Bs) and increased exon‑skipping events.; Live imaging in the nanobioreactor demonstrates migration of transduced HSPCs toward the SurgiFoam niche and a shift from RFP (exon inclusion) to GFP (exon skipping) over 72 h.; FACS analysis confirms a significant increase in GFP⁺ cells in APOBEC3C‑overexpressing samples compared with empty vector.

metadata.speaker: Emma Clarkin
metadata.talk_title: 3D nanobioreactor imaging of APOBEC3C‑driven splicing alterations in aged human HSPCs

text: Ex vivo microtumor platform predicts ADC and combination therapy responses in ovarian cancer | Speaker: Felix Berg | Tumors: ovarian cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: Microtumor fragments retain native tumor architecture and microenvironment, enabling high‑content imaging of drug‑induced cytotoxicity; ADC mirvetuximab soravtansine shows variable efficacy across FRα‑expressing ovarian samples, correlating with paclitaxel sensitivity due to shared microtubule‑targeting mechanisms, and synergizes with olaparib in a subset of patients. | Findings: Ex vivo microtumor responses to carboplatin/paclitaxel correlate with clinical C125 biomarker and predict progression‑free survival.; Mirvetuximab soravtansine efficacy varies widely among 25 ovarian patient samples, matching FRα expression heterogeneity.; ADC response correlates with paclitaxel sensitivity, reflecting shared microtubule inhibition.; Combination of mirvetuximab with olaparib yields synergistic killing in a subset of samples, while others are driven mainly by olaparib alone.; Target antigen profiling reveals intra‑patient FRα heterogeneity, influencing ADC efficacy.

metadata.speaker: Felix Berg
metadata.talk_title: Ex vivo microtumor platform predicts ADC and combination therapy responses in ovarian cancer

text: eLive cytokine profiling defines immune phenotypes and predicts ICI response in fresh tumor fragments | Speaker: Erika Van Aeou | Tumors: multiple solid tumors | MOA: Fresh tumor fragments are sliced, encapsulated in a proprietary gel, and cultured with checkpoint inhibitors; multiplex Luminex cytokine profiling identifies responder versus non‑responder signatures, which cluster into four distinct immune phenotypes (TH1‑inflamed, mixed T‑reg/myeloid, cytotoxic, polyfunctional myeloid‑angiogenic) that predict clinical ICI outcomes. | Findings: A nine‑cytokine eLive index predicts ICI response with 93% accuracy in a validation cohort.; Unsupervised clustering of cytokine responses defines four immune phenotypes, each with distinct cytokine patterns (e.g., IFN‑γ, CXCL9, CCL22, IL‑10, VEGF).; Subcluster 1 (TH1‑inflamed) shows CD8⁺ T‑cell activation (CD69⁺) and immune triads in NSCLC samples.; Subcluster 3 (cytotoxic) displays granzyme A/B up‑regulation and VEGF, indicating combined cytotoxic and angiogenic remodeling.; Multiplex IF confirms spatial co‑localization of T cells, B cells, and macrophages in responder biopsies.

metadata.speaker: Erika Van Aeou
metadata.talk_title: eLive cytokine profiling defines immune phenotypes and predicts ICI response in fresh tumor fragments

text: Targeting RNA Polymerase I and BCL2 synergy in acute myeloid leukemia | Speaker: Putzer Hung | Tumors: AML | MOA: Pol I degradation reduces rRNA synthesis, inducing differentiation and G1 arrest in AML cells, and synergizes with BCL2 inhibition to trigger apoptosis independent of TP53 status. | Findings: Nascent and mature rRNA levels are elevated in primary AML blasts versus healthy hematopoietic cells.; HOXA9 activation drives Pol I expression and rRNA synthesis; HOXA9 inactivation reduces rRNA production before cell cycle changes.; Targeted degradation of POLR1A with dTAG decreases rRNA synthesis, induces G1 arrest, differentiation, and reduces viability.; Pol I degradation synergizes with venetoclax (Z-score >10) to enhance AML cell killing, independent of TP53 mutation.

metadata.speaker: Putzer Hung
metadata.talk_title: Targeting RNA Polymerase I and BCL2 synergy in acute myeloid leukemia

text: LncRNA CYP4A22-AS1/YBX1/PK1 axis drives radiation resistance in cervical adenocarcinoma | Speaker: Dr. Zhao | Tumors: cervical adenocarcinoma | MOA: CYP4A22-AS1 binds YBX1, enhancing transcription of PK1, which drives glycolysis and confers radiation resistance; depletion of the lncRNA or PK1 sensitizes cells to radiation-induced DNA damage and apoptosis. | Findings: CYP4A22-AS1 is upregulated in cervical adenocarcinoma and predicts poor survival.; Knockdown of CYP4A22-AS1 increases radiation-induced apoptosis and DNA damage markers.; CYP4A22-AS1 regulates glycolysis via upregulation of PK1 through YBX1 interaction.; PK1 depletion reverses glycolytic enhancement and radiosensitizes CYP4A22-AS1 overexpressing cells.; In vivo, CYP4A22-AS1 overexpression accelerates tumor growth in mouse models.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Zhao
metadata.talk_title: LncRNA CYP4A22-AS1/YBX1/PK1 axis drives radiation resistance in cervical adenocarcinoma

text: Ultrasmall lactoferrin nanoassemblies delivering miR-196b antagomir and COP TF II inhibitor for RCC CAF remodeling | Speaker: Ahmed Ziyadeh | Tumors: renal cell carcinoma | MOA: An ultra‑small lactoferrin‑stabilized nanoassembly co‑delivers a miR‑196b antagomir and the COP TF II inhibitor CIA1 to RCC cancer‑associated fibroblasts, suppressing activation markers, ECM production, and secreted cytokines, thereby reducing CAF‑driven tumor growth and enhancing immune infiltration. | Findings: Nanoassembly size ~6.3 nm enables renal filtration and accumulation in tumor kidney.; Both miR‑196b antagomir and CIA1 independently down‑regulate CAF activation (α‑SMA) and ECM markers (collagen I, LOX).; Conditioned media from treated CAFs reduces RCC cell apoptosis resistance, EMT markers, and migration.; In orthotopic RENCA mice, combined nanoassembly markedly reduces tumor volume and weight without systemic toxicity.; Treatment increases intratumoral CD8⁺ T cells, dendritic cells, and NK cells while decreasing Tregs and suppressive myeloid cells.

metadata.speaker: Ahmed Ziyadeh
metadata.talk_title: Ultrasmall lactoferrin nanoassemblies delivering miR-196b antagomir and COP TF II inhibitor for RCC CAF remodeling

text: Mitochondrial tRNA‑Arg fragments modulate breast cancer metastasis | Speaker: Katie Schwankert | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Strain‑specific SNPs in mitochondrial tRNA^Arg alter its secondary structure, influencing cleavage into ~50‑nt fragments; these fragments correlate with primary tumor latency and pulmonary metastasis, suggesting a non‑coding RNA signaling role in metastatic progression. | Findings: Mitochondrial SNPs in tRNA^Arg D‑loop differ among mouse strains and associate with metastatic burden.; Northern blots reveal 40‑50 nt tRNA^Arg fragments whose abundance varies with mitochondrial genotype.; Enzymatic end‑repair and demethylation enable detection of these fragments by small‑RNA‑seq.; MINX mice with mismatched mitochondria show altered primary tumor latency and number of lung metastases.; Fragment production is higher in strains with higher metastatic propensity, implicating a functional role.

metadata.speaker: Katie Schwankert
metadata.talk_title: Mitochondrial tRNA‑Arg fragments modulate breast cancer metastasis

text: Urinary extracellular vesicle microRNA panel for early detection and prognosis of lung cancer | Speaker: Yoriko Ando | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: Urinary extracellular vesicles enriched for tumor‑derived miRNAs provide a non‑invasive source of cancer‑specific signatures; a machine‑learning model using selected miRNAs discriminates early‑stage lung cancer from controls and stratifies recurrence risk after surgery. | Findings: Urinary EV isolation increases miRNA read proportion fivefold.; A 11‑miRNA feature set yields AUC 0.94 for cancer detection; performance holds in age‑matched subset.; Three‑miRNA prognostic panel (selected from 11) predicts recurrence‑free survival with HR 8.3 and 3‑year AUC 0.80.; Age and other clinical covariates do not confound the detection score.

metadata.speaker: Yoriko Ando
metadata.talk_title: Urinary extracellular vesicle microRNA panel for early detection and prognosis of lung cancer

text: Multimodal miR‑15a conjugates overcome olaparib resistance in epithelial ovarian cancer | Speaker: Amartya Pal | Tumors: epithelial ovarian cancer | MOA: A chemically modified miR‑15a mimic incorporates 5‑FU, gemcitabine, and methotrexate, delivering tumor‑suppressive miRNA activity plus chemotherapeutic payloads; it down‑regulates DNA repair/checkpoint proteins (CHEK1, E1) and induces DNA damage, forcing cells into mitotic catastrophe and synergizing with olaparib. | Findings: Modified miR‑15a reduces viability of ovarian cancer cells at low nanomolar concentrations without delivery vehicle.; The construct retains potency in olaparib‑resistant cells, showing similar IC50 values.; RNA‑seq reveals up‑regulation of DNA damage pathways and down‑regulation of WNT, mTOR, AMPK signaling.; Western blots confirm down‑regulation of CHEK1 and E1, and activation of CDK1/CDC25A.; Bliss analysis demonstrates strong synergy between the modified miR‑15a and olaparib.

metadata.speaker: Amartya Pal
metadata.talk_title: Multimodal miR‑15a conjugates overcome olaparib resistance in epithelial ovarian cancer

text: Therapy‑induced senescent cells promote early dissemination via JUP‑mediated clustering | Speaker: Alaleh | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Therapy‑induced senescent breast cancer cells acquire a JUP‑dependent adhesive phenotype that forms multicellular clusters, enhancing early lung dissemination and, in immunocompetent hosts, promoting metastatic outgrowth through immune modulation. | Findings: Doxorubicin or fractionated irradiation induces dose‑dependent senescence in TNBC xenografts (X‑gal staining, beta‑gal activity).; Co‑injection of senescent cells with parental 231 cells does not affect primary tumor size but increases lung metastases (p<0.01).; Senescent cells accelerate early dissemination: 3‑day tail‑vein experiments show higher lung luciferase signal versus parental cells alone.; 3D imaging reveals larger tumor cell clusters and extravasation of senescent cells themselves in the lung.; RNA‑seq identifies up‑regulation of adhesion pathways; JUP (plakoglobin) is highly expressed in senescent cells.

metadata.speaker: Alaleh
metadata.talk_title: Therapy‑induced senescent cells promote early dissemination via JUP‑mediated clustering

text: Extracellular matrix stiffness regulates TYK2‑mediated EMT and breast cancer metastasis | Speaker: Zemin Hu | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Reduced matrix stiffness maintains TYK2 activity at the cell membrane via IFN‑α1 binding; loss of TYK2 at high stiffness releases EPHA2 and Nyn activity, leading to Twist1 phosphorylation, nuclear translocation, and EMT‑driven invasion and lung dissemination. | Findings: Normal breast tissue stiffness ~100‑200 Pa; invasive tumors reach 5‑6 kPa (30‑fold increase).; TAK2 knockdown or pharmacologic inhibition in 3D hydrogel (≤150 Pa) increases cell invasion and mesenchymal marker expression (vimentin, N‑cadherin).; TAK2 phosphorylation is high at low stiffness and drops sharply with increased matrix rigidity.; TAK2 inhibition (Tucabasertib) phenocopies knockdown, enhancing EMT and lung dissemination in orthotopic mouse models.; TAK2 interacts with IFN‑α1 and EPHA2 at low stiffness; high stiffness disrupts these interactions, activating Nyn‑mediated Twist1 phosphorylation.

metadata.speaker: Zemin Hu
metadata.talk_title: Extracellular matrix stiffness regulates TYK2‑mediated EMT and breast cancer metastasis

text: Spatial profiling reveals SPP1‑positive macrophages as central architects of colorectal brain metastasis | Speaker: Anuja Sath | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Macrophage‑derived SPP1 engages integrin/CD44 receptors on neighboring tumor and stromal cells, driving collagen‑rich ECM remodeling, immunosuppression, and enhanced tumor cell invasion in the colorectal brain metastasis niche. | Findings: SPP1‑high macrophages are present in >80 % of CRC brain metastasis samples and co‑localize with tumor cells and fibroblasts.; Spatial neighborhood analysis identifies two macrophage‑enriched niches; one directly contacts tumor cells, the other contacts stromal cells.; SPP1 knockout in macrophages reduces expression of lipid‑metabolism genes (e.g., SQLE) and diminishes tumor cell invasion in co‑culture.; Macrophage SPP1 loss decreases tumor cell expression of metastasis‑related genes (e.g., S100 family, VIM).; Organ‑on‑a‑chip assays show a ~40 % reduction in macrophage migration speed when SPP1 is deleted.

metadata.speaker: Anuja Sath
metadata.talk_title: Spatial profiling reveals SPP1‑positive macrophages as central architects of colorectal brain metastasis

text: KPC1 ubiquitin ligase suppresses melanoma mesenchymal transition by degrading ZEB1 | Speaker: Dave Hoon | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: KPC1 ubiquitinates ZEB1, targeting it for proteasomal degradation; loss of KPC1 stabilizes ZEB1, driving EMT, N‑cadherin up‑regulation and poor melanoma prognosis. | Findings: Low KPC1 expression correlates with high ZEB1 and CDH2 (N‑cadherin) in metastatic melanoma samples (p<0.001).; KPC1 knockout in melanoma cells increases ZEB1 protein levels without changing mRNA, indicating post‑translational regulation.; Cycloheximide chase shows prolonged ZEB1 half‑life in KPC1‑deficient cells.; Co‑IP demonstrates direct binding of KPC1 to ZEB1.; High KPC1 / low ZEB1 cohort exhibits significantly better overall survival (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.30‑0.68).

metadata.speaker: Dave Hoon
metadata.talk_title: KPC1 ubiquitin ligase suppresses melanoma mesenchymal transition by degrading ZEB1

text: Jagged1 expression in breast cancer cells drives lymph node metastasis via Notch4‑mediated endothelial remodeling | Speaker: Jan Kadlecky | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Tumor‑cell Jagged1 engages Notch4 on lymphatic endothelial cells in a non‑canonical manner, disrupting VE‑cadherin junctions, increasing endothelial permeability, and facilitating tumor cell trans‑endothelial migration and colonization of lymph nodes. | Findings: Jagged1‑positive breast cancer cells show >3‑fold increase in lymphovascular invasion compared with Jagged1‑negative controls (p<0.001).; Jagged1 overexpression leads to larger lymph node tumor burden (RFP‑PanCK area) and earlier colonization.; Coating lymphatic endothelial cells with Jagged1 protein disrupts VE‑cadherin junctions and creates intercellular gaps.; Notch4 neutralizing antibody blocks Jagged1‑induced endothelial gap formation and reduces transendothelial migration (≈45 % reduction).; VEGF‑R3 soluble trap reduces lymph node metastasis but does not affect primary tumor growth.

metadata.speaker: Jan Kadlecky
metadata.talk_title: Jagged1 expression in breast cancer cells drives lymph node metastasis via Notch4‑mediated endothelial remodeling

text: Allogeneic CAR Cells: Are They the New Black? | Speaker: Franco Locatelli | Tumors: B-cell malignancies, multiple myeloma, T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia, neuroblastoma, solid tumors | MOA: Allogeneic CAR‑T cells engineered to lack TCR and HLA molecules (or co‑knockdown CD52) avoid GvHD and host rejection, allowing robust expansion and MRD‑negative complete remissions across B‑ALL, T‑ALL, AML and neuroblastoma; CD7‑CAR‑T utilizes a protein‑expression blocker to target CD7 without fratricide, and GD2‑CAR‑T shows superior outcomes when administered early with low tumor burden. | Findings: Allogeneic CD19 CAR‑T in 19 high‑risk pediatric B‑ALL patients achieved 100% MRD‑negative CR with a 3‑year PFS of 42% and no grade 3‑4 CRS/ICANS.; Only two cases of acute GvHD occurred (both grade 2, resolved with steroids/JAK1/2 inhibitor) despite use of unmanipulated donor cells.; CD7 CAR‑T with a protein‑expression blocker induced complete MRD‑negative remissions in two pediatric patients, one remaining disease‑free at 2 years post‑allograft.; GD2 CAR‑T in neuroblastoma (n=35) yielded >50% 5‑year EFS in low‑burden disease, with better outcomes when cells were collected at diagnosis.; Pre‑clinical data showed that knocking down TCR/HLA and CD52 together markedly improves expansion and persistence of allogeneic CAR‑T cells.

metadata.speaker: Franco Locatelli
metadata.talk_title: Allogeneic CAR Cells: Are They the New Black?

text: Allogeneic CAR NK Cell Platforms and Clinical Data | Speaker: Katy Rezvani | Tumors: hematologic malignancies, Hodgkin lymphoma, diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma, solid tumors, glioblastoma | MOA: Cord‑blood derived allogeneic NK cells are engineered with an IL‑15 armoured CD70‑CAR (or CD5‑CAR) and a safety switch; they expand robustly in patients, persist for months, and mediate tumor cell killing directly and via ADCC, while a bispecific engager (AFM13) redirects NK cells to CD30‑positive Hodgkin lymphoma, achieving >90% ORR. | Findings: Cord‑blood derived CD70 CAR‑NK cells from optimal units (frozen ≤24 h, nucleated RBC ≈ 80 M) yielded 70% 1‑year PFS and 95% 1‑year OS, whereas delayed‑freeze units performed poorly.; In a 42‑patient Hodgkin lymphoma study combining AFM13 with CAR‑NK, overall response rate exceeded 90% with two‑thirds achieving CR, despite lack of bridging therapy.; CAR‑NK cells persisted up to 6 months in peripheral blood, with early clonal expansion (clone 0) followed by emergence of a memory‑like clone (clone 4) linked to long‑term persistence.; CD5 CAR‑NK therapy in T‑PLL achieved CR in 3 of 4 heavily pre‑treated patients, with donor NK cells tracking to disease clearance.; Manufacturing from a single cord‑blood unit can produce 250 patient doses at <$600 per dose, enabling off‑the‑shelf scalability.

metadata.speaker: Katy Rezvani
metadata.talk_title: Allogeneic CAR NK Cell Platforms and Clinical Data

text: Allogeneic CAR T Strategies to Overcome Rejection and Enhance Efficacy | Speaker: David Cheng | Tumors: large B‑cell lymphoma, renal cell carcinoma, solid tumors, autoimmune disorders | MOA: Allogeneic CAR‑T cells are engineered to eliminate TCR (prevent GvHD) and CD52 (allow anti‑CD52 lymphodepletion), or to express HLA‑E and knock‑out β2‑microglobulin (stealth), enabling robust expansion after standard lymphodepletion; CD70 is leveraged both as a tumor antigen and as a target to deplete alloreactive host T cells, improving persistence and efficacy in RCC and lymphoma. | Findings: In the MRD‑guided ALO‑501A trial, 7 of 8 patients cleared MRD after a single dose of allogeneic CD19 CAR‑T with standard flu‑cyclophosphamide lymphodepletion, without CRS/ICANS.; CD70‑targeted allogeneic CAR‑T (LO316) achieved a 31% ORR in CD70‑high RCC, with durable responses >12 months in most responders.; Gene‑editing approaches (TCR knockout, CD52 knockout, HLA‑E insertion) enable allogeneic CAR‑T expansion comparable to autologous products despite HLA‑agnostic lymphodepletion.; Selective depletion of alloreactive host T cells via CD70 targeting (the “dagger” approach) enhances CAR‑T persistence and reduces rejection.

metadata.speaker: David Cheng
metadata.talk_title: Allogeneic CAR T Strategies to Overcome Rejection and Enhance Efficacy

text: SOX2 as a master regulator of classical squamous cell carcinoma | Speaker: Riley Walter | Tumors: squamous cell carcinoma | MOA: SOX2 amplification in classical SCC drives a transcriptional program by maintaining chromatin accessibility at enhancers, forming enhancer‑promoter loops that upregulate ferroptosis suppressors, thereby conferring resistance to ferroptosis. | Findings: Classical SCC shows focal 3q amplification of SOX2 and a selective dependency on SOX2 for proliferation.; SOX2 knockdown reduces chromatin accessibility at thousands of sites and downregulates the classical SCC gene signature.; SOX2 overexpression restores accessibility and upregulates ferroptosis suppressor genes (GPX2, GSR, AKR1C3, SLC25A10).; SOX2‑deficient classical SCC cells exhibit increased lipid peroxidation and apoptosis upon ferroptosis inducer ML162 treatment.

metadata.speaker: Riley Walter
metadata.talk_title: SOX2 as a master regulator of classical squamous cell carcinoma

text: FOXP2B as a driver of neuroendocrine transformation in lung cancer | Speaker: Amin Sabit | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer, small cell lung cancer | MOA: FOXP2B overexpression in EGFR‑mutant LUAD with p53/Rb loss suppresses EGFR signaling and induces neuroendocrine markers, an effect amplified by REST inhibition, suggesting FOXP2B drives neuroendocrine transdifferentiation. | Findings: FOXP2B is highly up‑regulated in transformed small‑cell samples compared with de novo small‑cell.; FOXP2B overexpression reduces total and phospho‑EGFR levels and induces neuroendocrine markers (ASCL1, synaptophysin, chromogranin) in p53/Rb‑deficient LUAD cells.; Combined FOXP2B overexpression and REST inhibition further enhances neuroendocrine marker expression.; FOXP2B directly binds the EGFR locus, suggesting transcriptional repression of EGFR.

metadata.speaker: Amin Sabit
metadata.talk_title: FOXP2B as a driver of neuroendocrine transformation in lung cancer

text: MBD4 regulates FOXA1 lineage‑specific enhancers to promote prostate tumorigenesis | Speaker: Xuanrong Chen | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: MBD4 binds FOXA1‑motif enhancers in AR‑positive prostate cells, restricting FOXA1 pioneer activity; loss of MBD4 expands FOXA1 enhancer occupancy, reprogramming AR signaling toward an oncogenic program and altering lineage specification. | Findings: CRISPR screen identified MBD4 as a top gene whose loss rescues growth suppression caused by AR‑ARE activation.; MBD4 knockout in LNCaP cells expands FOXA1‑motif enhancer accessibility and increases AR and H3K27ac signals at these sites.; Overexpression of MBD4 reduces FOXA1 enhancer sites, while knockout in normal prostate organoids drives luminal differentiation (CK8/18 up, CHOP2 down).; MBD4 interacts with HDAC1/2, suggesting a deacetylase‑mediated mechanism restricting FOXA1 activity.

metadata.speaker: Xuanrong Chen
metadata.talk_title: MBD4 regulates FOXA1 lineage‑specific enhancers to promote prostate tumorigenesis

text: First‑in‑class oral small molecule DPX8743 dissolves MYC condensates | Speaker: Borja (last name not provided) | Tumors: ovarian cancer, esophageal cancer, pan‑cancer (MYC‑driven) | MOA: DPX8743 selectively dissolves MYC‑containing transcriptional condensates in MYC‑high cancer cells, leading to down‑regulation of MYC target genes, G1 cell‑cycle arrest, and apoptosis, while sparing global transcriptional condensates. | Findings: DPX8743 dissolves MYC condensates in MYC‑high tumor cells but not in normal cells with basal MYC levels.; Condensate dissolution correlates with G1 arrest, reduced MYC target expression, and tumor regression in MYC‑amplified CDX/PDX models.; Compound activity is potentiated by higher MYC protein levels and MYC genetic dependency; MYC knockdown desensitizes cells.; Seven‑day rat toxicology shows no weight loss or major organ toxicity except reversible thymus atrophy, indicating a therapeutic index >4×.

metadata.speaker: Borja (last name not provided)
metadata.talk_title: First‑in‑class oral small molecule DPX8743 dissolves MYC condensates

text: NSD3 as a co‑factor stabilizing BRD4‑NUT condensates in NUT carcinoma | Speaker: Kyle Egan | Tumors: NUT carcinoma | MOA: NSD3 deposits H3K36me2 within BRD4‑NUT mega‑domains, stabilizing BRD4‑NUT occupancy and nuclear condensate intensity, thereby maintaining long‑range chromatin contacts and MYC‑driven transcriptional programs in NUT carcinoma. | Findings: NSD3 interacts with BRD4‑NUT and deposits H3K36me2 at mega‑domains.; NSD3 knockdown reduces H3K36me2, diminishes BRD4‑NUT chromatin binding, and lowers condensate intensity while increasing condensate number.; Hi‑C reveals ~2‑fold loss of long‑range contacts between mega‑domains upon NSD3 depletion.; Genes within mega‑domains, especially MYC targets, are down‑regulated, leading to modest growth inhibition and differentiation markers up‑regulation.

metadata.speaker: Kyle Egan
metadata.talk_title: NSD3 as a co‑factor stabilizing BRD4‑NUT condensates in NUT carcinoma

text: Extrachromosomal DNA generates oncogenic fusion transcripts such as PVT1‑MYC | Speaker: Hairun Yi | Tumors: multiple cancer types (pan‑cancer) | MOA: ecDNA harbors high‑frequency structural rearrangements that generate fusion transcripts; the PVT1‑MYC fusion places PVT1 as a 5′ UTR, enhancing MYC mRNA stability and translation, leading to amplified MYC target activation and a proliferative advantage. | Findings: ecDNA exhibits the highest DNA and RNA fusion frequencies across cancers.; PVT1‑MYC is the most prevalent fusion on ecDNA, with >98% of fusions placing PVT1 at the 5′ end.; PVT1‑MYC transcripts show greater RNA stability and drive six‑fold stronger MYC‑target activation than canonical MYC.; In MYC‑depleted cells, PVT1‑MYC rescues viability more efficiently than canonical MYC.

metadata.speaker: Hairun Yi
metadata.talk_title: Extrachromosomal DNA generates oncogenic fusion transcripts such as PVT1‑MYC

text: VNTR2‑1 antisense transcript regulates DNA replication via METTL3‑dependent translation | Speaker: Brennan Papenberg | Tumors: multiple cancers (pan‑cancer) | MOA: The VNTR2‑1 repeat in TERT intron 2 encodes an antisense transcript with an open reading frame whose length scales with repeat number; METTL3‑mediated m6A modification enhances its translation, driving DNA replication gene programs and promoting cell proliferation. | Findings: VNTR2‑1 antisense transcript is expressed and contains multiple DRACH motifs for METTL3‑dependent m6A modification.; M6A‑intact reporter shows higher luciferase activity; METTL3 inhibition reduces this activity.; Flag‑tagged VNTR2‑1AS construct produces protein, confirming translational competence.; Overexpression of VNTR2‑1AS up‑regulates DNA replication and cell‑cycle pathways; knockout reduces these pathways and slows proliferation.; Translation‑deficient start‑codon mutant fails to enhance proliferation, indicating translation‑dependent function.

metadata.speaker: Brennan Papenberg
metadata.talk_title: VNTR2‑1 antisense transcript regulates DNA replication via METTL3‑dependent translation

text: AACR Progress and the GLITZ Clinical Trial | Speaker: Lillian Siu | Tumors: gastroesophageal cancer | MOA: The speaker introduced the GLITZ clinical trial, which utilizes a multi-biomarker informed treatment approach to determine if patients with gastroesophageal cancer can safely avoid surgery. The trial's IND application has been approved by the FDA and Health Canada. | Findings: The GLITZ Clinical Trial IND application was approved by the US FDA and Health Canada to assess multi-biomarker informed treatment in gastroesophageal cancer.; Cancer mortality has decreased by nearly 35% since the peak in the 1990s.; The number of cancer survivors in the US has increased by approximately 6.6 million over the last 15 years.; Over 20 new anticancer therapeutics were FDA approved between July 2024 and June 2025.

metadata.speaker: Lillian Siu
metadata.talk_title: AACR Progress and the GLITZ Clinical Trial

text: Targeting Programmed Cell Death in Leukemia | Speaker: Anthony Letai | Tumors: chronic lymphocytic leukemia, acute myelogenous leukemia | MOA: The speaker described the translational journey from basic protein chemistry to the clinical application of targeting programmed cell death pathways. This work culminated in the development and use of venetoclax for the treatment of AML and CLL. | Findings: Targeting programmed cell death pathways is an effective strategy for treating chronic lymphocytic leukemia and acute myelogenous leukemia.; Venetoclax was successfully translated from laboratory research into a standard of care for AML patients.

metadata.speaker: Anthony Letai
metadata.talk_title: Targeting Programmed Cell Death in Leukemia

text: How Cancer Cells Escape Targeted Therapy by Changing Identity | Speaker: Dr. Charles L. Sawyers | Tumors: prostate cancer, small cell lung cancer, pancreatic cancer | MOA: Loss of RB1 primes prostate adenocarcinoma cells for lineage plasticity; extracellular matrix engagement via integrin‑β1 restrains YAP/TAZ‑TEAD activity, while Notch signaling also suppresses neuroendocrine transition. Disruption of matrix signaling, inhibition of LATS kinase, or pharmacologic blockade of YAP/TEAD or Notch releases this brake, inducing ASCL1 expression and a neuroendocrine phenotype that can be reversed pharmacologically. FOXA1 relocalization and TEAD binding rewire chromatin, enabling MYC paralog‑TIP60 co‑activator dependence in the neuroendocrine state. | Findings: RB loss combined with PTEN or TP53 loss drives adenocarcinoma-to‑neuroendocrine transition in mouse prostate models.; Matrix withdrawal or β1‑integrin deletion induces ASCL1 expression within 7 days in organoids.; LATS inhibition restores YAP activity and blocks ASCL1 up‑regulation, demonstrating reversibility of lineage transition.; Combined TEAD and Notch inhibition drives >90% of organoid cells to a neuroendocrine state.; FOXA1 relocalization to TEAD‑bound enhancers is required for transition; FOXA1 knockout prevents neuroendocrine differentiation.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Charles L. Sawyers
metadata.talk_title: How Cancer Cells Escape Targeted Therapy by Changing Identity

text: Beyond Blood: The Evolution of CAR T Therapy for Solid Malignancies | Speaker: Dr. Carl H. June | Tumors: glioblastoma, pancreatic cancer, ovarian cancer, gastroesophageal cancer, mesothelioma | MOA: Engineered autologous T cells expressing chimeric antigen receptors target tumor‑associated antigens (e.g., CD19, mesothelin, claudin‑18.2, EGFRvIII/IL‑13Rα2). Armoring CARs with cytokines (IL‑18) or delivering CAR constructs via lipid nanoparticles enhances persistence and stromal targeting (anti‑FAP). Dual‑target CARs and regional delivery (Ommaya reservoir) improve trafficking and efficacy in solid tumors such as glioblastoma, while NK cell infiltration and low Treg density correlate with better outcomes. | Findings: IL‑18‑armored CAR T cells achieved 75% complete response in CAR‑refractory lymphoma with no increase in CRS.; Dual‑target EGFRvIII/IL‑13Rα2 CAR T delivered via Ommaya achieved 2 PRs and ~70% disease control in 18 glioblastoma patients.; Higher intratumoral NK cell levels predicted longer PFS, whereas higher Treg levels predicted resistance in glioblastoma CAR T trials.; Sequential anti‑FAP followed by anti‑mesothelin CAR T in KPC mice markedly improved survival compared with either monotherapy.; Lipid‑nanoparticle‑delivered anti‑FAP CAR RNA achieved superior tumor control versus retroviral CAR T in pancreatic cancer models.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Carl H. June
metadata.talk_title: Beyond Blood: The Evolution of CAR T Therapy for Solid Malignancies

text: Chemical Rewiring of Biological Circuits for Cancer Therapy: Targeted Protein Degradation and Beyond | Speaker: Dr. Georg E. Winter | MOA: PROTACs and molecular glues induce proximity between an E3 ligase (e.g., CRBN, VHL, FBXO3, DCAF16) and a target protein, leading to ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Novel mechanisms include intermolecular bivalent gluing (IBG‑1 bridges two bromodomains of RAD4 to recruit DCAF16) and inhibitor‑induced supercharging of native degradation pathways (kinase inhibitors promote native E3 ligase recognition). SERDs such as fulvestrant act by inducing SUMOylation of ERα, which then triggers RNF4/RNF111‑mediated ubiquitination; however, degradation is dispensable for anti‑estrogenic activity, while SUMOylation is essential for transcriptional repression. | Findings: Identified UBE2M as a global regulator of >200 E3 ligases, enabling phenotypic discovery of molecular glues.; Discovered DHTC3, a molecular glue that recruits FBXO3 to degrade BET4 via a chemically derived exit vector.; Revealed IBG‑1 acts via intermolecular bivalent gluing, bridging two RAD4 bromodomains and recruiting DCAF16 despite low affinity.; Showed that many kinase inhibitors cause “supercharging” of native degradation, leading to target destabilization without a dedicated E3 ligase.; Demonstrated that fulvestrant induces SUMOylation of ERα, which is required for transcriptional repression, while degradation by RNF4/RNF111 is dispensable.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Georg E. Winter
metadata.talk_title: Chemical Rewiring of Biological Circuits for Cancer Therapy: Targeted Protein Degradation and Beyond

text: Rethinking Cancer Diagnosis and Treatment with AI from Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Management | Speaker: Dr. Regina Barzilay | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Deep learning models (e.g., SPARK, Mirai) integrate routine pathology slides or mammograms with spatial transcriptomics to predict molecular pathway activity and long‑term clinical outcomes. The models learn patch‑level annotations of ~40 molecular programs from paired imaging‑omics data, enabling risk stratification, early detection, and mechanistic insight into tumor biology. | Findings: SPARK predicts 40 molecular programs from routine pathology slides with AUC ~0.90 and Pearson ~0.74.; Adding program-level information to image features improves prediction of disease‑free survival and treatment response across multiple cancer types.; Mirai mammography model achieves a 5‑year c‑index of 0.80, outperforming density (c‑index 0.50) and questionnaire‑based risk models (c‑index 0.63).; High‑risk patients identified by Mirai correspond to risk levels exceeding those of BRCA1 carriers.; Prospective trials (UMass, UCSF, Israel, MiPEBS) are underway to evaluate AI‑driven risk‑adapted screening.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Regina Barzilay
metadata.talk_title: Rethinking Cancer Diagnosis and Treatment with AI from Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Management

text: Mechanistic analysis of CTLA-4 and PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor colitis in human patients | Speaker: Patrick Dugan | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: CTLA-4 and PD-1 blockade induce colitis by reactivating resident memory CD8 T cells and expanding Th1/Th17 CD4 effector populations; regulatory T cells are not depleted in human colitis, and S1PR1+ Tregs expand uniquely in CTLA-4 colitis, suggesting distinct mechanistic pathways for each checkpoint. | Findings: Both CTLA-4 and PD-1 colitis show expansion of resident memory CD8 T cells and Th1/Th17 CD4 effector cells.; Regulatory T cells are broadly expanded rather than depleted in human colitis biopsies.; CTLA-4 colitis uniquely expands S1PR1+ Treg populations not seen in PD-1 colitis.; Clonotypic expansion is observed in effector cells, with resident memory clones dominating in healthy controls and effector clones dominating in colitis.

metadata.speaker: Patrick Dugan
metadata.talk_title: Mechanistic analysis of CTLA-4 and PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor colitis in human patients

text: Wild microbiota–driven CTLA-4 blockade colitis model and Fc‑dependent toxicity separation | Speaker: Gabriel Nunez | Tumors: colorectal cancer, melanoma | MOA: Gavage of wild mouse microbiota into antibiotic‑treated mice creates a microbiota‑dependent, CD4‑Th1–driven colitis upon CTLA‑4 blockade; Fc‑effector function of the anti‑CTLA‑4 antibody is required for colitis but not for anti‑tumor efficacy, allowing separation of toxicity from therapeutic benefit. | Findings: Wild‑derived microbiota, but not standard SPF microbiota, enables severe colitis after anti‑CTLA‑4 treatment.; Colitis is CD4‑Th1 dependent; depletion of CD4 T cells or neutralization of IFN‑γ abolishes disease.; Peripheral Treg depletion (Helios‑negative FoxP3+ cells) occurs with CTLA‑4 antibody; thymic Tregs remain.; Fc‑null CTLA‑4 antibody (H11 extender) retains anti‑tumor activity while eliminating colitis, demonstrating Fc‑dependence of toxicity.; Clonotypic analysis reveals oligoclonal expansion of Th1 cells recognizing microbial antigens in colitic mice.

metadata.speaker: Gabriel Nunez
metadata.talk_title: Wild microbiota–driven CTLA-4 blockade colitis model and Fc‑dependent toxicity separation

text: Bench to bedside in epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (EHE) | Speaker: Brian Rubin | Tumors: epithelioid hemangioendothelioma | MOA: The TAZ-CAMTA1 fusion drives EHE by constitutively activating the Hippo pathway effector TAZ, leading to nuclear TEAD transcriptional programs. Trametinib inhibits MAPK signaling downstream of the fusion, reducing colony formation in vitro and tumor growth in mouse models. CDK9 inhibition (dinaciclib) disrupts transcriptional elongation complexes essential for fusion-driven transcription, showing synergistic tumor regression when combined with MEK inhibition. | Findings: TAZ-CAMTA1 fusion activates MAPK pathway; MEK inhibitor trametinib shows IC50 <10 nM in colony assays.; Phase 2 trial of trametinib in unresectable/metastatic EHE yielded 20 responders among 24 patients but did not meet primary endpoint for FDA approval.; Genetically engineered TAZ-CAMTA1 homozygous mice develop histologically identical EHE tumors, providing a faithful preclinical model.; CDK9 inhibitors (dinaciclib, CGP) induce apoptosis in EHE cell lines and dramatically reduce lung tumor burden in xenograft models.; Combination of MEK inhibition with TEAD inhibition (MGH CP1) shows synergistic growth suppression in vitro.

metadata.speaker: Brian Rubin
metadata.talk_title: Bench to bedside in epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (EHE)

text: Project Cure CRC Integrated Adaptive Clinical Trial Platform | Speaker: Kim Newcomer | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: The Alliance has built an integrated ecosystem (BlueHQ, Blue Lake, adaptive trial) that links patient-reported data, genomic profiling, and real-world outcomes to accelerate colorectal cancer drug development, with patients shaping trial windows and governance. | Findings: Received 525 research proposals in the past cycle.; Allocated $15 M to 34 projects across 150 investigators.; Engaged 20 industry partners in the adaptive trial platform.; Goal to increase 5‑year metastatic CRC survival from 13% to 35% within five years.

metadata.speaker: Kim Newcomer
metadata.talk_title: Project Cure CRC Integrated Adaptive Clinical Trial Platform

text: Lineberger Excellence in Advocacy Program Impact Metrics | Speaker: Lourdes Baiz Conde-Carbonatti | MOA: LEAP consolidates multiple patient/community advisory structures into a single program that tracks engagement metrics, provides training, matches advocates to research projects, and integrates patient voices into grant review and protocol development at a comprehensive cancer center. | Findings: Advocate pool composition: 83% female, 17% male.; Processed 86 matching requests with 250 advocate responses.; Reviewed 328 pilot grants with participation of 36 individual advocates.; Implemented systematic evaluation surveys with >90% positive scores on respect and impact.

metadata.speaker: Lourdes Baiz Conde-Carbonatti
metadata.talk_title: Lineberger Excellence in Advocacy Program Impact Metrics

text: Patient Advocate Involvement in Matchmakers Preclinical Immunotherapy Project | Speaker: Annie Ellis | MOA: The Matchmakers team integrates patient advocates into a preclinical T‑cell receptor engineering program, providing monthly meetings, co‑created educational deliverables, and bidirectional feedback that improves scientific relevance and trainee communication skills. | Findings: 70+ patient advocates contributed to 21 preclinical immunotherapy teams.; Advocate involvement increased trainee awareness of patient relevance from 0% to ~50% in surveys.; Co‑created lay summaries, glossaries, and videos improved communication of complex TCR science.; Advocates reported enhanced understanding of basic research, while trainees noted better non‑scientist communication.

metadata.speaker: Annie Ellis
metadata.talk_title: Patient Advocate Involvement in Matchmakers Preclinical Immunotherapy Project

text: Spatial single-cell analysis of supratentorial ependymoma subtypes | Speaker: Mariella | Tumors: pediatric ependymoma | MOA: Single-cell RNA‑seq and 10x Xenium spatial transcriptomics were used to map developmental cell states across supratentorial ependymoma subtypes, revealing that YAP1‑driven tumors are differentiated ependymal‑like, while CEFTA/RELA tumors retain neuroepithelial and embryonic‑like stem states; spatial organization correlates with a mesenchymal‑hypoxia cell state, and in vitro/in vivo models show that differentiation requires microenvironmental cues. | Findings: Assembled a cohort of >60 supratentorial ependymoma samples covering all molecular subclusters.; YAP1‑fusion tumors project to later developmental stages and consist almost exclusively of differentiated ependymal‑like cells.; CEFTA/RELA‑fusion tumors contain a mixture of neuroepithelial‑like stem cells, embryonic‑like cells, and differentiated ependymal/neuronal states.; Spatial transcriptomics identified two global tumor architectures (organized vs disorganized) driven by the presence of a mesenchymal‑hypoxia cell state.; In vitro cultures grown as PDX or neuron/astrocyte co‑cultures recapitulate the full differentiation hierarchy, whereas neurosphere‑only cultures enrich for stem‑like cells.

metadata.speaker: Mariella
metadata.talk_title: Spatial single-cell analysis of supratentorial ependymoma subtypes

text: Targeting ACOD1‑itaconate axis to suppress ZFTA‑RELA fusion in ependymoma | Speaker: Suram | Tumors: pediatric ependymoma | MOA: ZFTA/RELA fusion upregulates ACOD1, leading to increased production of itaconate; itaconate acts as an oncometabolite that inhibits KDM5 histone demethylases, raising H3K4me3 at the fusion promoter and sustaining fusion expression. Pharmacologic or genetic inhibition of ACOD1 (dimethyl itaconate, citraconate analogs) or upstream glutamine metabolism (GHU‑083) reduces itaconate levels, lowers H3K4me3, down‑regulates fusion mRNA and protein, and prolongs survival in mouse models. | Findings: ZFTA/RELA fusion drives strong up‑regulation of ACOD1 and accumulation of itaconate in both mouse and human ependymoma cells.; shRNA knockdown of the fusion or ACOD1 reduces cell viability and ACOD1 expression.; ACOD1 whole‑body or tumor‑cell specific knockout in mice dramatically improves survival (median age 25 days → >50 % long‑term survivors).; Dimethyl itaconate treatment lowers fusion mRNA and protein levels in vitro and in vivo; rescue with exogenous itaconate restores fusion expression.; Itaconate inhibits KDM5 demethylases (IC50 ~470 µM), increasing H3K4me3; KDM5 inhibition phenocopies itaconate’s effect on fusion expression.

metadata.speaker: Suram
metadata.talk_title: Targeting ACOD1‑itaconate axis to suppress ZFTA‑RELA fusion in ependymoma

text: Anti‑GM‑CSF therapy reverses immunotolerance in pediatric brain tumors | Speaker: Richard Gilbertson | Tumors: supratentorial ependymoma, choroid plexus carcinoma, group 3 medulloblastoma | MOA: Tumor‑derived GM‑CSF in the CSF drives expansion of MHC‑II⁺ hematopoietic stem cells in calvarial bone marrow, which differentiate into immunosuppressive myeloid cells and promote T‑reg development; intrathecal or intravenous Lenzilumab blocks GM‑CSF, reducing stem‑cell proliferation, myeloid suppression, and restoring CD8⁺ T‑cell anti‑tumor activity, leading to tumor regression in multiple pediatric brain tumor models. | Findings: CSF of tumor‑bearing mice contains high GM‑CSF levels, absent in tumor‑free controls.; GM‑CSF promotes expansion of CD34⁺MHC‑II⁺ hematopoietic stem cells in calvarial marrow, which migrate to dura and tumor.; These stem cells differentiate into immunosuppressive myeloid cells; CD4⁺ T cells skew toward FoxP3⁺ Tregs.; Intrathecal Lenzilumab lowers CSF GM‑CSF, reduces skull HSC proliferation, decreases tumor‑infiltrating myeloid cells, and increases CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration.; Tumor regression observed in ZFTA‑RELA ependymoma, choroid plexus carcinoma, and group 3 medulloblastoma models; effect replicated with intravenous dosing.

metadata.speaker: Richard Gilbertson
metadata.talk_title: Anti‑GM‑CSF therapy reverses immunotolerance in pediatric brain tumors
