text: Dysregulated AKT Signaling Reprograms Osteosarcoma to Drive Selective Reliance on EP300 | Speaker: Adam Durbin | Tumors: osteosarcoma | MOA: JQUAD1 is a cereblon-recruiting PROTAC that selectively degrades EP300, sparing CBP, leading to loss of enhancer acetylation and transcriptional reprogramming in AKT‑activated osteosarcoma. Co‑inhibition of AKT with MK‑2206 or capivasertib reduces translation rates, enhancing EP300 degradation and synergistic tumor growth inhibition. | Findings: JQUAD1 selectively degrades EP300 with minimal effect on CBP in vitro.; AKT‑dysregulated osteosarcoma lines (PTEN loss or AKT amplification) are uniquely sensitive to JQUAD1.; Combining JQUAD1 with AKT inhibitors (MK‑2206 or capivasertib) yields synergistic cell death in ~10‑15% of 800 screened cell lines.; Synergy is linked to reduced translational capacity in sensitive lines, as shown by puromycin incorporation assays.; In orthotopic osteosarcoma xenografts, the JQUAD1 + MK‑2206 combination markedly suppresses tumor growth and prolongs survival compared to either agent alone.

metadata.speaker: Adam Durbin
metadata.talk_title: Dysregulated AKT Signaling Reprograms Osteosarcoma to Drive Selective Reliance on EP300

text: Cell‑free DNA Profiling in Relapsed/Refractory Neuroblastoma | Speaker: Gudrun Schillenbacher | Tumors: neuroblastoma | MOA: Low‑coverage whole‑genome and high‑coverage exome sequencing of plasma cfDNA enables detection of tumor‑specific copy‑number alterations and SNVs, allowing longitudinal monitoring of clonal dynamics, emergence of resistance mutations (e.g., ALK, FGFR1), and prognostic assessment via cfDNA quantity in relapsed/refractory neuroblastoma. | Findings: cfDNA quantity at enrollment predicts poorer survival independent of disease burden.; Relapsed neuroblastoma shows enrichment of ALK and RAS/MAPK pathway mutations, including FGFR1.; Longitudinal cfDNA dynamics correlate with treatment response: decrease during response, re‑increase at progression.; Clonal hematopoiesis events (e.g., JAK3) were detected in cfDNA, highlighting need for careful interpretation.; Predicted gene expression from cfDNA fragment patterns identifies activation of oncogenes (e.g., ALK, TERT) at relapse.

metadata.speaker: Gudrun Schillenbacher
metadata.talk_title: Cell‑free DNA Profiling in Relapsed/Refractory Neuroblastoma

text: Spatial TCR Profiling Reveals Barriers to T Cell Engagement in High‑Risk Neuroblastoma | Speaker: January Zhang | Tumors: neuroblastoma | MOA: Custom Xenium spatial transcriptomics probes track specific TCR clonotypes in situ, revealing that gamma‑delta T cells preferentially infiltrate neural‑blast rich tumor domains and adopt an exhausted phenotype (LAG3 high), while alpha‑beta clones show variable localization, linking spatial context to T‑cell functional states in high‑risk neuroblastoma. | Findings: Gamma‑delta T cells are the most spatially privileged population, with ~45% of nearest neighbors being neural blast cells.; T cells in neural‑blast rich domains express exhaustion marker LAG3, whereas those in immune‑rich domains express activation markers CD4 and FOS.; Cross‑patient gamma‑delta clone 2 is detected in tumor, blood, and cfDNA across multiple patients and time points, often adjacent to tumor cells.; Alpha‑beta TCR pairing can be inferred by co‑detection of alpha and beta probes within the same cell, confirming clonotype identity in situ.; Predicted antigen specificity for clone 2 includes NY‑ESO‑1, present in ~23% of neuroblastoma tumors.

metadata.speaker: January Zhang
metadata.talk_title: Spatial TCR Profiling Reveals Barriers to T Cell Engagement in High‑Risk Neuroblastoma

text: Co‑targeting GPC2 and B7H3 with Bicistronic CAR T Cells in Neuroblastoma and Medulloblastoma | Speaker: Patrick Scheuer | Tumors: neuroblastoma, medulloblastoma | MOA: Bicistronic CAR T cells co‑express GPC2‑specific and B7H3‑specific CARs in a single vector, enabling simultaneous targeting of two tumor antigens; this prevents antigen escape (GPC2 down‑regulation) and improves T‑cell proliferation, cytokine secretion, and tumor infiltration, leading to durable tumor control in neuroblastoma and medulloblastoma PDX models. | Findings: Bicistronic GPC2/B7H3 CAR T cells outperform single‑antigen CARs and co‑transduced mixtures in vitro and in vivo.; Dual CARs achieve complete tumor regressions and long‑term survival in neuroblastoma and medulloblastoma PDX models.; B7H3 expression remains stable under CAR pressure, while GPC2 is frequently down‑regulated, supporting the need for dual targeting.; Mice cured with dual CARs retain persisting memory T cells in bone marrow, conferring protection against rechallenge.; Relapse after dual CAR therapy is associated with increased MDSC infiltration.

metadata.speaker: Patrick Scheuer
metadata.talk_title: Co‑targeting GPC2 and B7H3 with Bicistronic CAR T Cells in Neuroblastoma and Medulloblastoma

text: Surface‑Localized Nuclear Envelope Proteins as Targets in MYC‑Driven Group 3 Medulloblastoma | Speaker: Sheila Xing | Tumors: medulloblastoma | MOA: Single‑domain camelid antibodies against LBR and TMPO are engineered into second‑generation CARs; these antigens are aberrantly presented on the plasma membrane of MYC‑driven Group 3 medulloblastoma due to nuclear envelope fragmentation, enabling CAR‑T mediated cytotoxicity against a proliferative tumor subpopulation. | Findings: LBR and TMPO are mislocalized to the cell surface specifically in MYC‑driven Group 3 medulloblastoma, not in normal neural cells.; LBR+ tumor cells display high proliferation signatures (G2/M enrichment).; LBR‑CAR and TMPO‑CAR T cells achieve potent killing in vitro at low E:T ratios.; Bispecific CAR combining LBR and TMPO binders yields superior tumor remission and durability in vivo.; Therapy‑adapted mouse models show enrichment of LBR expression after standard chemoradiotherapy, indicating a post‑treatment target.

metadata.speaker: Sheila Xing
metadata.talk_title: Surface‑Localized Nuclear Envelope Proteins as Targets in MYC‑Driven Group 3 Medulloblastoma

text: Neuronal Activity‑Regulated Mechanisms Promote Growth of Diffuse Hemispheric Glioma H3‑G34 Mutant | Speaker: Samuel Wu | Tumors: diffuse hemispheric glioma H3‑G34 mutant | MOA: Neuronal activity, via both glutamatergic and GABAergic circuits, enhances proliferation of H3‑G34 glioma cells through synaptic integration and release of activity‑regulated secreted factors; proteomic analysis identified N‑cadherin and neurofascin as novel paracrine mediators that promote tumor growth and migration. | Findings: Electron microscopy shows ~10% neuron‑to‑glioma synapses and glioma‑to‑glioma synapses in G34 xenografts.; Glioma cells exhibit evoked EPSCs and spontaneous activity, indicating functional integration.; Pharmacologic blockade of neuronal activity (TTX, NBQX) abolishes neuron‑induced proliferation boost.; Optogenetic activation of either glutamatergic or GABAergic neurons increases tumor proliferation in vivo.; Proteomics of activity‑stimulated conditioned media identifies N‑cadherin and neurofascin as upregulated secreted factors.

metadata.speaker: Samuel Wu
metadata.talk_title: Neuronal Activity‑Regulated Mechanisms Promote Growth of Diffuse Hemispheric Glioma H3‑G34 Mutant

text: Targeting MIB and REM4 with REM422 in Pediatric T‑ALL | Speaker: Richard Locke | Tumors: T‑cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia | MOA: REM422 is an oral small‑molecule that promotes inclusion of a poison exon in MIB pre‑mRNA, triggering nonsense‑mediated decay and loss of MIB protein, thereby inhibiting NOTCH pathway signaling essential for T‑ALL survival. | Findings: REM422 induces rapid (2‑24 h) depletion of MIB protein in ALL PDX cells at nanomolar concentrations.; In vivo, daily oral REM422 (5 mg/kg) is well tolerated and extends EFS across diverse ALL subtypes.; T‑ALL PDXs show greater benefit (median +33 days, T/C = 3.6) than B‑ALL.; Seven of ten T‑ALL models achieve complete or maintained complete responses, including durable remissions beyond treatment cessation.; MIB expression alone does not fully predict response, indicating additional determinants of sensitivity.

metadata.speaker: Richard Locke
metadata.talk_title: Targeting MIB and REM4 with REM422 in Pediatric T‑ALL

text: Development and impact of prophylactic HPV virus‑like particle vaccines | Speaker: Douglas R. Lowy | Tumors: cervical cancer, anal cancer, oropharyngeal cancer, vulvar cancer, vaginal cancer | MOA: HPV L1 virus‑like particles self‑assemble into 360‑subunit VLPs that present repetitive neutralizing epitopes, inducing durable, high‑titer antibodies that persist for >15 years and provide sterilizing immunity by blocking the slow, basement‑membrane‑mediated entry of HPV into wounded epithelium. | Findings: A monovalent HPV16 VLP trial showed 0 persistent infections in the vaccine arm versus 41 in placebo, demonstrating sterilizing immunity.; Single‑dose HPV vaccination achieved non‑inferior efficacy (97%–98%) compared with two doses in the ESCUDO trial, supporting dose de‑escalation.; Antibody titers after a single dose remain flat over 16 years, declining <2.5% per year, indicating long‑lived plasma cell maintenance.; Real‑world data from Denmark show ~90% protection against cervical cancer precursors in women vaccinated ≤16 y.; Global vaccine uptake has risen from 72% to 78% (≥1 dose) and 75% to 80% (up‑to‑date) among US adolescents, contributing to an estimated 1.4 million future deaths averted.

metadata.speaker: Douglas R. Lowy
metadata.talk_title: Development and impact of prophylactic HPV virus‑like particle vaccines

text: Therapeutic applications of HPV VLPs and VLP‑IR700 conjugates | Speaker: John T. Schiller | Tumors: ocular melanoma, bladder cancer, pan-cancer (HSPG‑modified tumors) | MOA: HPV VLPs bind preferentially to cancer cells displaying EMT‑associated, modified heparan‑sulfate proteoglycans; conjugation with the infrared‑activatable dye IR700 enables light‑triggered membrane disruption and necrotic cell death, while simultaneously releasing neoantigens that prime secondary T‑cell responses, creating a dual‑mode therapeutic platform. | Findings: HPV VLPs bind >90% of a 129‑cell‑line panel, with binding strongly correlated to EMT/TGF‑β transcriptional programs.; In a Phase I/II ocular melanoma trial, the therapeutic VLP‑IR700 regimen markedly prolonged time to standard‑of‑care referral compared with sub‑therapeutic dosing.; Therapeutic dosing halted tumor growth in ocular melanoma patients, suggesting disease‑modifying activity.; A bladder cancer window‑of‑opportunity study showed complete pathological response after intravesical VLP‑IR700 plus light, indicating potent local tumor ablation.; The VLP‑IR700 platform leverages dual specificity (tumor binding + light activation) to achieve on‑target cytotoxicity with minimal off‑target effects.

metadata.speaker: John T. Schiller
metadata.talk_title: Therapeutic applications of HPV VLPs and VLP‑IR700 conjugates

text: AI-augmented drug discovery across biologics, small molecules, and multimodal biomarkers | Speaker: Susan Galbraith | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: AstraZeneca embeds AI models to predict protein structures for de novo mini‑protein binders (17% hit rate, 28 nM affinity) and to guide small‑molecule optimization (potency, clearance, exposure) for an intractable target, while computational pathology AI quantifies membrane‑cytoplasm optical density to predict ADC internalization, and multimodal foundation models integrate EHR, imaging, and omics to improve patient selection and trial design. | Findings: AI‑designed mini‑protein library yielded 45 binders (17% success) with highest affinity of 28 nM in just one month, a three‑fold speedup over traditional methods.; Reinvent AI tool accelerated small‑molecule lead optimization for a confidential target, reducing the design cycle from ~8 months to ~4 months while achieving target‑level potency, clearance, exposure, and tumor growth inhibition.; Computational pathology model identified membrane‑to‑cytoplasm optical density difference as a surrogate for internalization of the TROP2 ADC datupizumab duoxetecane, now entering prospective validation in a phase‑III trial.; A multimodal foundation model built with Tempus and Pathos integrates longitudinal EHR, labs, histology, and genomics to predict control‑arm performance and patient response, aiming to improve phase‑III success rates.

metadata.speaker: Susan Galbraith
metadata.talk_title: AI-augmented drug discovery across biologics, small molecules, and multimodal biomarkers

text: Chromatin remodeling complexes as AI‑guided therapeutic targets | Speaker: Sigal Kadish | Tumors: lung cancer, pediatric malignancies, solid tumors | MOA: AI‑driven AlphaFold‑based modeling identified a novel immunoglobulin‑like SWIFT domain within BAF chromatin remodelers that mediates transcription‑factor interactions; hydrogen‑deuterium exchange validated TF‑SWIFT binding sites, and CRISPR dependency screens revealed synthetic lethalities (e.g., SMARCA2 dependence in SMARCA4‑mutant lung cancer), establishing these interfaces as emerging therapeutic targets. | Findings: AI‑predicted SWIFT domain structures correctly identified three PU.1 TAD binding motifs, validated by pull‑down and HDX experiments.; Fitness correlation across >1,000 cancer cell lines highlighted SWIFT‑containing paralogs (SMARCD1‑3) as top codependencies, suggesting selective vulnerability.; Histone modification profiling showed that specific nucleosome acetylation patterns dramatically modulate BAF complex remodeling activity, revealing allele‑specific inhibition opportunities.; Synthetic‑lethal relationship between SMARCA2 and SMARCA4 mutations was confirmed, positioning SMARCA2 as a high‑value target in SMARCA4‑mutant lung cancer.

metadata.speaker: Sigal Kadish
metadata.talk_title: Chromatin remodeling complexes as AI‑guided therapeutic targets

text: AI‑driven de novo antibody design with atomic precision | Speaker: Josh Meyer | Tumors: solid tumors, hematologic malignancies | MOA: Chai Discovery uses diffusion‑based generative models and high‑resolution folding predictions to design full‑length antibodies (including VHH) that directly target defined epitopes on GPCRs, peptide‑MHC complexes, and cytokine interfaces, achieving nanomolar affinities and functional agonism/antagonism without library screening, while agentic AI enforces developability constraints and off‑target avoidance. | Findings: Design of antibodies against >50 diverse targets succeeded with ≤20 designs per target, yielding binders for ~50% of targets (≈10‑fold improvement over prior 0.1% rates).; Atomic‑resolution predictions matched cryo‑EM structures (global RMSD <2 Å, CDR loop RMSD <1 Å) for five test cases, confirming near‑perfect epitope modeling.; GPCR VHH agonist for CCR8 achieved functional signaling after testing only 10 designs, with 1 agonist hit, demonstrating feasibility of de novo agonist design.; Peptide‑MHC antibody selectively bound KRAS G12V peptide‑MHC complex while sparing WT KRAS and alternative MHCs, illustrating precise epitope discrimination.; Developability metrics (expression, stability, viscosity, polyreactivity) of AI‑generated antibodies matched or exceeded those of clinically approved mAbs on first‑pass designs.

metadata.speaker: Josh Meyer
metadata.talk_title: AI‑driven de novo antibody design with atomic precision

text: Adolescent adherence to Planetary Health Dietary Index and breast cancer risk | Speaker: Phuong Anh Le | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Higher adherence to the EAT-Lancet planetary health diet during adolescence is linked to a lower incidence of ER-negative breast cancer, particularly among premenopausal women with lower BMI, suggesting a protective effect of plant-forward dietary patterns on hormone‑negative tumor development. | Findings: Adolescent high PHDI reduced overall invasive breast cancer risk by >30% for ER-negative tumors.; Association remained significant after adjustment for weight change since age 18.; Effect was strongest in premenopausal women and those with BMI <21 kg/m2 at age 18.; Whole fruits were protective; added saturated and trans fats increased risk.

metadata.speaker: Phuong Anh Le
metadata.talk_title: Adolescent adherence to Planetary Health Dietary Index and breast cancer risk

text: Cardiorespiratory multimorbidity and lung cancer risk in the UK Biobank | Speaker: Wang Peng | Tumors: lung cancer | MOA: Co-occurrence of chronic respiratory disease and cardiovascular disease markedly increases lung cancer incidence, with a hazard ratio of 4.11 versus healthy individuals, and healthy lifestyle factors (non‑smoking, diet) attenuate progression risk by up to 57%. | Findings: Cardiorespiratory multimorbidity (CRM) confers the highest lung cancer risk (HR 4.11) compared with single disease states.; 22% of CRD patients progressed to CRM versus 4.9% of CVD patients.; CRM shows the shortest transition time to lung cancer among disease states.; Healthy lifestyle reduces progression from single disease to CRM by 34‑54% and from CRM to lung cancer by 57%.

metadata.speaker: Wang Peng
metadata.talk_title: Cardiorespiratory multimorbidity and lung cancer risk in the UK Biobank

text: Generational immigration status and gastric cancer incidence among Japanese descendants | Speaker: Catherine De La Torre | Tumors: gastric cancer | MOA: Risk of gastric cancer remains elevated across generations of Japanese immigrants in the US, decreasing from a five‑fold increase in first‑generation to a 2.5‑fold increase in third‑generation, indicating persistent ancestry‑related susceptibility beyond environmental assimilation. | Findings: First‑generation Japanese immigrants have ~5× higher gastric cancer risk than NHW.; Risk declines across generations but remains ~2.5× higher in third generation.; Pattern is strongest for non‑cardia gastric cancer.; No effect modification by family history, education, BMI, smoking, or sodium intake.

metadata.speaker: Catherine De La Torre
metadata.talk_title: Generational immigration status and gastric cancer incidence among Japanese descendants

text: PRIME: Parsimonious EHR risk model for pancreatic cancer | Speaker: Lucas Mavromatis | Tumors: pancreatic cancer | MOA: An interpretable elastic‑net derived EHR model (PRIME) using 19 routine clinical variables predicts pancreatic cancer risk with AUC ≈0.75, identifying a high‑risk 1% subgroup with a 0.61% three‑year absolute risk, comparable to germline mutation carriers. | Findings: PRIME achieved AUC 0.76 (24 mo) and 0.75 (36 mo) in US validation health systems.; Top 1% risk group has 0.61% 3‑year absolute PDAC risk (1 in 128) and captures 5.8% of incident cases.; Model performance modestly declines in UK Biobank (AUC 0.71) but remains well‑calibrated.; High‑risk individuals have similar prevalence of known PDAC pathogenic germline variants as the general population, indicating capture of sporadic risk.

metadata.speaker: Lucas Mavromatis
metadata.talk_title: PRIME: Parsimonious EHR risk model for pancreatic cancer

text: Basal metabolic rate and survival in colorectal cancer (COLO-CARE) | Speaker: Sheetal Hardikar | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Higher predicted basal metabolic rate, reflecting greater physiological reserve, is associated with improved overall and colorectal‑cancer‑specific survival, especially pronounced in younger male patients. | Findings: Patients in the highest BMR quartile had 23% lower risk of overall death (HR 0.77).; Highest BMR quartile showed 36% lower risk of CRC‑specific death (HR 0.64).; Benefit was strongest in men under 50, with ~70% better survival.; BMR correlated positively with BMI and was higher in men than women.

metadata.speaker: Sheetal Hardikar
metadata.talk_title: Basal metabolic rate and survival in colorectal cancer (COLO-CARE)

text: Telehealth utilization disparities among older cancer patients | Speaker: Sakshat Chintala | MOA: Older cancer patients exhibit marked disparities in telehealth adoption, with lower uptake among Black, low‑income, and non‑English‑speaking groups, and provider/system factors (e.g., academic setting, female providers) influencing delivery. | Findings: 14.1% of older cancer patients used telehealth at least once in the first year post‑diagnosis.; Utilization peaked in 2020 (21.2%) then declined to 16.2% in 2021.; Black patients had the lowest utilization (11.2%); Asian/Pacific Islanders highest (17.9%).; Provider type (APPs, female clinicians) and academic facilities increased telehealth delivery.

metadata.speaker: Sakshat Chintala
metadata.talk_title: Telehealth utilization disparities among older cancer patients

text: CONFLUENCE: Multi‑ancestry GWAS of breast cancer | Speaker: Houyi Zhang | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: A massive multi‑ancestry GWAS (CONFLUENCE) uncovered 545 independent breast cancer risk loci, including 273 novel signals, and a 544‑variant PRS derived from these loci outperforms the standard 313‑variant score across European, African, and admixed American populations. | Findings: CONFLUENCE includes >2 M participants, tripling effective sample size of prior multi‑ancestry studies.; Identified 545 independent loci, of which 273 are novel.; A 544‑variant PRS improves AUC by 2‑3% across EUR, AFR, and AMR cohorts versus the 313‑variant PRS.; Resource will be publicly released with summary statistics and data access platform.

metadata.speaker: Houyi Zhang
metadata.talk_title: CONFLUENCE: Multi‑ancestry GWAS of breast cancer

text: Plasma proteomic signature of persistent smoking effects and cancer risk | Speaker: Hui Li | Tumors: lung cancer, upper aerodigestive tract cancer | MOA: The PSPSE proteomic signature captures persistent protein alterations after smoking cessation, reflecting cumulative exposure and biological memory, and its elevated levels predict higher incidence of smoking-related cancers, particularly lung cancer, independent of self-reported smoking metrics. | Findings: Identified 18 proteins forming a PSPSE score that distinguishes current, former, and never smokers.; Higher PSPSE score significantly associated with increased lung cancer risk (HR ~1.5) in UK Biobank former smokers.; PSPSE score improves PLCOm2012 lung cancer risk prediction, especially in quitters >20 years.; Signature validated in an independent Asian cohort (Shanghai Men's Health Study) with consistent risk association.

metadata.speaker: Hui Li
metadata.talk_title: Plasma proteomic signature of persistent smoking effects and cancer risk

text: Adult height genetics and fatal prostate cancer risk | Speaker: Anqi Wang | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: Genetically determined adult height, captured by a polygenic risk score, drives the observed association with fatal prostate cancer, likely via growth‑related pathways such as androgen signaling, rather than early‑life nutrition. | Findings: Height PRS strongly associated with fatal prostate cancer (HR 1.30 per SD).; Residual height after accounting for PRS shows no association, indicating genetics drive the risk.; Androgen response pathway upregulated in tumors of taller men, linking height to prostate cancer biology.

metadata.speaker: Anqi Wang
metadata.talk_title: Adult height genetics and fatal prostate cancer risk

text: Copy number alteration subtypes in high‑grade serous ovarian cancer and racial survival disparities | Speaker: Irma Wasak | Tumors: high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma | MOA: Unsupervised clustering of genome‑wide copy‑number profiles from methylation arrays defines three HSOC subtypes (loss‑dominant, CNA‑quiet, gain‑dominant); CNA‑quiet tumors show higher immune infiltration and better survival, while Black patients in the gain‑dominant subtype experience higher mortality, suggesting ancestry‑linked biological contributors to disparity. | Findings: Identified three CNA‑based clusters: loss‑dominant (44%), CNA‑quiet (40%), gain‑dominant (16%).; CNA‑quiet tumors have significantly higher immune cell infiltration and improved overall survival.; Within the gain‑dominant cluster, Black women have a 60% higher hazard of death compared to White women.

metadata.speaker: Irma Wasak
metadata.talk_title: Copy number alteration subtypes in high‑grade serous ovarian cancer and racial survival disparities

text: Spatial context of T‑cell infiltration and exhaustion predicts ovarian cancer survival in Black women | Speaker: Brett Reid | Tumors: high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma | MOA: Multiplex immunofluorescence of whole‑section ovarian tumors reveals that cytotoxic CD8+ T cells confer survival benefit when enriched in the tumor compartment versus stroma, and tumor‑localized TIM‑3+ exhausted T cells paradoxically mark better outcomes, indicating spatially resolved immune functionality drives prognosis in Black women. | Findings: Tumor‑dominant cytotoxic T‑cell enrichment predicts improved survival (HR 0.68).; Stroma‑dominant cytotoxic enrichment predicts worse survival.; Tumor TIM‑3+ exhaustion associated with better survival among tumors with ≥2% T cells.

metadata.speaker: Brett Reid
metadata.talk_title: Spatial context of T‑cell infiltration and exhaustion predicts ovarian cancer survival in Black women

text: Pathways enriched in primary breast tumors with disseminated tumor cells | Speaker: Kayli Lawson-Micho | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: In early‑stage hormone‑receptor‑positive breast cancer, presence of disseminated tumor cells correlates with somatic mutations in Wnt, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and NRF2 pathways; Wnt mutations drive EMT and a stem‑like migratory phenotype, while PI3K alterations promote proliferation and resistance, together facilitating dormancy and later metastasis. | Findings: DTC‑positive tumors enriched for mutations in Wnt, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and NRF2 pathways.; Wnt‑mutated DTC‑positive tumors show increased EMT and decreased proliferation signatures.; PI3K‑mutated DTC‑positive tumors display upregulated proliferative pathways and reduced apoptosis.; APOBEC mutagenesis activity nearly doubled in DTC‑positive patients.

metadata.speaker: Kayli Lawson-Micho
metadata.talk_title: Pathways enriched in primary breast tumors with disseminated tumor cells

text: Colorectal cancer polygenic risk across birth cohorts | Speaker: Xinyu Wang | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: A colorectal cancer polygenic risk score shows progressively stronger association with disease risk in later birth cohorts, suggesting gene‑environment interactions where modern lifestyle exposures amplify genetic susceptibility, particularly for distal colon and rectal cancers. | Findings: PRS distribution unchanged across birth cohorts, but effect size increases in recent cohorts.; Stronger PRS‑CRC association observed in individuals <55 years, unscreened, without family history, and for distal colon/rectal cancers.; Innate immune system pathways enriched among SNPs showing birth‑cohort interaction.

metadata.speaker: Xinyu Wang
metadata.talk_title: Colorectal cancer polygenic risk across birth cohorts

text: Functional characterization of STARD13 as a BRCA2 modifier in breast cancer | Speaker: Shiv Prakash Verma | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: A non‑coding variant rs3742324 within an enhancer region regulates STARD13 expression; loss of STARD13 in BRCA2‑mutant breast epithelial cells amplifies EMT‑related genes (e.g., MMP9) and proliferative pathways, suggesting STARD13 acts as a genetic modifier of BRCA2‑associated breast cancer risk. | Findings: rs3742324 region shows allele‑specific enhancer activity and regulates STARD13 expression.; CRISPR deletion of the enhancer reduces STARD13 transcript levels.; STARD13 knockdown leads to greater downregulation of LATAS2 in BRCA2‑mutant cells.; RNA‑seq reveals upregulation of EMT and extracellular matrix genes (e.g., MMP9) when STARD13 is reduced in BRCA2‑mutant background.

metadata.speaker: Shiv Prakash Verma
metadata.talk_title: Functional characterization of STARD13 as a BRCA2 modifier in breast cancer

text: Building infrastructure for population genomics research at Roswell Park | Speaker: Ken Onel | Tumors: AML, myeloma, lymphoma | MOA: Ken Onel described the creation of a universal consent program, a large biorepository of serial blood and bone marrow samples, and an integrated clinical-genomic data commons (Insight) to enable population‑scale genetic studies in hematologic malignancies, linking germline and tumor sequencing with detailed exposure and demographic data. | Findings: Implemented universal consent with >80% accrual across >50,000 patients.; Biorepository contains 1.3 million biospecimens, including 220,000 bone marrow/blood samples from heme malignancy patients.; Insight tool identified 523 AML patients with germline testing versus 1,195 without, revealing ancestry‑linked testing disparities.

metadata.speaker: Ken Onel
metadata.session_title: Advances in Hemologic Malignancies: Population Sciences for Hematological Malignancies
metadata.talk_title: Building infrastructure for population genomics research at Roswell Park

text: Genetic ancestry and outcome disparities in acute myeloid leukemia | Speaker: Anne Katherine Eisfeldt | Tumors: AML | MOA: Eisfeldt presented data showing that genetic ancestry profoundly modifies AML biology: African ancestry patients exhibit distinct mutation frequencies (e.g., lower NPM1, higher PHIP, novel Rho GTPase mutations) and altered epigenetic landscapes, leading to poorer survival even when harboring traditionally favorable lesions such as NPM1. | Findings: Black AML patients have ~12‑year shorter median OS compared with White patients, especially pronounced in <30 y age group.; NPM1 mutation, usually favorable, predicts adverse outcome in African‑American patients (near‑universal relapse).; PHIP mutations occur in ~7% of African‑American AML and confer aggressive disease in mouse models.; Rho GTPase family mutations are present in 12% of African‑American/A Hispanic AML, a novel finding.; Clonal hematopoiesis is present in 15% of African‑American AML and associates with 80% relapse rate.

metadata.speaker: Anne Katherine Eisfeldt
metadata.session_title: Advances in Hemologic Malignancies: Population Sciences for Hematological Malignancies
metadata.talk_title: Genetic ancestry and outcome disparities in acute myeloid leukemia

text: Overview of Pediatric Extrapolation in Oncology Drug Development | Speaker: Lauren Price | MOA: Pediatric extrapolation leverages similarity in disease biology, drug pharmacology, and response between adult (or older pediatric) reference populations and younger pediatric patients to support safe and efficient drug development without repeating full efficacy trials. | Findings: More than 50% of new pediatric oncology indications (2013‑2024) used pediatric extrapolation.; ICH E11A (2024) formalizes guidance, including allowance for safety extrapolation when supported by data.; Three‑step framework: concept development, plan creation, and plan execution with iterative updates.; Early FDA engagement (early advice meetings, pediatric study plans) is encouraged to reduce uncertainty.

metadata.speaker: Lauren Price
metadata.talk_title: Overview of Pediatric Extrapolation in Oncology Drug Development

text: Model‑Informed Drug Development (MIDD) to Support Pediatric Extrapolation | Speaker: Jiang Liu | MOA: MIDD integrates PK/PD, PBPK, population PK, and QSP models to bridge adult and pediatric data, enabling exposure matching, dose optimization, and trial design for pediatric oncology drugs. | Findings: MIDD methods (population PK, PBPK, QSP) can predict pediatric exposure and support dose selection without extensive pediatric trials.; Examples: gadolinium‑based contrast agents, RILACE, itolizumab, rituximab—all received pediatric indications down to neonates via MIDD.; Renal maturation modeling shows GFR normalizes after ~2 years, informing GBCA dosing in infants.; FDA recommends early, iterative MIDD discussions (type D, MIDD‑focused meetings) to reduce uncertainty.

metadata.speaker: Jiang Liu
metadata.talk_title: Model‑Informed Drug Development (MIDD) to Support Pediatric Extrapolation

text: Pediatric Extrapolation for Lutathera in Adolescents with SSTR‑Positive GEP‑NETs | Speaker: Nicole Dresner | Tumors: gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumor | MOA: Lutathera delivers beta‑emitting 177Lu to SSTR‑expressing neuroendocrine tumor cells, causing DNA damage and tumor regression; adult NETTER‑1 showed a 79% reduction in progression risk (HR 0.21) and 13% ORR, supporting extrapolation to adolescents with similar SSTR expression. | Findings: Adult NETTER‑1 trial demonstrated PFS benefit (HR 0.21) and ORR 13% for Lutathera in SSTR‑positive GEP‑NETs.; NETTER‑P enrolled 9 adolescents; safety profile matched adults (lymphopenia, neutropenia).; Organ dosimetry (kidney, bone marrow) in adolescents was comparable to adults, though predicted high‑dose kidney probability exceeded 20% at the 95th percentile.; FDA concluded extrapolation appropriate despite limited pediatric efficacy data, issuing PMRs for long‑term renal and hematologic safety.; Lutathera received FDA approval for adolescents with SSTR‑positive GEP‑NETs in 2024, marking a successful pediatric extrapolation case.

metadata.speaker: Nicole Dresner
metadata.talk_title: Pediatric Extrapolation for Lutathera in Adolescents with SSTR‑Positive GEP‑NETs

text: Pediatric Extrapolation for Blinatumomab in B‑ALL | Speaker: Mansi Dalal | Tumors: B‑cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia | MOA: Blinatumomab is a CD19‑directed CD3 bispecific T‑cell engager that forms an immunologic synapse, activating T‑cells to lyse CD19‑positive B‑ALL blasts; PK exposure matching between adults and children supports similar efficacy and safety extrapolation. | Findings: Adult BLAST study showed 81% MRD‑negative conversion, providing a robust efficacy signal for extrapolation.; Pediatric dose‑finding study (MT103205) demonstrated tolerability and similar cytokine release syndrome rates to adults.; Meta‑analysis of three randomized trials (adult E1910, pediatric 201/20215, AALL 1331) plus BLIM‑FANT showed consistent survival benefit across ages, supporting extrapolation to pediatric consolidation therapy.; FDA granted age‑agnostic indications for blinatumomab in MRD‑positive B‑ALL and in consolidation, relying on adult efficacy and pediatric safety/PK data.; Post‑marketing requirements include long‑term safety follow‑up for neurotoxicity and cytokine release syndrome.

metadata.speaker: Mansi Dalal
metadata.talk_title: Pediatric Extrapolation for Blinatumomab in B‑ALL

text: African Cancer Atlas (TACA) project and early genomic findings | Speaker: Yaw Bediako | Tumors: breast cancer, colorectal cancer, lung cancer | MOA: The TACA initiative generates paired whole-genome sequencing of African cancer patients to uncover ancestry-specific mutational signatures, driver alterations such as TP53 enrichment, and novel candidate drivers like LEPR and KRTAP10-6, aiming to improve cancer biology understanding and drug discovery for African and global populations. | Findings: Phase 1 of TACA funded to generate 3,000 genomes from 1,500 African cancer patients across 7 countries.; Median sequencing coverage achieved 41X for germline and 121X for somatic samples, comparable to reference datasets.; Tumor mutational burden in African breast cancer cohort comparable to TCGA, suggesting eligibility for checkpoint blockade.; Enrichment of TP53 mutations and novel driver candidates (e.g., LEPR in TNBC, KRTAP10-6 in luminal) relative to European datasets.; Geographic subtype distribution observed: higher triple‑negative breast cancer prevalence in West Africa versus luminal B in East Africa.

metadata.speaker: Yaw Bediako
metadata.talk_title: African Cancer Atlas (TACA) project and early genomic findings

text: Proteomics studies in African cancer cohorts and the African ClinMap multi‑omic platform | Speaker: Irechen | Tumors: breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, gallbladder cancer | MOA: Proteomic profiling of African tumor specimens reveals ECM remodeling, altered lipid metabolism, and distinct protein signatures (e.g., decreased CD36 in breast cancer, high LGR1 in pancreatic cancer) that differentiate tumor from normal tissue and suggest ancestry‑specific therapeutic vulnerabilities. | Findings: Breast cancer proteomics (n=28) identified >2,000 proteins with a five‑fold decrease in CD36 compared to US cohorts.; Machine‑learning classifier achieved AUC 0.96 distinguishing tumor vs normal tissue using proteomic data.; Pancreatic cancer plasma proteomics showed ECM remodeling and inflammatory mediators; LGR1 achieved AUC 0.94 for cancer vs benign.; Prostate cancer tissue proteomics (n>150) uncovered a five‑protein panel linked to neurogenous metastasis.; Gallbladder cancer proteomics identified nine key proteins associated with ECM and smooth muscle contraction loss.

metadata.speaker: Irechen
metadata.talk_title: Proteomics studies in African cancer cohorts and the African ClinMap multi‑omic platform

text: Ancestry‑driven genomic and transcriptomic landscape of aggressive endometrial cancer | Speaker: Nyasha Chambwe | Tumors: endometrial cancer | MOA: Whole‑genome and transcriptomic profiling of African‑ancestry endometrial cancers reveals ancestry‑specific driver alterations (e.g., enriched MECOM short‑isoform amplifications) and reduced CD8 T‑cell infiltration, indicating distinct molecular and immune landscapes that may affect therapeutic response. | Findings: African ancestry patients showed lower CD8 T‑cell infiltration after adjusting for tumor purity and subtype.; MECOM short‑isoform focal amplifications were present in ~35% of African ancestry tumors versus ~10% in European ancestry, linked to poorer progression‑free survival in TCGA.; FBXW7 mutations enriched in African ancestry copy‑number‑high endometrial cancers.; Overall fewer clinically actionable mutations (OncoKB) in African ancestry tumors compared with European ancestry.; Ancestry‑specific expression of PLXNA3 and other genes correlated with admixture proportion.

metadata.speaker: Nyasha Chambwe
metadata.talk_title: Ancestry‑driven genomic and transcriptomic landscape of aggressive endometrial cancer

text: Biomarker‑guided precision prevention and chemoprevention of HCC | Speaker: Yujin Hosoda | Tumors: hepatocellular carcinoma | MOA: Hosoda demonstrated that a liver‑tissue risk signature (PLS) can be modulated by targeting EGFR signaling in myofibroblasts with low‑dose erlotinib, leading to dose‑dependent suppression of phospho‑EGFR, reduction of early HCC nodules, and improvement of the risk signature; similar modulation is observed with lipophilic statins, bariatric surgery, and GLP‑1 agonists, supporting the signature as a surrogate endpoint for chemoprevention trials. | Findings: Risk‑stratified HCC screening using the PLS risk signature improves cost‑effectiveness and predicts incident HCC in >2,000 US patients and a 1,300‑patient NIH cohort.; Low‑dose erlotinib (25‑75 mg) suppresses phospho‑EGFR in cirrhotic liver tissue, with risk‑signature improvement at ≥50 mg and no grade ≥3 toxicity.; Erlotinib reduces early HCC nodules in a rat fibrosis model in a dose‑dependent manner, but has minimal effect on larger established tumors due to poor tumor cell uptake.; Lipophilic statins (atorvastatin) and bariatric surgery improve the PLS risk signature, correlating with lower long‑term HCC incidence.; The EGFR‑driven myofibroblast signature can serve as a surrogate endpoint for future chemoprevention trials (ECHO‑B, CATCH‑B, TOSS).

metadata.speaker: Yujin Hosoda
metadata.talk_title: Biomarker‑guided precision prevention and chemoprevention of HCC

text: Personalized care in advanced HCC: gamma‑delta T cells, liver decompensation AI model, and genomics‑driven targeted therapy | Speaker: Manon Allaire | Tumors: hepatocellular carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, mixed hepatocholangiocarcinoma | MOA: Allaire identified a blood‑based gamma‑delta T cell signature that predicts response to atezolizumab‑bevacizumab in HCC, demonstrated that CT‑derived AI modeling (HepatoSAJ) can stratify patients at high risk of portal‑hypertension‑driven decompensation, and showed that genomics‑driven molecular tumor boards enable targeted therapy for ~65% of liver cancer patients, yielding disease control in one‑third of treated cases. | Findings: High baseline gamma‑delta T cell levels in blood correlate with disease control and longer PFS/OS in atezo‑bev‑treated HCC.; Interferon‑γ is elevated at baseline in responders, supporting a Th1‑type immune milieu.; The HepatoSAJ CT‑AI model predicts liver decompensation risk (AUC ≈ 0.84) better than conventional clinical scores.; Portal hypertension identified by AI is a stronger predictor of mortality than tumor‑related factors in real‑world HCC cohorts.; Genomic profiling revealed targetable alterations in 65% of liver cancer patients; genotype‑matched therapy achieved disease control in 32% with a median PFS of 12 months.

metadata.speaker: Manon Allaire
metadata.talk_title: Personalized care in advanced HCC: gamma‑delta T cells, liver decompensation AI model, and genomics‑driven targeted therapy

text: Therapy-associated clonal hematopoiesis and risk of secondary hematologic malignancies in cancer survivors | Speaker: Ms. Berneo | Tumors: solid tumors, hematologic malignancies | MOA: Therapy (chemo/radiation) promotes expansion of clonal hematopoiesis, especially DNA‑damage‑response CHIP mutations and copy‑neutral loss‑of‑heterozygosity MCAs, which in turn increase the risk of secondary hematologic malignancies in cancer survivors. | Findings: CHIP prevalence rises from 4.5% in cancer‑free individuals to 7.5% in treated cancer survivors (≈50% relative increase).; MCA prevalence rises from 3% to 4% in treated survivors (≈19% relative increase).; Therapy‑associated MCAs are distinct from those linked to secondary hematologic malignancy risk.; Presence of any autosomal MCA confers a hazard ratio of ~4.8 for secondary hematologic malignancy.; CHIP confers a hazard ratio of ~2.8 for secondary hematologic malignancy, with TP53 and PPM1D mutations linking therapy and malignancy risk.

metadata.speaker: Ms. Berneo
metadata.talk_title: Therapy-associated clonal hematopoiesis and risk of secondary hematologic malignancies in cancer survivors

text: Somatic APC mosaicism and colibactin‑producing bacteria in unexplained colorectal adenomatous polyposis | Speaker: Dr. Druwesh | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Somatic APC mosaicism arising early in embryogenesis drives polyposis in one‑third of unexplained cases, while colibactin‑producing E. coli induces a mutational signature that co‑occurs with APC mutations, together contributing to adenoma burden and earlier disease onset. | Findings: APC mosaicism was identified in ~33% of tested unexplained polyposis patients.; Mosaic carriers presented at a younger median age (45 y) and had higher adenoma counts than non‑mosaic patients.; Colibactin‑associated mutational signatures were present in 40% of patients and often co‑occurred with APC mutations within the same lesion.; Blood detection of low‑frequency mosaic APC variants was possible in two cases, confirming systemic mosaicism.; Both mosaic APC and colibactin exposure represent distinct etiologic pathways for unexplained adenomatous polyposis.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Druwesh
metadata.talk_title: Somatic APC mosaicism and colibactin‑producing bacteria in unexplained colorectal adenomatous polyposis

text: Intrinsic and extrinsic determinants of racial disparities in breast cancer biology | Speaker: Dr. DeWitt | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Black women’s breast tumors exhibit higher collagen deposition and a CD4‑dominant, immunosuppressive T‑cell milieu; poverty amplifies the CD4 signature, and collagen‑rich environments enhance invasive potential of Black‑derived tumor cells, linking intrinsic ancestry‑related biology with extrinsic socioeconomic stressors. | Findings: Tumors from Black women show significantly increased collagen content compared with White women.; CD4 T‑cell infiltration is enriched and CD8 depleted in Black women’s tumors; poverty burden further raises CD4 dominance.; Black‑derived HR‑positive cell lines require collagen‑containing matrix for 3D growth, unlike White‑derived lines.; HCC1500 xenografts (Black origin) form palpable tumors with radial collagen alignment; MDA‑175 (White) do not.; In silico invasion modeling predicts collagen density boosts invasion only for Black‑derived cells.

metadata.speaker: Dr. DeWitt
metadata.talk_title: Intrinsic and extrinsic determinants of racial disparities in breast cancer biology

text: Microdysplastic cytomorphologic signatures in normal breast tissue predict future cancer risk | Speaker: Dr. Abubakar | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Quantitative single‑cell analysis of H&E slides identifies epithelial nuclear enlargement and stromal inflammation signatures that reflect early oncogenic and immune alterations, conferring a two‑fold or greater future breast cancer risk independent of age and histologic atypia. | Findings: Four microdysplastic signatures (absent, epithelial, stromal, mixed) were defined based on nuclear and stromal metrics.; Presence of any signature conferred >2‑fold increased breast cancer risk after multivariable adjustment.; Stromal signature strongly predicted ER‑negative cancers, especially in stroma‑rich tissue.; Signatures were predictive across age groups (<50 and ≥50) and in benign disease cohorts.; RNA‑seq of signature‑positive tissues showed immune and wound‑repair pathways activation.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Abubakar
metadata.talk_title: Microdysplastic cytomorphologic signatures in normal breast tissue predict future cancer risk

text: Deep plasma proteomics for early‑stage breast cancer detection in dense breasts | Speaker: Dr. Advani | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: A mass‑spectrometry‑based deep proteomic platform quantifies ~7,000 plasma proteins; a machine‑learning classifier distinguishes early‑stage breast cancer, achieving high sensitivity especially in women with dense breast tissue where conventional imaging is limited. | Findings: Deep proteomics identified ~7,000 proteins per sample in both cancer and healthy cohorts.; Classifier achieved AUC 0.96, 86.2% sensitivity and 90.4% specificity overall.; In women with high breast density, sensitivity rose to 90.2% at fixed 90.4% specificity.; Stage‑0, I, II cancers detected with sensitivities of 84.6%, 88%, and 97% respectively.; Prospective pilot (n≈300) showed 89% sensitivity and 93% NPV, supporting clinical utility.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Advani
metadata.talk_title: Deep plasma proteomics for early‑stage breast cancer detection in dense breasts

text: Multi‑analyte liquid biopsy for early detection of pancreatic cancer in high‑risk individuals | Speaker: Dr. Bergamaschi | Tumors: pancreatic cancer | MOA: A multi‑analyte liquid biopsy combines 5‑hmC epigenomic profiling, cfDNA fragment‑size analysis, and genotype‑adjusted CA19‑9 to generate a machine‑learning classifier that discriminates pancreatic cancer from non‑cancer high‑risk individuals with >80% sensitivity and >97% specificity. | Findings: Training set achieved 80.5% overall sensitivity and 97.5% specificity for pancreatic cancer detection.; Independent validation (n=1,445) confirmed 82.6% sensitivity and 97.5% specificity.; Performance remained consistent across three additional high‑risk validation cohorts.; Specificity loss across 11 non‑pancreatic cancers was negligible (<0.05%).; Pathway analysis of selected features recapitulated cancer hallmarks, confirming biological relevance.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Bergamaschi
metadata.talk_title: Multi‑analyte liquid biopsy for early detection of pancreatic cancer in high‑risk individuals

text: Risk-based breast cancer screening: evidence, models, and implementation challenges | Speaker: Graham Colditz | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Colditz presented a framework for risk-based breast cancer screening that stratifies women by absolute five‑year risk using calibrated models (e.g., Gail, Tyrer‑Cuzick) and assigns screening frequency accordingly, aiming to increase mortality reduction while decreasing false‑positive workups. | Findings: Risk‑based screening could improve breast cancer deaths averted while reducing false‑positive workups by up to 25% (CISNET analysis).; No consensus exists on a universal five‑year risk cut‑point for initiating annual screening; proposed cut points: >3% for annual + supplemental imaging, 1.67–3% for annual, <1.67% for biennial.; Implementation challenges include lack of consistent risk thresholds across trials, guideline variability, and need for model‑agnostic frameworks.

metadata.speaker: Graham Colditz
metadata.talk_title: Risk-based breast cancer screening: evidence, models, and implementation challenges

text: Development and validation of blood‑based biomarkers to guide mammography interval | Speaker: Chris Lee | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Lee described a PROBE‑compliant pipeline that used pre‑clinical plasma from WHI and CHS cohorts to discover protein and auto‑antibody markers (e.g., REG4, JAK2) associated with future hormone‑receptor‑positive breast cancer, then combined them into a four‑marker panel achieving 50% sensitivity at 95% specificity to guide individualized mammography recall intervals. | Findings: From 3,000 screened proteins and 3,000 auto‑antibodies, 6 protein and 5 auto‑antibody markers met pre‑specified statistical criteria.; A four‑marker panel (including REG4 and JAK2) achieved 50% sensitivity at 95% specificity, exceeding the minimal performance needed to inform six‑month recall.; Validated markers in an independent CHS cohort (p<0.05 for 6 proteins, 5 auto‑antibodies).; Developed clinical‑grade MSD assays for top markers and plan prospective validation in the MD Anderson MERIT cohort (n≈250 cancers).

metadata.speaker: Chris Lee
metadata.talk_title: Development and validation of blood‑based biomarkers to guide mammography interval

text: Precision screening and surveillance strategies for colorectal cancer | Speaker: Mingyang Song | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Song presented epidemiologic and genetic risk models that estimate individual 10‑year colorectal cancer risk, showing that high‑risk individuals could start colonoscopy up to six years earlier and low‑risk individuals could delay up to six years; post‑colonoscopy risk varies by polyps, colonoscopy quality (ADR), and polygenic risk scores, supporting personalized surveillance intervals. | Findings: High‑risk individuals (top risk score) reach the 10‑year CRC risk benchmark at age 44, suggesting screening 6 years earlier than standard age 50.; Low‑risk individuals (bottom risk score) reach the benchmark at age 56, indicating possible delay of screening by 6 years.; Negative colonoscopy confers sustained risk reduction for up to 20 years, but risk varies widely by underlying risk score, allowing interval extension up to 25 years for very low‑risk patients.; Only 64% of patients with high‑risk polyps receive recommended surveillance, and only 21% adhere to the guideline‑specified interval.; Polygenic risk scores add modest predictive value (AUC increase ~0.02) for post‑colonoscopy CRC and polyp recurrence.

metadata.speaker: Mingyang Song
metadata.talk_title: Precision screening and surveillance strategies for colorectal cancer

text: Mapping the Molecular Landscape of Head and Neck Cancer to Inform Pan‑Tumor Targeting | Speaker: Lillian L. Siu | Tumors: head and neck cancer | MOA: Dr. Siu demonstrated that ultrasensitive tumor‑informed ctDNA (RADAR) and HPV‑DNA assays can detect molecular residual disease months before radiographic recurrence in head‑and‑neck cancer. Randomization of MRD‑positive patients to a PD‑1‑targeting bispecific antibody (revagostumab) resulted in durable disease‑free survival, supporting the concept of early immunotherapy interception based on real‑time MRD status. | Findings: Feasibility study (PREMERIDIAN) showed 100% blood sample capture in 17 patients and identified ctDNA lead times of 100–245 days before clinical recurrence.; In MERIDIAN, only 5/42 evaluable patients were ctDNA‑positive at early post‑treatment time points, and most of those already had macroscopic disease, highlighting the need for radiologic confirmation of MRD.; MRD‑negative patients (≈35) had excellent relapse‑free outcomes (30/35 alive without recurrence, median follow‑up >22 months).; The single patient randomized to revagostumab remained disease‑free for >22 months, whereas the observation patient progressed, providing proof‑of‑concept for MRD‑guided immunotherapy interception.; Longitudinal ctDNA sampling (multiple post‑treatment windows) increased detection sensitivity compared with single landmark testing.

metadata.speaker: Lillian L. Siu
metadata.talk_title: Mapping the Molecular Landscape of Head and Neck Cancer to Inform Pan‑Tumor Targeting

text: Risk for Pediatric Cancer in Newborn Screening | Speaker: Dr. Sharon Plon | Tumors: retinoblastoma, pinealoblastoma, pediatric solid tumors | MOA: Newborn screening using targeted NGS panels identifies pathogenic variants in cancer predisposition genes (e.g., RB1, TP53) from dried blood spots, enabling early surveillance and treatment to reduce mortality and treatment-related toxicity in high‑risk children. | Findings: Modeling predicts newborn cancer‑risk screening could reduce deaths before age 20 by 8% and by up to 54% in carriers of predisposition syndromes.; Retrospective analysis of 2,000 Michigan newborn spots found 6.8% carried pathogenic variants, with 5/5 RET carriers developing medullary thyroid cancer and RB1 carriers developing retinoblastoma or pinealoblastoma.; Estimated incidence of cancer among newborns with a positive screen is ~1 in 30,000, comparable to other rare screened conditions.; Prospective NCARE trial will randomize 10,000 mothers to focused vs. broad panels to assess feasibility, acceptability, and downstream clinical impact.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Sharon Plon
metadata.talk_title: Risk for Pediatric Cancer in Newborn Screening

text: Therapeutic Precision Cancer Prevention: The Power of Canaries | Speaker: John Burn | Tumors: colorectal cancer, upper GI cancer, hepatobiliary cancer, duodenal cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer | MOA: Low‑dose aspirin reduces cancer incidence in Lynch syndrome by inhibiting platelet‑derived thromboxane A2, thereby enhancing anti‑tumor T‑cell responses; dose‑finding trials (CAP3) show the smallest dose (100 mg) yields the fewest cancers with minimal toxicity. | Findings: CAP3 trial (1,547 participants) demonstrated the lowest cancer incidence in the 100 mg aspirin arm, with 30% of participants experiencing the fewest cancers after 8 years.; Serious adverse events were absent in the 100 mg group, indicating a favorable safety profile compared with higher doses.; Combined analysis of CAP2 and CAP3 yields HR 0.67 versus historic placebo, confirming a protective effect of aspirin across Lynch‑syndrome cancer sites.; Guideline update in the UK will recommend ~81 mg aspirin starting five years before the first colonoscopy for Lynch carriers.

metadata.speaker: John Burn
metadata.talk_title: Therapeutic Precision Cancer Prevention: The Power of Canaries

text: Vaccines for Cancer Prevention and Intervention | Speaker: Nora Disis | Tumors: breast cancer, colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer, Lynch syndrome-associated cancers, obesity‑related breast cancer | MOA: Vaccines deliver tumor‑associated antigens (e.g., HER2, MUC1, frameshift neoantigens) via dendritic cell loading or viral vectors to elicit robust type‑1 CD4⁺/CD8⁺ T‑cell and antibody responses that can eradicate pre‑invasive lesions (interception) or provide prophylactic immunity in high‑risk individuals such as Lynch syndrome carriers. | Findings: HER2/neu dendritic‑cell vaccination induced type‑1 T‑cell and antibody responses and led to loss of HER2 expression in 7/11 evaluable DCIS patients.; Pathologic complete responses were observed in ~30% of HER2‑positive, ER‑negative DCIS patients receiving the vaccine.; NAUS209 (viral‑vector frameshift vaccine) was safe (8% grade 3 AEs) and immunogenic, with 100% of 45 Lynch syndrome participants generating T‑cell responses, persisting in 85% at 12 months.; Adipocyte‑directed Advac vaccine reduced visceral CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration, restored regulatory T‑cells, improved insulin sensitivity, and prevented tumor development in 60% of obese breast‑cancer‑prone mice.

metadata.speaker: Nora Disis
metadata.talk_title: Vaccines for Cancer Prevention and Intervention

text: AI in Cancer Diagnosis: Promise, Performance, and the Human‑AI Factor | Speaker: Joanne Elmore | Tumors: breast cancer, melanoma, skin lesions | MOA: AI models process imaging (mammography, pathology slides) to generate diagnostic predictions; variability studies reveal human inter‑observer inconsistency, while AI can improve reproducibility but may introduce automation bias, highlighting the need for rigorous evaluation and human‑in‑the‑loop designs. | Findings: In a large mammography cohort, AI assistance was associated with a statistically significant increase in recall rate, suggesting potential over‑diagnosis.; Only 10% of 36 pathologists agreed with expert consensus on a challenging skin biopsy, illustrating high diagnostic variability.; Repeated reads by the same pathologists after six months showed poor intra‑observer reproducibility, underscoring the need for decision support.; Human‑AI interaction studies (PRISM) are enrolling 400,000 exams to assess real‑world impact of AI cue timing and presentation.

metadata.speaker: Joanne Elmore
metadata.talk_title: AI in Cancer Diagnosis: Promise, Performance, and the Human‑AI Factor

text: STING agonists amplify BH3 mimetic activity via p53- and cGAS-STING-dependent apoptosis loops | Speaker: Andreas Strasser | Tumors: CLL, AML, non-Hodgkin lymphoma | MOA: STING agonists activate cGAS-STING signaling leading to IRF3-dependent transcription of BH3-only proteins (BIM, NOXA, PUMA) and p53 activation, creating a feed‑forward loop that amplifies apoptosis; combined with BH3 mimetics (venetoclax or MCL‑1 inhibitors) this overcomes resistance by releasing BIM from anti‑apoptotic proteins, resulting in enhanced tumor cell killing in vitro and in mouse models. | Findings: STING agonists induce p53‑independent IRF3 activation and upregulation of BIM, NOXA, and PUMA in lymphoma and leukemia cells.; Loss of Bax/Bak abolishes STING‑agonist‑mediated apoptosis, confirming dependence on the intrinsic pathway.; Combination of STING agonist with BH3 mimetics (MCL‑1 inhibitor or venetoclax) yields synergistic killing in vitro and improves survival in immune‑deficient and immune‑competent mouse models.; High STING expression in AML patient samples predicts sensitivity to STING agonist monotherapy and to the combination with venetoclax.; In vivo, dual treatment leads to ~50% survival benefit in Rag‑KO mice and extends median survival three‑fold in Cas9‑transgenic mice.

metadata.speaker: Andreas Strasser
metadata.talk_title: STING agonists amplify BH3 mimetic activity via p53- and cGAS-STING-dependent apoptosis loops

text: Mitochondrial priming, BCL2 family dependencies and resistance mechanisms in multiple myeloma | Speaker: Larry Boyes | Tumors: multiple myeloma, Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia | MOA: Myeloma cells exhibit high mitochondrial priming driven by BIM up‑regulation; venetoclax releases BIM from BCL2 but BIM can be re‑sequestered by MCL1, especially after IL6‑mediated signaling or BIM phosphorylation, leading to resistance. Combination with dexamethasone or IL6 blockade restores priming and sensitizes cells, while t(11;14) myeloma shows intrinsic BCL2 dependence and higher venetoclax response. | Findings: BIM is up‑regulated in myeloma and drives mitochondrial priming, making cells vulnerable to BH3 mimetics.; Venetoclax treatment releases BIM from BCL2, which then binds MCL1, causing resistance in BCL2‑dependent lines.; Dexamethasone increases total BIM and restores venetoclax sensitivity across resistant myeloma samples.; Stromal IL6 shifts BIM binding to MCL1, conferring resistance; IL6 neutralization or Tocilizumab pretreatment re‑sensitizes cells to venetoclax.; BIM phosphorylation at Ser94 (and Ser87) reduces sensitivity to MCL1 inhibition, indicating a post‑translational resistance mechanism.

metadata.speaker: Larry Boyes
metadata.talk_title: Mitochondrial priming, BCL2 family dependencies and resistance mechanisms in multiple myeloma

text: Domain Alteration Chimeras (DALTACs) reprogram AR-p300 enhancer complexes in prostate cancer | Speaker: Arul Chinnaiyan | Tumors: prostate adenocarcinoma | MOA: The DALTAC heterobifunctional molecule simultaneously binds the androgen receptor ligand‑binding domain and the p300 bromodomain, inducing a ternary complex that repositions p300 from its native chromatin sites to AR‑bound enhancers. This relocalization extinguishes N‑terminal H2B acetylation, suppresses AR‑target gene transcription, and creates neomorphic complexes that impair transcriptional elongation, leading to selective cytotoxicity in AR‑positive prostate cancer cells. | Findings: DALTAC induced ternary complex formation between AR and p300 confirmed by proximity ligation assay and IP‑mass spec.; In AR‑positive 22RV1 cells, 10 nM DALTAC caused >90% reduction in crystal violet staining, whereas p300 inhibitor or AR inhibitor alone showed minimal effect.; Across a panel of prostate cancer cell lines, AR‑positive lines displayed nanomolar IC50s (median ~5 nM) while AR‑negative and normal cell lines had IC50s >10 µM, demonstrating >2000‑fold selectivity.; In castrated VCAP xenografts, oral DALTAC modestly inhibited tumor growth; intraperitoneal dosing achieved tumor regression in all treated mice with no regrowth after drug withdrawal.; Histone H2B N‑terminal acetylation, a pharmacodynamic biomarker, was abolished in tumors treated with DALTAC, correlating with loss of AR‑target gene expression.

metadata.speaker: Arul Chinnaiyan
metadata.talk_title: Domain Alteration Chimeras (DALTACs) reprogram AR-p300 enhancer complexes in prostate cancer

text: Phase I/II trial of heterobifunctional BRD4‑AR degrader (RIPTag) in heavily pre‑treated CRPC | Speaker: Johan de Bono | Tumors: castration‑resistant prostate cancer | MOA: The heterobifunctional RIPTag molecule simultaneously binds BRD4 bromodomain and the AR ligand‑binding domain, creating a non‑degradative ternary complex that locks AR and BRD4 together, disrupting AR transcriptional programs without classic AR antagonism, leading to PSA reductions and radiographic tumor regressions in heavily pre‑treated CRPC. | Findings: No dose‑limiting toxicities observed; MTD not reached up to the highest tested dose (~1000 Da molecule).; Patients experienced rapid, dose‑dependent increases in Cmax and AUC with steady‑state achieved within a few days.; Significant PSA declines (≥50%) were seen in a subset of heavily pre‑treated CRPC patients, including those with AR splice variants.; Radiographic regressions were documented in liver metastases and primary prostate lesions, indicating drug penetration into sanctuary sites.; Common adverse events were mild nausea, anemia, and fatigue; overall tolerability was favorable.

metadata.speaker: Johan de Bono
metadata.talk_title: Phase I/II trial of heterobifunctional BRD4‑AR degrader (RIPTag) in heavily pre‑treated CRPC

text: DLL3‑targeted T‑cell engager gocatumig in neuroendocrine prostate cancer | Speaker: Misha Beltran | Tumors: neuroendocrine prostate cancer | MOA: Gocatumig is a bispecific T‑cell engager that binds DLL3 on neuroendocrine prostate cancer cells and CD3 on T cells, with an albumin‑binding domain to improve half‑life. Engagement redirects cytotoxic T cells to DLL3‑expressing tumor cells, inducing tumor regression; a by‑stander effect may contribute to activity against DLL3‑negative cells within heterogeneous tumors. | Findings: Phase I/II trial showed an overall response rate of ~50% and disease control rate of 72% in heavily pre‑treated NEPC patients.; Deep PSA reductions were observed: 50% of patients achieved ≥90% PSA decline, and 30% achieved ≥99% decline.; Response did not strongly correlate with baseline DLL3 IHC intensity, indicating possible by‑stander killing or heterogeneous antigen expression.; Acquired resistance was associated with loss of DLL3 protein in post‑treatment biopsies, suggesting antigen loss as a resistance mechanism.; Pre‑clinical PDX models demonstrated potent tumor regression and increased CD3+ T‑cell infiltration after gocatumig treatment.

metadata.speaker: Misha Beltran
metadata.talk_title: DLL3‑targeted T‑cell engager gocatumig in neuroendocrine prostate cancer

text: Immunological considerations and B7H3-targeted radioligand therapy mechanisms | Speaker: Dave | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: BetaBART is a humanized anti‑B7H3 antibody with 20 pM affinity for the tumor‑specific 4‑Ig isoform; when labeled with Y‑90 it delivers beta radiation that induces DNA damage, immunogenic cell death and a CD8‑dependent in situ vaccination, leading to long‑term tumor control and immune memory in murine models. | Findings: MIL‑33B (Zr‑89) specifically localizes to 4IG‑expressing tumors in vivo, with loss of signal in B7H3‑KO or excess cold antibody controls.; A single 100 µCi Y‑90‑MIL‑33B injection yields 56% long‑term survival in IR‑resistant CT26 tumors, whereas controls die.; CD8 T‑cell depletion abolishes the survival benefit, indicating CD8‑mediated adaptive immunity is essential.; Treated mice develop immune memory, rejecting rechallenge with the same tumor cells at >100 days post‑treatment.; Cold (non‑radiolabeled) MIL‑33B antibody at high dose shows no anti‑tumor effect, confirming radiation drives the response.

metadata.speaker: Dave
metadata.talk_title: Immunological considerations and B7H3-targeted radioligand therapy mechanisms

text: Granzyme‑B targeted PET imaging to monitor immune activation during PSMA‑RLT plus pembrolizumab | Speaker: Mike Evans | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: A Cu‑64‑labeled GRIP peptide is proteolytically activated by granzyme B released from cytotoxic T cells; the activated probe inserts into nearby membranes, retaining signal on PET and enabling non‑invasive visualization of immune‑mediated tumor killing during PSMA‑targeted radioligand therapy combined with pembrolizumab. | Findings: Granzyme‑B PET signal appears in bone lesions after sub‑ablative PSMA‑617 (Pluvicto) plus pembrolizumab, coinciding with PSA reductions.; Serial granzyme PET scans show increased SUV in existing lesions and emergence of new PET‑avid lesions, reflecting evolving immune activation.; Granzyme PET uptake is absent in control mice lacking granzyme B, confirming probe specificity.; Probe uptake correlates with peripheral blood granzyme B induction and with clinical response, suggesting a pharmacodynamic biomarker for RLT‑IO combinations.; No significant off‑target uptake observed in most patients; occasional uptake in sarcoma of unclear relevance.

metadata.speaker: Mike Evans
metadata.talk_title: Granzyme‑B targeted PET imaging to monitor immune activation during PSMA‑RLT plus pembrolizumab

text: Immunostimulatory radioligand therapy to enhance checkpoint blockade and CAR‑T efficacy | Speaker: Ravi Patel | Tumors: melanoma, breast cancer, neuroblastoma, glioma, solid tumors, liquid tumors | MOA: Low‑dose targeted radionuclide therapy (e.g., NM600 or Cu‑67‑LLP‑2A) delivers localized radiation that modulates the tumor microenvironment, increases pro‑inflammatory cytokines and CD8 infiltration, and can serve as a lymphodepleting conditioning regimen for checkpoint blockade or CAR‑T cells, while sparing systemic lymphocytes when using small‑molecule agents. | Findings: NM600 at 50–100 µCi (2.5–5 Gy) combined with checkpoint blockade yields ~50% complete responses in B78 melanoma, whereas either monotherapy is ineffective.; In 4T1 metastatic breast cancer, low‑dose NM600 alone controls primary tumor but not micrometastases; combination with checkpoint blockade controls both primary and metastatic disease.; Whole‑body 2.5 Gy radiation abrogates the synergy, indicating systemic lymphocyte depletion impairs efficacy, whereas tumor‑restricted dosing preserves benefit.; Cu‑67‑LLP‑2A enhances lymphodepletion, improving engraftment and persistence of adoptively transferred T cells (Flucy conditioning) and boosting CAR‑T efficacy in B16‑PMEL and neuroblastoma models.; Copper‑67 conditioning reduces exhaustion markers (TIM3, LAG3, PD‑1) on CAR‑T cells and shifts tumor‑associated macrophages from M2 to a less suppressive phenotype.

metadata.speaker: Ravi Patel
metadata.talk_title: Immunostimulatory radioligand therapy to enhance checkpoint blockade and CAR‑T efficacy

text: Clinical application of radiopharmaceutical theranostics in neuroendocrine tumors and prostate cancer | Speaker: Dr. Jonathan McConathy | Tumors: neuroendocrine tumor, prostate cancer | MOA: Radiolabeled somatostatin analogs (DOTATATE) and PSMA‑targeted ligands (PSMA‑617) bind cell‑surface receptors on neuroendocrine tumors or prostate cancer cells, are internalized, and deliver beta‑particle radiation (Lu‑177) that induces DNA double‑strand breaks, leading to tumor cell death while allowing PET imaging of target expression for patient selection and dosimetry. | Findings: DOTATATE therapy (NETTER‑1) provided a marked progression‑free survival benefit compared with high‑dose octreotide in Grade 1‑2 GEP‑NETs.; PSMA‑617 therapy (VISION) improved overall survival by 4 months versus standard of care in mCRPC after ARPI and taxane.; Higher baseline PSMA PET SUVmean (>10) predicted greater PSA response and longer PFS in PSMA‑targeted trials.; Patients with high circulating tumor DNA or PTEN loss had poorer outcomes on PSMA therapy, suggesting genomic biomarkers of resistance.; Combination of PSMA‑targeted radioligand therapy with PARP inhibitors or immune checkpoint blockade is feasible and shows early safety signals.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Jonathan McConathy
metadata.talk_title: Clinical application of radiopharmaceutical theranostics in neuroendocrine tumors and prostate cancer

text: Overview of RAS inhibitor landscape, resistance mechanisms and combination strategies | Speaker: Channing | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: KRAS G12C inhibitors achieve modest response rates (~40%) with limited duration (<10 months) due to primary and acquired resistance driven by MAPK pathway reactivation, secondary KRAS mutations, and non‑genetic transcriptional programs such as TEAD, MYC, and ERK activation. | Findings: 73 RAS inhibitors have entered clinical evaluation with ~150 actively recruiting trials as of 2026.; Median ORR for G12C inhibitors across trials is ~40% with median DOR <10 months.; Acquired resistance mechanisms are split roughly 50% genomic (e.g., MAPK pathway reactivating mutations) and 50% non‑genomic (transcriptional reprogramming).; Pan‑RAS inhibitors (e.g., daraxasib) show activity without reactivation of RAS alleles but face toxicity challenges.

metadata.speaker: Channing
metadata.talk_title: Overview of RAS inhibitor landscape, resistance mechanisms and combination strategies

text: BMAL2 as a KRAS‑linked hypoxia driver in pancreatic cancer | Speaker: Alvaro (post‑doc, Ken Olive lab) | Tumors: pancreatic cancer | MOA: BMAL2 functions as a KRAS‑responsive transcription factor that links KRAS signaling to hypoxia responses; it promotes EMT, cell proliferation, and glycolytic metabolism via interaction with HIF‑1α/2α, and its loss delays tumor growth in orthotopic PDA models. | Findings: Regulatory network analysis identified BMAL2 as the top KRAS‑associated master regulator across >200 PDA samples.; BMAL2 activity decreases after treatment with KRAS inhibitor RNC7977 in vitro and in KPC mouse tumors.; BMAL2 knockout reduces proliferation, EMT markers, and glycolysis; overexpression induces mesenchymal morphology and increases proliferation.; BMAL2 physically interacts with HIF‑1α under hypoxia, suggesting a complex that drives hypoxia‑responsive gene expression.; Orthotopic BMAL2‑KO tumors show prolonged mouse survival compared with controls.

metadata.speaker: Alvaro (post‑doc, Ken Olive lab)
metadata.talk_title: BMAL2 as a KRAS‑linked hypoxia driver in pancreatic cancer

text: Rewiring RTK signaling under RAS inhibition in pancreatic cancer | Speaker: Sandra Massali | Tumors: pancreatic cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: RAS inhibition induces dynamic up‑regulation of RTKs (EGFR, HER2, ERBB3) in pancreatic cancer, altering receptor internalization and creating windows for ADC delivery; stromal fibroblasts secrete neuregulin to activate ERBB3, and combined RTK blockade enhances tumor regression. | Findings: RAS inhibition increases HER2 and ERBB3 protein levels in a subset of PDAC models, while EGFR remains stable.; Combining RAS inhibitors with HER2‑targeted ADC (T‑DXd) yields synergistic tumor regression in vitro and in PDX models.; Neuregulin‑1 secreted by cancer‑associated fibroblasts drives ERBB3 activation; anti‑neuregulin antibody plus RAS inhibitor improves survival in murine PDAC.; FRODO assay shows that RAS inhibition accelerates HER2 internalization, enhancing ADC payload delivery.

metadata.speaker: Sandra Massali
metadata.talk_title: Rewiring RTK signaling under RAS inhibition in pancreatic cancer

text: KRAS-targeted therapy Phase III trial results in pancreatic cancer | Speaker: Julie Fleshman | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: A KRAS-directed small‑molecule inhibitor was evaluated in a Phase III trial for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, demonstrating a favorable safety profile and evidence of clinical activity that supports KRAS as a therapeutic target in this disease. | Findings: Revolution Medicines reported positive Phase III trial results for a KRAS‑targeted therapy in pancreatic cancer.; The trial represents a major step forward for KRAS‑directed treatment strategies in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

metadata.speaker: Julie Fleshman
metadata.talk_title: KRAS-targeted therapy Phase III trial results in pancreatic cancer

text: Implementation gaps and early data from the TUBAWISP-2 salpingectomy trial | Speaker: Rebecca Stone | Tumors: ovarian cancer | MOA: Stone outlined the epidemiologic and health‑policy data supporting salpingectomy as a primary ovarian cancer prevention strategy, presented early enrollment data from the TUBAWISP-2 preference trial comparing standard risk‑reducing salpingo‑oophorectomy to early salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy, and highlighted implementation barriers (coding, coverage, disparities) that limit adoption despite a 0.22 hazard ratio for serous ovarian cancer. | Findings: 56% of BRCA1 carriers and ~33% of BRCA2 carriers delay risk‑reducing surgery beyond recommended ages, increasing lifetime serous cancer risk.; Presence of STIC at risk‑reducing surgery confers ~30% 10‑year risk of peritoneal high‑grade serous carcinoma.; Opportunistic salpingectomy reduces serous ovarian cancer risk by ~80% (HR 0.22) in the BC, Canada population‑based cohort.; US adoption of opportunistic salpingectomy at inpatient hysterectomy has plateaued at ~60% since 2018, with lower uptake in outpatient settings (11‑14%).; Racial and insurance disparities exist: Black women and Medicaid recipients are less likely to receive salpingectomy during tubal ligation or postpartum sterilization.

metadata.speaker: Rebecca Stone
metadata.talk_title: Implementation gaps and early data from the TUBAWISP-2 salpingectomy trial

text: OVASEEK: hyperspectral and fluorescence imaging platform for whole fallopian tube screening | Speaker: Angela Belcher | Tumors: ovarian cancer | MOA: Belcher described the OVASEEK system that combines near‑infrared hyperspectral imaging, >1000 nm fluorescent nanoparticle labeling, and machine‑learning segmentation to scan entire excised fallopian tubes in ~15 minutes, identify regions with atypical optical signatures, and predict BRCA mutation status and nanoparticle binding with >90% accuracy, enabling whole‑organ detection of STIC and pre‑cancer lesions. | Findings: Imaged 86 fallopian tubes; initial prototype required 8 hours per tube, later optimized toward 15‑minute workflow.; Machine‑learning model predicts presence of gold‑nanoparticle binding sites with 86% accuracy based on hyperspectral data alone.; BRCA1/2 mutation status can be inferred from optical spectra with 90% accuracy at the whole‑tube level and 95% at the cellular level.; Detected a previously missed STIC in a colon‑surgery patient by highlighting a <200 µm atypical region for targeted pathology.; Developed a seventh‑generation instrument and custom edge‑computing chips (first batch expected June) to enable rapid on‑site analysis.

metadata.speaker: Angela Belcher
metadata.talk_title: OVASEEK: hyperspectral and fluorescence imaging platform for whole fallopian tube screening

text: Orion FISH platform reveals polyclonal copy‑number heterogeneity in STIC lesions | Speaker: Dr. Drapkin | Tumors: ovarian cancer | MOA: Using the Orion FISH platform, Drapkin performed simultaneous 16‑plex immunofluorescence and multiplex DNA‑FISH on single tissue sections, revealing that MYC and CCNE1 amplifications in STIC lesions are polyclonal and spatially heterogeneous, with MYC‑amplified cells often adjacent to immune infiltrates, while CCNE1‑amplified regions are immune‑cold; unexpected copy‑number gains of MDM4 were also detected in morphologically normal epithelium, especially in BRCA1 carriers. | Findings: STIC lesions display polyclonal copy‑number alterations: distinct sub‑clones harbor MYC amplification, CCNE1 amplification, or both.; MYC‑amplified regions are enriched for neighboring immune cells, whereas CCNE1‑amplified regions show reduced immune infiltration.; Copy‑number gains of MYC and CCNE1 are also observed in adjacent histologically normal tubal epithelium.; MDM4 copy‑number gain occurs in both secretory (PAX8+) and ciliated (FOXP1+) cells of normal tubes, more frequently in BRCA1 carriers.; Validation with the clinically approved BioView platform confirms the accuracy of Orion FISH copy‑number calls.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Drapkin
metadata.talk_title: Orion FISH platform reveals polyclonal copy‑number heterogeneity in STIC lesions

text: Mechanisms of ADC resistance informing novel combination therapy strategies | Speaker: Dr. Leif Ellison | Tumors: triple-negative breast cancer, HR-positive breast cancer | MOA: SG (sacituzumab govitecan) binds TROP2, is internalized, releases SN-38 topoisomerase I inhibitor; resistance arises via TROP2 missense mutations that mislocalize the antigen and TOP1 point mutations that prevent SN-38 binding. Sequential PARP inhibition after SG exposure stabilizes TOP1 cleavage complexes, enhancing cytotoxicity. | Findings: Acquired TROP2 missense mutations redirect the protein intracellularly, conferring resistance to SG.; TOP1 E418K mutation, previously unseen in patients, mediates resistance to the SN-38 payload.; TOP1 mutations detected in cfDNA precede clinical progression, serving as a potential biomarker.; Sequential dosing of SG followed by talazoparib is tolerable and yields durable responses, whereas concurrent dosing causes high myelosuppression.; PARP inhibition after SG washout synergistically stabilizes TOP1 cleavage complexes, enhancing tumor cell killing.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Leif Ellison
metadata.talk_title: Mechanisms of ADC resistance informing novel combination therapy strategies
