This mechanotransduction‑driven mitotic error produces copy‑number losses (and later gains) that scale with collagen‑I‑driven tissue stiffness across multiple cancer types. | Findings: Across TCGA, tumor collagen I transcript levels strongly correlate with total copy‑number variation burden.; In 3D spheroids, mutation (chromosome loss) rate per division increases ~10‑fold when stiffness rises from 0 to 30 kPa.; Stiff agarose gels suppress proliferation but increase per‑division mutation frequency, yielding a super‑Poisson variance pattern.; Myosin II knockdown exacerbates mutation rates in stiff environments, implicating contractile rounding forces in genome stability.; Micronuclei frequency is higher in stiff spheroids and in the cores of tumors, linking mechanical confinement to missegregation.

metadata.speaker: Dennis Discher
metadata.talk_title: Stiffness‑induced copy number variation across pan‑cancer

text: Spatial ecosystem analysis reveals mechanobiology‑driven relapse niches in breast cancer | Speaker: Christina Curtis | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Curtis integrated multi‑modal spatial data (MIBI proteomics, CosMX transcriptomics, AFM‑derived stiffness maps, and glycomics) to define a tumor‑dense niche (niche zero) where cancer cells co‑localize with perivascular‑like cells and fibroblasts within a stiff, collagen‑rich microenvironment. This spatial ecosystem predicts poor long‑term outcomes independent of genomic risk classifiers, suggesting that mechanobiology‑driven ECM remodeling creates vascular niches that bypass VEGF signaling and foster relapse. | Findings: Spatial niche zero (high cancer cell density) is a strong independent predictor of 20‑year relapse in ER+ HER2‑ breast cancer.; Perivascular‑like cells and fibroblasts co‑localize within niche zero, forming collagen‑rich vascular niches associated with relapse.; Stiffness measured by AFM‑CNN correlates with niche zero prevalence and doubles relapse risk in the top 20% stiffness group.; Integrative analysis shows that genomic high‑risk subtypes (focal CN amplifications) acquire distinct microenvironmental signatures, refining risk stratification.; Spatial glycomics reveals enrichment of COL6A1, COL3A1, COL1A2 in tumor‑dense regions, linking specific collagen isoforms to aggressive niches.

metadata.speaker: Christina Curtis
metadata.talk_title: Spatial ecosystem analysis reveals mechanobiology‑driven relapse niches in breast cancer

text: Historical context and biological implications of extrachromosomal DNA in cancer | Speaker: Paul Michiel | Tumors: glioblastoma, NSCLC, esophageal adenocarcinoma, lung squamous cell carcinoma, pan-cancer | MOA: Michiel described how extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) forms via double-strand breaks or chromothripsis, lacks centromeres leading to random segregation, creates high copy-number heterogeneity, and drives rapid oncogene amplification, transcriptional hyperactivity, and therapeutic resistance. | Findings: ecDNA particles are large (1–5 Mb), chromatinized but highly accessible, and absent in normal tissues.; ecDNA amplifies oncogenes (e.g., EGFR, MYC) leading to rapid copy-number changes upon drug treatment and withdrawal.; ecDNA formation is linked to p53 loss and can arise during high-grade dysplasia, predicting progression to invasive cancer.

metadata.speaker: Paul Michiel
metadata.talk_title: Historical context and biological implications of extrachromosomal DNA in cancer

text: Computational tools for ecDNA detection and structural reconstruction | Speaker: Vineet Bafna | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Bafna presented AmpliconSuite, a graph‑based pipeline that parses whole‑genome sequencing to identify focal high‑copy amplifications, classify them as ecDNA cycles, breakage‑fusion‑bridge events, or linear amplicons, and reconstruct possible ecDNA structures using long‑read and short‑read data. | Findings: AmpliconSuite has processed >60,000 WGS samples, providing first‑level ecDNA classification.; In lung cancer cohorts, ~20% of patients harbor computationally confident ecDNA, matching prior pan‑cancer estimates.; Long‑read data resolve ambiguous cycles, enabling validation of complex ecDNA structures (e.g., PC3DM, Polo3.20).; Experimental CRISPR‑Cas cuts and multi‑FISH confirm predicted ecDNA structures in cell lines.

metadata.speaker: Vineet Bafna
metadata.talk_title: Computational tools for ecDNA detection and structural reconstruction

text: Longitudinal whole‑genome analysis of ecDNA in TRACERx lung cancer cohort | Speaker: Myall‑Ghanayem | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: Ghanayem showed that ecDNA, identified via AmpliconArchitect in longitudinal whole‑genome data, is frequently truncal in NSCLC, often harbors oncogenes (e.g., ERBB2) or immune‑modulatory genes, correlates with aggressive clinical phenotypes, rapid metastatic growth, and resistance to EGFR‑TKI therapy. | Findings: ~20% of early‑stage NSCLC tumors contain ecDNA; prevalence rises to ~30% in metastatic lesions.; ecDNA is predominantly truncal, present across all sampled regions, and usually carries at least one oncogene.; Patients with ecDNA have worse overall survival, higher rates of extra‑thoracic metastasis, and faster lesion growth on imaging.; In a case of EGFR‑mutant NSCLC, ERBB2 ecDNA emerged at progression and was present in all resistant metastases, suggesting a role in TKI resistance.; Unichromosomal ecDNA dominate, but multi‑chromosomal ecDNA also occur, often co‑amplifying immune‑related genes.

metadata.speaker: Myall‑Ghanayem
metadata.talk_title: Longitudinal whole‑genome analysis of ecDNA in TRACERx lung cancer cohort

text: GV20-0251 anti-IGSF8 antibody phase 1/2 study in melanoma | Speaker: Dr. Memi | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: GV20-0251 is an IgG4 anti-IGSF8 antibody that blocks IGSF8, enhancing NK cell cytotoxicity and dendritic cell antigen presentation, leading to tumor regression especially in IGSF8-high, PD-L1-negative melanoma. | Findings: GV20-0251 monotherapy yielded an ORR of 33.3% and DCR of 77.8% in primary ICI‑resistant melanoma (n=9).; Responses were observed in patients with high tumor IGSF8 expression and low PD‑L1.; The antibody showed a favorable safety profile with no dose‑limiting toxicities and a 26‑day half‑life.; Pharmacodynamics demonstrated full target occupancy on circulating T cells at >3 mg/kg and increased intratumoral NK and CD8 T‑cell infiltration.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Memi
metadata.talk_title: GV20-0251 anti-IGSF8 antibody phase 1/2 study in melanoma

text: First-in-human Phase 1 study of PLN101-095 dual integrin inhibitor with pembrolizumab | Speaker: Dr. Timothy Yap | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma | MOA: PLN101-095 blocks integrin αVβ8/αVβ1, preventing local activation of TGF‑β in the tumor microenvironment, thereby reducing immunosuppression and enhancing IFN‑γ–driven anti‑tumor immunity, especially when combined with pembrolizumab. | Findings: Overall ORR was 19% (4/16) with disease control rate of 56% in the dose‑escalation cohort.; In patients with secondary ICI resistance, ORR increased to 30% and DCR to 60%.; Responses included a complete response in cholangiocarcinoma and partial responses in NSCLC and melanoma.; Pharmacodynamics showed dose‑proportional exposure and >24‑hour IC75 coverage at ≥1000 mg BID.; Elevated plasma IFN‑γ and PD‑L1 after 14 days correlated with clinical responses.

text: Phase I study of AMG 355 anti‑CCR8 antibody alone and with pembrolizumab | Speaker: Dr. Marwan Fakhry | Tumors: melanoma, gastric cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: AMG 355 is an afucosylated IgG1 anti‑CCR8 antibody engineered for enhanced FcγRIIIa binding, depleting CCR8‑positive intratumoral Tregs via ADCC, thereby reducing immunosuppression. | Findings: AMG 355 monotherapy yielded a single partial response (melanoma) and limited activity overall.; Combination with pembrolizumab produced one complete response (gastric) and modest disease control (33%).; Pharmacodynamic analyses showed robust CCR8+ cell depletion in tumor biopsies across dose levels.; Safety profile was favorable with ≤5% grade 3 toxicities; infusion reactions were common but mild.

metadata.talk_title: Phase I study of AMG 355 anti‑CCR8 antibody alone and with pembrolizumab

text: Safety of prolonged atezolizumab exposure in alveolar soft part sarcoma | Speaker: Dr. Alice Chen | Tumors: alveolar soft part sarcoma | MOA: Atezolizumab, an anti‑PD‑L1 antibody, provides durable checkpoint inhibition in ASPS, with long‑term treatment (>2 years) showing low incidence of new grade 2‑3 immune‑related adverse events. | Findings: Extended atezolizumab treatment (>2 years) was feasible with only 3 of 17 patients developing new grade 2‑3 toxicities.; No grade 4‑5 immune‑related events were observed after prolonged exposure.; Median treatment duration reached 124 cycles in the longest‑treated patient.; Overall response rate remained at 37% consistent with earlier reports.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Alice Chen
metadata.talk_title: Safety of prolonged atezolizumab exposure in alveolar soft part sarcoma

text: Phase I study of DKY709 IKZF2 degrader alone and with PDR001 | Speaker: Dr. Giralda | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer, melanoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma | MOA: DKY709 is a cereblon‑recruiting molecular glue that selectively degrades IKZF2 (Helios) in regulatory T cells, reducing their suppressive function and enhancing effector T‑cell activity; combined with PD‑1 blockade (PDR001) to further potentiate anti‑tumor immunity. | Findings: Robust IKZF2 degradation (>90%) observed in peripheral Tregs at doses ≥6 mg.; Monotherapy yielded 2 confirmed PRs and 1 CR in melanoma; combination added 3 PRs across tumor types.; Peripheral neuropathy was dose‑dependent, occurring mainly >10 mg but reversible with dose adjustments.; Recommended Phase 2 dose established at 6 mg QD for both monotherapy and combination.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Giralda
metadata.talk_title: Phase I study of DKY709 IKZF2 degrader alone and with PDR001

text: Phase 2 trial of tislelizumab with anti‑TIM‑3 and anti‑LAG‑3 in recurrent/metastatic HNSCC | Speaker: Dr. Hyeryoun Kim | Tumors: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma | MOA: Tislelizumab blocks PD‑1, while cirgelicimab and LBA‑007 inhibit TIM‑3 and LAG‑3 respectively, aiming to overcome adaptive resistance by targeting multiple immune checkpoints in HNSCC. | Findings: Overall ORR was similar across all arms (25‑27.5%).; Complete responses were observed only in LAG‑3‑containing arms (3 CRs).; In PD‑L1 low (CPS 1‑19) subgroup, combination arms showed numerically longer median PFS (5.4 mo) than monotherapy (1.4 mo).; Safety was comparable; most AEs were grade 1‑2 with no additive toxicity in combinations.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Hyeryoun Kim
metadata.talk_title: Phase 2 trial of tislelizumab with anti‑TIM‑3 and anti‑LAG‑3 in recurrent/metastatic HNSCC

text: 10‑year survival and cfDNA methylation in melanoma brain metastases treated with ipilimumab + nivolumab | Speaker: Dr. Di Giacomo | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: Combined CTLA‑4 and PD‑1 blockade synergistically activates T‑cells, leading to durable intracranial and systemic responses in melanoma brain metastases; cfDNA tumor fraction and methylation scores serve as surrogate biomarkers of long‑term survival. | Findings: 10‑year OS was 32% with ipilimumab + nivolumab versus 30% with fuio‑mustine and 7% with ipilimumab + fuio‑mustine.; Melanoma‑specific 10‑yr OS reached 36% in the combination arm.; Low baseline tumor fraction and t‑methylation scores predicted superior survival.; Decreases in TF and t‑methylation at week 12 correlated with longer overall survival.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Di Giacomo
metadata.talk_title: 10‑year survival and cfDNA methylation in melanoma brain metastases treated with ipilimumab + nivolumab

text: Digital Tissue Twins: AI‑Powered Prediction of Single‑Cell Spatial Omics from H&E Slides | Speaker: Mingyao Li | Tumors: lung adenocarcinoma, pan-cancer | MOA: Li's group developed AI models (iSTAR, iSCALE, AURORA) that learn the relationship between H&E morphology and spatial gene expression, using bulk RNA‑seq as a dynamic‑range constraint to predict single‑cell resolution transcriptomic maps and cell‑type annotations across whole‑slide images. | Findings: AURORA achieved the highest Pearson correlation and lowest false‑positive rate among competing methods when predicting gene expression on held‑out LUAD samples (5 patients).; Virtual prediction of 4,000 TCGA LUAD slides reproduced known tumor pathology patterns (e.g., KRT8 expression).; Mature TLS area quantified by AURORA correlated with improved patient survival in TCGA LUAD.; Higher tumor‑TLS co‑localization was associated with better cancer survival.; Spatial cuff structures identified by AURORA predicted poorer survival, recapitulating findings from Wang et al. Cancer Cell.

metadata.talk_title: Digital Tissue Twins: AI‑Powered Prediction of Single‑Cell Spatial Omics from H&E Slides

text: Rosie: Generative AI for In‑Silico Spatial Proteomics from H&E Slides | Speaker: James Zou | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Rosie trains a hierarchical deep‑learning model on paired H&E and CODEX images to impute multiplex protein expression at 8 µm resolution, enabling rapid, low‑cost generation of in‑silico spatial proteomics maps. | Findings: Rosie generates in‑silico CODEX images for up to 50 protein markers in minutes for <$1 cost, matching key structures seen in experimental CODEX.; Performance across external validation sites remained robust, with Pearson correlations ranging from high (99th percentile) to moderate (25th percentile).; Imputed proteomic maps enable accurate segmentation of tissue structures (stroma, tumor epithelium, endothelium) comparable to ground‑truth CODEX.

metadata.talk_title: Rosie: Generative AI for In‑Silico Spatial Proteomics from H&E Slides

text: Virtual Biotech and AI‑Driven Spatial Omics for Therapeutic Strategy Design | Speaker: Unnamed Session Chair | Tumors: lung cancer, pan-cancer | MOA: The virtual biotech platform uses AI agents to integrate multi‑omic and clinical data, identifying CD276 (B7H3) as a fibroblast‑derived immune checkpoint; agents propose an ADC (CD276‑DXd) strategy, later validated by an FDA breakthrough designation for a similar ADC. | Findings: AI agents identified CD276 highly expressed in tumor‑associated fibroblasts in lung cancer.; Spatial analysis showed CD276‑high fibroblast neighborhoods depleted of immune cells.; High CD276 expression correlated with poorer overall and disease‑specific survival.; Agents independently designed a CD276‑DXd ADC strategy, later mirrored by Merck's FDA‑breakthrough ADC.

metadata.speaker: Unnamed Session Chair
metadata.talk_title: Virtual Biotech and AI‑Driven Spatial Omics for Therapeutic Strategy Design

text: Multiplexed functional assay of BRCA2 missense variants in HAP1 cells | Speaker: Faris | Tumors: breast cancer, ovarian cancer | MOA: A multiplexed assay of variant effects (MAVE) was performed in haploid HAP1 cells where BRCA2 missense variants were introduced at the endogenous locus; cells were cultured and viability ratios (day 5 vs day 14) were sequenced to generate functional scores that distinguish loss‑of‑function (pathogenic strong) from benign variants, enabling calibration to ACMG classification and risk association. | Findings: 502 missense variants (≈10‑11% of all missense) were classified as pathogenic strong, far exceeding the 30‑50 pathogenic missense in ClinVar.; Sensitivity and specificity of the BRCA2 MAVE against known standards were 93‑95% across multiple metrics.; Integration of functional scores with ACMG criteria reduced VUS from ~7,000 to 608 variants (≈90% reclassification).; Combined analysis of two independent BRCA2 MAVEs (HAP1 and mouse ESC) using an integrated VarCall model captured ~95% of variants and further reduced VUS to 396.; Case‑control analysis of pathogenic‑strong missense variants yielded an odds ratio of 4.5 for breast/ovarian cancer risk, comparable to truncating mutations (OR ~5.5).

metadata.speaker: Faris
metadata.talk_title: Multiplexed functional assay of BRCA2 missense variants in HAP1 cells

text: Saturation MAVE of Lynch syndrome mismatch‑repair genes and clinical risk integration | Speaker: Jacob Kitzman | Tumors: colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer | MOA: Saturation MAVE libraries covering >73,000 missense variants across the four Lynch‑syndrome mismatch‑repair genes were introduced into haploid cells; 6‑thioguanine treatment selects for loss‑of‑function variants, and deep sequencing quantifies variant depletion, producing functional scores that correlate with clinical pathogenicity and cancer risk. | Findings: Generated functional maps for >73,000 missense variants across MSH2, MLH1, MSH6, and PMS2.; Proline substitution patterns validated assay performance, showing expected loss‑of‑function in ordered protein regions.; 47 of 48 clinically classified missense variants (independent of functional evidence) were concordant with MAVE results, providing strong evidence for assay reliability.; Retrospective reclassification of 10 individuals in Ambry Genetics database as Lynch syndrome carriers based on MAVE data.; Population‑scale analysis linked loss‑of‑function missense scores to increased colorectal cancer risk, recapitulating known penetrance differences (high for MLH1/MSH2, lower for MSH6/PMS2).

metadata.talk_title: Saturation MAVE of Lynch syndrome mismatch‑repair genes and clinical risk integration

text: Inducing viral mimicry to turn cold small cell lung cancer hot via DHX9, TREX1 and spliceosome inhibition | Speaker: Israel Cañadas | Tumors: small cell lung cancer | MOA: Inhibition or genetic loss of DHX9, TREX1, or spliceosome components leads to accumulation of dsRNA, DNA‑RNA hybrids and crRNA, activating MDA5/MAVS and cGAS‑STING pathways, inducing type I interferon, cytokine production and necroptosis, which remodels the tumor microenvironment, increases CD8+ T‑cell infiltration and sensitizes small cell lung cancer to anti‑PD‑1 therapy. | Findings: DHX9 knockdown in small cell lung cancer cells increases dsRNA and DNA‑RNA hybrids, activating STING and MDA5 pathways.; DHX9 loss reduces tumor growth and enhances CD8+ T‑cell infiltration in immunocompetent mice.; Combination of DHX9 knockdown with anti‑PD‑1 dramatically improves tumor control and survival versus anti‑PD‑1 alone.; Spliceosome inhibition (Pladienolide B) induces crRNA accumulation, ZBP1‑dependent necroptosis, and tumor regression.; Spliceosome inhibitor plus anti‑PD‑1 shows synergistic tumor suppression; effect is lost in CBP1‑deficient mice.

metadata.speaker: Israel Cañadas
metadata.talk_title: Inducing viral mimicry to turn cold small cell lung cancer hot via DHX9, TREX1 and spliceosome inhibition

text: Epigenetic regulation of viral mimicry and its impact on immunotherapy response | Speaker: Catherine Chapinelli | Tumors: melanoma, ovarian cancer, NKT cell lymphoma, high-grade serous ovarian cancer | MOA: DNMT and HDAC inhibition demethylates and opens chromatin, reactivating transposable element transcription that forms dsRNA or DNA‑RNA hybrids, which are sensed by MDA5/MAVS and cGAS‑STING pathways, driving type I interferon signaling, upregulating antigen presentation and PD‑L1, and reshaping the tumor microenvironment to enhance checkpoint blockade efficacy; ADAR1 editing dampens this response, and TP53 status modulates TE expression and drug responsiveness. | Findings: DNMT inhibitors reactivate endogenous retroviruses, generating dsRNA that triggers innate immunity.; Combining DNMTi with HDACi amplifies TE transcription and interferon responses.; ADAR1 knockdown synergizes with DNMTi to improve survival and shift macrophage polarization in ovarian cancer models.; Wild‑type TP53 binds to LTRs and enhances TE transcription upon DNMTi; TP53 loss reduces DNA methylation globally, increasing TE expression.; TP53‑null cells show the strongest interferon response to DNMTi, whereas R175H mutants are less responsive.

metadata.speaker: Catherine Chapinelli
metadata.talk_title: Epigenetic regulation of viral mimicry and its impact on immunotherapy response

text: Viral mimicry enhances cancer vaccine efficacy via interferon‑dependent tumor remodeling | Speaker: Nicolas Verret | Tumors: melanoma, colon carcinoma, lymphoma, MC38 colon cancer | MOA: Azacitidine demethylates tumor DNA, reactivating transposable elements that generate dsRNA and DNA‑RNA hybrids, activating MDA5/MAVS and cGAS‑STING pathways, leading to type I interferon production, upregulation of MHC‑I and PD‑L1, and remodeling of myeloid populations; this creates a permissive microenvironment for vaccine‑elicited T cells to infiltrate, expand, and mediate tumor control, an effect lost when MAVS or STING are knocked out in tumor cells. | Findings: Azacitidine strongly induces transposable element transcription and a type I interferon response in B16 melanoma, dependent on MAVS and STING.; Vaccination alone fails therapeutically, but combined with azacitidine leads to tumor control and improved survival across multiple tumor models.; The combination increases tumor cell MHC‑I expression and expands vaccine‑specific CD8+ T‑cell clones within the TME.; MAVS/STING knockout tumors do not respond to the combination, confirming the necessity of tumor‑intrinsic viral mimicry.; Single‑cell analysis reveals increased cDC1 dendritic cells and reduced immunosuppressive Arg1+ macrophages only when viral mimicry is intact.

metadata.speaker: Nicolas Verret
metadata.talk_title: Viral mimicry enhances cancer vaccine efficacy via interferon‑dependent tumor remodeling

text: Clinical advances and patient experiences with KRAS inhibitors | Speaker: Ignacio Garrido Laguna | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, gastroesophageal cancer, cholangiocarcinoma | MOA: KRAS inhibitors bind either the GDP‑bound or GTP‑bound conformations of mutant KRAS, blocking downstream MAPK signaling and inducing tumor regression. Pan‑KRAS agents target multiple KRAS alleles, while allele‑specific inhibitors (e.g., QTX‑3034) selectively inhibit G12D. Tricomplex inhibitors form a ternary complex with KRAS and an adaptor, achieving potent inhibition across alleles. Early clinical data show high response and disease‑control rates in KRAS‑driven pancreatic, colorectal, and gastro‑esophageal cancers. | Findings: A patient with metastatic KRAS‑mutant pancreatic cancer achieved a complete response after enrollment in the FMC6236 first‑in‑human study (Nov 2022) and remains in remission.; Early‑phase KRAS inhibitor trials report overall response rates around 30% and disease‑control rates of 80‑90% in pancreatic cancer, markedly exceeding historical chemotherapy control rates.; Pan‑KRAS inhibitors show activity in KRAS‑amplified gastro‑esophageal cancers but face pharmacokinetic challenges and limited efficacy against GTP‑bound KRAS.; Allele‑specific G12D inhibitor QTX‑3034 demonstrated a signal in a small endometrial cancer cohort, highlighting the need for mutation‑focused development.; Resistance mechanisms such as KRAS amplification can be detected by ctDNA, suggesting adaptive dosing or combination strategies.

text: Speaker noted that current 3D imaging studies are limited by cost and scale, suggesting an opportunity for CrisPRO to provide computationally efficient synthetic 3D reconstructions that reduce experimental burden. | CrisPRO can generate high‑fidelity synthetic 3D volumes from sparse 2D sections, enabling larger cohort analyses without full 3D acquisition. | Speaker said: "The biggest downside is that 3D imaging is tedious and expensive, so it's infeasible to think of studies on the scale of thousands of tissues."

text: The speaker notes limited use of complex NAMs (only eight INDs) and a need for fit‑for‑purpose validation, opening a niche for CrisPRO to provide robust computational validation frameworks for complex in‑vitro models. | CrisPRO can generate in‑silico validation pipelines that correlate complex NAM readouts with clinical outcomes, strengthening regulatory confidence. | Speaker said: "Only eight INDs discussing complex NAMs were identified, and four of these proposed the NAMs as part of a weight of evidence to replace animal studies."

metadata.speaker: Natalie Simpson
metadata.institution: FDA Division of Hematology, Oncology, Toxicology (DHOT)

text: Speaker proposes hypothetical designs that replace non‑rodent three‑month studies with weight‑of‑evidence; CrisPRO can provide quantitative risk models to support such designs and justify omission of animal data. | CrisPRO can integrate IND database, mechanistic toxicology, and NAM outputs to generate a safety confidence score, enabling regulators to accept reduced animal study designs. | Speaker said: "Could a three‑month rodent study and a weight of evidence assessment in lieu of a non‑rodent three‑month study be sufficient to support safety?"

metadata.speaker: Matthew Thompson
metadata.institution: FDA Division of Hematology, Oncology, Toxicology (DHOT) – Bioinformatics Unit

text: The extensive 8,000‑IND database offers a foundation for CrisPRO to develop predictive models of class‑specific toxicities, reducing reliance on animal studies. | Leverage this curated dataset to train machine‑learning models that predict toxicity risk, supporting weight‑of‑evidence assessments. | Speaker said: "We have a database of now over 8,000 commercial INDs in oncology, cataloguing the mechanisms, targets, and classes by product."

metadata.speaker: Matthew Thompson
metadata.institution: FDA Division of Hematology, Oncology, Toxicology (DHOT) – Bioinformatics Unit

text: Target the SPP1/POSTN tissue repair ligand program that drives melanoma dedifferentiation and immune evasion. | CrisPRO can model ligand-receptor networks to predict combinatorial inhibition of SPP1/POSTN signaling and identify biomarkers of response. | Speaker said: "We put POSTN on cancer cells and see dedifferentiation" and "SPP1 rescue protects cancer cells against immune cytokine killing"

Combine engineered bacteria with checkpoint blockade to enhance TLS formation and antibody responses. | CrisPRO can predict synergistic cytokine networks between bacterial payloads and checkpoint inhibition. | Speaker said: "We combined engineered bacteria with PD‑1 blockade and saw 50% cure versus 25% with PD‑1 alone"

Develop small‑molecule or antibody inhibitors of GPNMB to recapitulate knockout phenotype. | CrisPRO can model GPNMB‑driven signaling networks to prioritize inhibitor design and predict combinatorial effects with checkpoint blockade. | Speaker said: "We are working on making an inhibitor for it"

Identify patients with sufficient vaccine‑responsive T‑cell precursors to benefit from bystander CAR T boosting. | CrisPRO can integrate T‑cell repertoire data to predict responder thresholds for vaccine‑driven bystander activation. | Speaker said: "If you're below certain threshold, this therapy doesn't work"

Incorporate baseline T‑cell frequency as enrollment criterion for future trials of amphiphile vaccine + CAR T. | CrisPRO can model enrollment enrichment strategies based on immune profiling. | Speaker emphasized the need for sufficient precursor T cells

Target IL‑18‑driven myeloid activation pathways to enhance CAR T efficacy in heterogeneous tumors. | CrisPRO can map IL‑18‑induced signaling networks to identify combinatorial targets (e.g., IFN‑γ blockade, macrophage modulators). | Speaker highlighted macrophage expansion and interferon‑γ dependence for tumor control

Use CrisPRO to model emergency myelopoiesis and predict agents that disrupt MS1 programming. | CrisPRO can simulate hematopoietic differentiation trajectories to identify upstream regulators amenable to drug targeting. | Speaker described MS1 score emergence at GMP stage and IL‑6/IL‑10 driven reinforcement

Blastocystis prevalence correlates with plant‑based diet, favorable cardiometabolic markers, and lower colorectal cancer odds, suggesting a potential non‑invasive biomarker for cancer risk stratification. | CrisPRO can integrate multi‑omics and microbial sequencing to develop a predictive model linking Blastocystis subtypes to cancer risk, enabling patient‑level stratification. | Speaker said: "Blastocystis prevalence was positively associated with healthy diets and negatively associated with colorectal cancer"

The randomized dietary intervention showed modest Blastocystis expansion only in weight‑loss achievers; a more controlled trial could test causality for cancer prevention. | CrisPRO can simulate trial power and identify optimal enrollment criteria (e.g., baseline Blastocystis subtype, diet score) to avoid dilution of signal. | Speaker said: "In a randomized controlled trial of 1,100 individuals, blastocystis prevalence could expand modestly, particularly among people who were adhering to a higher quality diet"

Genetic loci linked to EBV persistence (e.g., antigen presentation genes) could be targeted to enhance viral clearance. | CrisPRO can prioritize druggable targets within the identified pathways and model their impact on EBV DNA load. | Speaker said: "We detected 25 conditionally independent loci... many genes that are reassuring that they probably have something to do with either B cells or viruses"

High‑EBV‑DNA individuals constitute a ~10% high‑risk subgroup for autoimmune and neoplastic diseases; a biomarker assay could stratify patients for surveillance. | CrisPRO can integrate EBV DNA quantification with host genotype to generate a risk score for longitudinal monitoring. | Speaker said: "These 10% of individuals have very high levels of persistent EBV... and are more likely to develop lung cancer, lymphomas, autoimmune diseases"

The described whole‑genome‑sequencing‑derived EBV detection platform can be extended to ~100 other viral species, offering a broader virome surveillance capability. | CrisPRO’s computational spine can be adapted to detect low‑abundance viral DNA across biobanks, outperforming conventional serology. | Speaker said: "We focused on EBV, given quite a bit of prior work, but this is one of probably 100 viral species that we've been able to characterize"

Systemic fluconazole reduces gut Candida and restores beneficial butyrate‑producing bacteria, suggesting a combination of antifungal and microbiome‑modulating therapy for colorectal cancer. | CrisPRO can model synergistic effects of antifungal agents with probiotic or FMT strategies to predict tumor‑microbiome response. | Speaker said: "Fluconazole cleared Candida from the gut and led to recovery of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia intestinalis"

Strain‑level variation in Candida albicans (candidalysin production, hyphal formation) may predict which patients benefit from antifungal therapy. | CrisPRO can incorporate strain‑specific genomic signatures to stratify patients for targeted antifungal trials. | Speaker said: "We observed phenotypical differences among Candida albicans strains; some produce hyphae and candidalysin, others do not"

Future trials should include longitudinal metagenomic and metabolomic endpoints to avoid dilution of signal seen in the current 8‑week pilot. | CrisPRO can simulate power calculations for multi‑omics endpoints and recommend optimal sampling intervals. | Speaker said: "We only looked at induction; longer follow‑up and more comprehensive omics would clarify ecological effects"

CrisPRO could provide computational deconvolution of ORF1P signal to infer tissue of origin using multi‑omics integration | Leverage machine‑learning on paired proteomic, ctDNA and clinical data to predict tumor source | Speaker said: "we don't know what kind of tissue the LINE‑1 is coming from"

CrisPRO can model LINE‑1 activation pathways to identify co‑targets that boost assay sensitivity in low‑shedding tumors | Integrate transcriptomic and epigenomic data to predict LINE‑1 expression dynamics | Speaker said: "we don't know why LINE‑1 is low in brain tumors"

Design a longitudinal, risk‑adapted trial in high‑risk cohorts (e.g., Li‑Fraumeni) with paired blood and tissue sampling to validate ORF1P kinetics | Use CrisPRO's simulation engine to power‑calculate optimal sampling intervals | Speaker said: "we know very little about shedding kinetics, especially in early‑stage cancers"

CrisPRO can integrate auto‑antibody signatures with ctDNA and proteomics to create a multi‑modal risk score | Use graph‑based integration of heterogeneous assay outputs to boost specificity and sensitivity | Speaker said: "multiple markers may be necessary" and showed modest AUCs for single antibodies

metadata.speaker: Dr. Qi Dang
metadata.institution: University of Pennsylvania / CRUK Grand Challenge

text: Develop computational models to predict low‑shedding tumors and integrate additional biomarkers (e.g., proteins, microRNA) to overcome the 0.1% tumor fraction detection limit. | CrisPRO can combine multi‑omic features with a probabilistic spine to enhance early‑stage detection beyond cfDNA alone. | Speaker noted: "Improving the algorithms using AI is unlikely to make much of a difference" due to detection limits.

Design trials with biomarker‑enriched enrollment (e.g., high‑risk subpopulations) to increase event rates and reduce dilution of signal. | CrisPRO can stratify participants in silico to identify optimal enrichment criteria for trial simulations. | Speaker emphasized that broad enrollment "may dilute signal" and that a targeted approach could accelerate evidence generation.

Apply CrisPRO’s multi‑omic integration to identify high‑risk subpopulations where early‑stage sojourn time is longer, improving trial enrichment. | CrisPRO can model tumor natural history and predict which cancers have sufficient early‑stage windows for detection. | Speaker noted that early‑stage opportunity for high‑grade cancers was less than four months, limiting down‑staging impact.

Develop a composite MCED platform that combines cfDNA with protein and microRNA markers to overcome the short detection window of DNA‑only tests. | CrisPRO’s computational spine can weight heterogeneous biomarkers to maximize early‑stage detection while controlling false positives. | Speaker emphasized that protein markers may improve sensitivity to early cancers at the expense of specificity.

Implement prevalence‑adjusted analysis pipelines using CrisPRO to retrospectively re‑evaluate existing trial data for stage‑specific outcomes. | CrisPRO can model lead‑time and overdiagnosis effects to refine surrogate endpoint interpretation. | Speaker suggested a "prevalence adjusted comparison" to improve power of stage‑based meta‑analyses.

Use CrisPRO to identify subpopulations where stage reduction is more predictive of mortality, enabling targeted trial enrichment. | CrisPRO’s predictive modeling can quantify the mortality impact of stage shifts for specific cancers. | Speaker noted variability in correlation between stage reduction and mortality across cancer types.

Dr. Lattai highlighted the need to develop and validate functional precision medicine assays using patient tumor tissue, noting logistical challenges such as tissue preservation and lack of standardized workflows. | CrisPRO can integrate multi-omics and phenotypic screening data to create predictive models that prioritize functional assay readouts, accelerating validation and standardization. | Speaker said: "We need to do a better job of demonstrating that functional precision medicine works so that then the tissues that we need will become more easily available."

The NCI vaccine program will fund three clinical trials to generate go/no‑go signals for therapeutic cancer vaccines, indicating an area where existing assets have limited data and could benefit from computational prioritization. | CrisPRO can analyze early trial biomarker data to identify patient sub‑populations most likely to respond, informing go/no‑go decisions and potential combination strategies. | Speaker said: "We are going to fund three different clinical trials over the next three years that will give us some go, no‑go signals in the cancer vaccine field."

Discussion of slow US trial activation compared to Australia suggests an opportunity to redesign trial contracting and IRB processes; CrisPRO could model optimal enrollment criteria to reduce dilution of signal. | CrisPRO can simulate trial enrollment scenarios, recommending biomarker‑driven eligibility criteria that improve signal detection while maintaining feasibility. | Speaker said: "Australia uses central contracting language and shared IRBs, which cuts activation time dramatically."

CrisPRO could provide a computational framework to predict performance metrics (sensitivity, specificity, throughput) for emerging IMAT technologies, helping applicants define quantitative targets required by reviewers. | Leverage CrisPRO's predictive modeling to generate realistic performance benchmarks for novel assays, strengthening grant applications. | Speaker emphasized the need for quantitative performance measures such as "I'm going to reduce assay time from X days to Y hours" to demonstrate impact.

CrisPRO can model protocol failure modes and suggest optimization pathways for high‑failure single‑cell assays. | Apply CrisPRO's simulation engine to predict reagent stability and reaction kinetics, reducing failure rates before wet‑lab testing. | Speaker noted "half the time it doesn't work at all, but it's proof of principle" for the ATAC‑seq method.

CrisPRO can add AI‑driven biomarker prioritization modules to Xena, enabling users to quickly identify clinically actionable signatures within multi‑omic datasets. | Integrate CrisPRO's predictive biomarker engine as a plug‑in for Xena, delivering actionable insights without requiring deep bioinformatics expertise. | Speaker highlighted the need for tools that "help us to better understand cancer" and emphasized usability for non‑computational users.

Need for metabolic health–based biomarkers beyond BMI to stratify cancer risk. | CrisPRO can develop predictive models integrating multi-omic metabolic signatures to define high‑risk subpopulations. | Speaker said: "We need to move beyond measuring body size and start measuring biology."

text: DES1 inhibitor program lacks clinical validation; opportunity to repurpose with CrisPRO‑identified metabolic signatures. | CrisPRO can model DES1 pathway dependencies and predict patient subsets likely to respond. | Speaker said: "We are testing a first‑in‑class DES1 inhibitor that lowers ceramide production."

metadata.speaker: Mary Playdon
metadata.institution: University of Utah, Huntsman Cancer Institute

text: Define circulating AFABP thresholds to select patients for anti‑AFABP therapy. | CrisPRO can integrate proteomic and metabolomic data to derive predictive cut‑offs for AFABP‑positive tumors. | Speaker said: "We are evaluating AFABP as a circulating biomarker and potential target for immunotherapy."

Leverage CrisPRO’s in‑silico screening to identify small‑molecule AFABP inhibitors with better tissue selectivity. | Computational docking and off‑target prediction can accelerate non‑antibody modalities. | Speaker said: "We have developed multiple anti‑AFABP antibody for immunotherapy and have confirmed the therapeutic efficacy in multiple mouse models."

Integrate lipidomic and metabolomic data with inflammatype to capture missing pathways. | CrisPRO can fuse multi‑omic layers to refine the inflammatory signature for better predictive power. | Speaker said: "We have a 384 inflammatory proteins panel, plus glycemic markers, but we may be missing other mediators."

Leverage MEDOC’s harmonized phenotyping to embed CrisPRO‑derived metabolic signatures into upcoming prevention trials. | CrisPRO can provide standardized computational pipelines that plug into MEDOC’s analytics backbone. | Speaker said: "Our common measures ensure we are truly comparing apples to apples, both in mice and human studies."

Researchers need pre-analytical standardization for biomarker assays, which is not addressed by existing funding mechanisms. | CrisPRO can provide computational models to predict optimal pre-analytical conditions and prioritize biomarkers for validation. | Speaker said: "the funding opportunity kind of fills the gap" for pre-analytics and assay validation.

text: The program seeks assays that can monitor treatment resistance; CrisPRO can model resistance pathways to guide assay design. | CrisPRO's computational spine can identify predictive resistance signatures for inclusion in multiplex assays. | Speaker described need for assays that predict "response or resistance to treatment".

text: Identify specific acetylcholine receptor subtypes (muscarinic/nicotinic) that correlate with tumor prognosis across organ sites. | CrisPRO can integrate multi‑omics to discover receptor‑specific expression signatures and predict patient subsets that would benefit from targeted modulation. | Speaker noted: "There are five muscarinic receptors, 16 nicotinic receptors… there may be dozens, if not 100 of these receptors."

Combine acetylcholine pathway modulators with checkpoint inhibitors to overcome T‑cell exhaustion mediated by cholinergic signaling. | CrisPRO can model synergistic effects of neuro‑immune modulators with immunotherapy using computational spine simulations. | Speaker discussed: "Acetylcholine from T cells may affect T‑cell exhaustion and immune surveillance."

Incorporate baseline neural imaging biomarkers to stratify patients and enrich for those with high tumor innervation. | CrisPRO can simulate enrichment strategies and predict power gains from biomarker‑guided enrollment. | Speaker emphasized need to localize celiac ganglion via MRI/PSMA PET for precise radiotherapy.

Leverage CrisPRO’s multi‑omics integration to map neuron‑tumor‑immune connectomes beyond Fast Blue labeling. | CrisPRO can model subcellular transcript distribution and predict functional impact of neuronal injury markers. | Speaker noted that Trace‑and‑Seek captures only cell‑body transcriptomes, missing axonal mRNA localization.

Repurpose existing migraine RAMP1 antagonists for melanoma by defining a biomarker‑driven patient subset with high tumor RAMP1 expression. | CrisPRO can integrate expression data to build a predictive model for RAMP1‑high melanoma responders. | Speaker noted: "Patients treated with RAMP1 antagonists seemed to do better than control patients."

Develop a composite nerve‑injury signature (ATF3, GAL, CGRP) to predict immunotherapy resistance. | CrisPRO can combine multi‑omics to generate a validated signature for trial enrichment. | Speaker described: "Nerve injury signature correlates with poor prognosis across cancer types."

FGFR2 fusion status and kinase‑domain mutation status are not used to select patients in the preclinical models, representing a gap for CrisPRO predictive biomarker integration. | CrisPRO can model the impact of specific FGFR2 fusions and resistance mutations on antibody binding and internalization to prioritize candidates. | Speaker said: "we thought that perhaps these antibodies would also work in inhibitor‑resistant settings" and created kinase‑domain resistant mutations for testing.

Biparatopic antibodies retain activity against FGFR2 kinase‑domain resistance mutations, suggesting a combinatorial strategy with FGFR inhibitors. | CrisPRO can predict synergistic combinations of biparatopic antibodies with FGFR inhibitors and forecast resistance trajectories. | Speaker said: "BC and BD have anti‑proliferative activity for both of the intracellular kinase domain mutations".

Combining biparatopic FGFR2 antibodies with small‑molecule FGFR inhibitors may overcome residual tumor growth. | CrisPRO can simulate pharmacodynamic interactions and optimal dosing schedules for antibody‑small molecule combos. | Speaker said: "the antibody plus the small molecule might end up to be a way to defeat resistance in a combination strategy".

Ribosome‑display nanobody platform enables rapid generation of diverse binders, addressing the limited combinatorial space of traditional biparatopic screening. | CrisPRO can prioritize nanobody clusters based on predicted epitope complementarity and developability, accelerating lead selection. | Speaker said: "we screened three different libraries, each 10^11 in size, and after six cycles we had 500,000 unique sequences".

Identify HER2 expression patterns or co‑mutations that predict the CDC‑mediated advantage of zenitatamab over trastuzumab + pertuzumab. | CrisPRO can integrate HER2 epitope mapping with CDC assay data to define a predictive biomarker panel. | Speaker said: "zenitatamab mediates very potent CDC, whereas the individual antibodies and the combination did not"

Explore whether HER2‑negative or low‑expressing tumor cells become susceptible via the bystander effect observed with zenitatamab. | CrisPRO can model diffusion of complement components and predict bystander cytotoxicity across heterogeneous tumor populations. | Speaker said: "we see robust killing of HER2‑negative cells in the admixed model"

Combine zenitatamab with checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., tislelizumab) to exploit the observed PD‑L1‑independent survival benefit. | CrisPRO can simulate immune‑cell recruitment and predict synergistic effects of CDC‑active antibodies with PD‑1 blockade. | Speaker said: "progression‑free and overall survival benefit was observed independent of PD‑L1 status"

Leverage CrisPRO’s structural modeling to design biparatopic HER2 antibodies with optimized trans‑binding geometry, potentially surpassing zenitatamab’s CDC activity. | CrisPRO can predict optimal epitope pairings and linker lengths to maximize clustering without inducing agonism. | Speaker said: "different formats may mediate different potencies, but not necessarily is the case where you see particular formats with very undesirable properties"

Develop a robust EMPP3 IHC/flow cytometry assay to enrich for responders and reduce exposure of EMPP3‑negative patients. | CrisPRO can model expression thresholds needed for avidity‑driven killing and define a quantitative biomarker cutoff. | Speaker said: "the two strongest progressors in this study actually had absolutely no EMPP3 expression"

Combine the EMPP3 2+1 engager with a CD28 co‑stimulatory bispecific to overcome T‑cell exhaustion observed after repeated dosing. | CrisPRO can simulate sequential dosing schedules and predict synergistic cytokine profiles. | Speaker said: "co‑dosing with CD28 bispecific rescued anti‑tumor activity after chronic restimulation"

Leverage CrisPRO to design 2+1 formats with optimized CD3 affinity tiers (medium vs high) to balance potency and CRS risk. | CrisPRO can predict kinetic avidity effects of varying CD3 affinities within the 2+1 scaffold. | Speaker said: "we have settled on the medium affinity for CD3 as the sweet spot"

CrisPRO can model the pan‑HIF degron interface to predict and design next‑generation glues that retain activity in HIF‑2α low tumors. | Use CrisPRO's protein‑protein interaction prediction to identify alternative neo‑substrate motifs for ARNT that overcome low HIF‑2α dependency. | Speaker hypothesized that HIF‑1α may drive pathology in HIF‑2α low models and that ARNT degradation captures that biology.

Develop a companion diagnostic measuring tumor ARNT/HIF‑2α levels to enrich for patients likely to respond to NEO811. | Leverage CrisPRO's expression‑driven modeling to correlate ARNT degradation kinetics with baseline HIF signatures. | Speaker noted lack of patient selection based on HIF‑2α status and admitted uncertainty about mechanism in the XP490 model.

CrisPRO can develop a predictive model for STEAP2 expression thresholds needed for optimal AZD8359 activity. | Use CrisPRO's tumor‑cell surface expression modeling to define cut‑offs for patient enrollment. | Speaker emphasized that STEAP2 homogenous high expression is critical for efficacy.

Identify synergistic agents that boost CD4 helper function without increasing CRS, complementing CD8 bias. | Leverage CrisPRO to simulate immune network effects of adding checkpoint inhibitors or cytokine modulators. | Speaker noted durability studies suggest indirect CD4 activation is still present.

CrisPRO can integrate FOCAD, MTAP, and SKI complex genomic data to define a high‑confidence patient cohort for TNG961. | Use CrisPRO's pathway‑level synthetic lethality modeling to prioritize patients with combined deletions. | Speaker noted that FOCAD loss co‑occurs with MTAP loss and that SKI complex destabilization predicts sensitivity.

Model potential GSPT1 cross‑reactivity to design next‑generation glues with improved selectivity. | Apply CrisPRO's off‑target prediction engine to redesign the degron interface. | Speaker mentioned that some analogues picked up GSPT1 activity at nanomolar range.

Identify additional synergistic agents (e.g., KRAS inhibitors) that exploit translational stress induced by HBS1L loss. | Simulate combination networks to prioritize agents that enhance ER stress without overlapping toxicity. | Speaker suggested broad safety profile could allow combination with many agents.

Use CrisPRO to model integrin β6 expression thresholds needed for effective EGFR degradation. | Predict patient subsets with sufficient β6 co‑expression to prioritize enrollment. | Speaker emphasized high and homogeneous integrin β6 expression in tumor types as a key selection criterion.

Demonstrate via CrisPRO that extracellular bispecific degradation removes EGFR scaffolding functions unavailable to small‑molecule inhibitors. | Quantify loss of downstream signaling networks after EGFR removal versus inhibition. | Speaker highlighted that degradation reduces phospho‑HER3 and c‑Jun more than blocking antibodies.

Identify synergistic agents (e.g., KRAS inhibitors) that complement EGFR degradation in KRAS‑mutant EGFR‑expressing tumors. | Model pathway cross‑talk to prioritize combination regimens. | Speaker showed preclinical synergy of EPI‑326 with sotorasib in CRC models.

Lack of prospective selection of patients with high tumor hypersialylation limits signal detection | CrisPRO can develop a quantitative hypersialylation signature to enrich for responders in early trials | Speaker said: "we only saw a modest clinical activity and only in the hypersialylated patients"

Transient desialylation suggests a need for sustained enzymatic activity or repeat dosing | CrisPRO can model optimal dosing schedules and predict PK/PD windows for durable target engagement | Speaker said: "the desialylation was only lasting a couple of days on tumors"

Need for robust CCNE1 amplification or cyclin E expression assay to enrich for responders | CrisPRO can develop a predictive gene‑expression signature for cyclin E‑driven CDK2 dependence | Speaker said: "tumors that have relatively high expression of cyclin E… do benefit… but PFS benefit is less"

Potential to pair ECI‑830 with agents that target adaptive resistance pathways beyond CDK4/6 | CrisPRO can simulate multi‑target network effects to prioritize synergistic combos | Speaker said: "the addition of ECI‑830 to ribociclib further suppresses phosphorylated Rb"

TRI‑611 can be positioned to replace failed ALK TKIs in patients with resistance mutations | CrisPRO can model degradation efficiency across the spectrum of ALK resistance mutations to prioritize patient subsets | Speaker said: "TRI‑611 is active against all of the mutations that we have put into this system"

Need for prospective selection of patients harboring ALK resistance mutations for trial enrollment | CrisPRO can integrate genomic profiling to generate a resistance‑mutation panel for enrichment | Speaker said: "we used the BAF‑3 system to explore activity against known and predicted ALK TKI resistance mutations"

Identify synergistic agents that further overcome P‑gp mediated resistance when combined with the dual‑payload ADC | CrisPRO can screen for small molecules that down‑regulate MDR1 expression to augment ADC efficacy | Speaker said: "we retained activity in P‑gp overexpressing resistant models"

Incorporate P‑gp expression as a stratification biomarker in early‑phase trials | CrisPRO can develop a predictive model linking MDR1 levels to expected ADC response | Speaker said: "the dual payload ADC showed activity where MMAE‑only ADC failed due to P‑gp"

RB loss and E2F‑high status are proposed biomarkers but were not incorporated into a prospective trial design; CrisPRO could develop a predictive model to prospectively select patients | Use CrisPRO's computational pipeline to integrate genomic (RB1 mutation) and proteomic (RB protein loss) data to generate a composite RB/E2F activity score for patient selection | Speaker said: "most patients will come on our trial, they'll be scored as having an RB alteration... we need to understand the type of alteration"

Preclinical data suggest synergy with CDK4/6 inhibitor‑resistant tumors; CrisPRO could model combination schedules with existing CDK4/6 inhibitors | Simulate pharmacodynamic interactions between CID‑078 and CDK4/6 inhibitors to prioritize dosing regimens | Audience question: "It should work in CD4/6 inhibitor‑resistant model, right?"

BRD9 dependency is inferred from AML subtype but not prospectively validated; CrisPRO could develop a transcriptomic signature of non‑canonical BAF reliance | Apply machine‑learning to AML RNA‑seq datasets to predict BRD9 dependency and enrich trial enrollment | Speaker: "BRD9 expression is elevated in AML, and SMARCB1 is downregulated"

Synergy observed with venetoclax; CrisPRO can model optimal dosing schedules for BRD9 degrader + BCL2 inhibition | Simulate pharmacodynamic interaction to prioritize combination cohorts | Speaker: "we saw synergy with venetoclax"

ENPP3 IHC positivity alone may not predict ADC delivery; CrisPRO could integrate tumor microenvironment features to refine patient selection | Combine IHC with spatial transcriptomics to model ADC penetration and payload release | Speaker: "we see broad ENPP3 expression, but also noted variable tumor regression timing"

Previous ENPP3 ADC attempts suffered heme toxicity; CrisPRO could redesign linker‑payload to reduce basophil activation | Use computational chemistry to screen alternative non‑auristatin payloads with lower basophil activation potential | Audience: "ENPP3 ADCs have been plagued by heme tox"

Develop a CrisPRO model to predict patient Vβ6/Vβ10 repertoire size from peripheral blood sequencing and select responders | Leverage CrisPRO's TCR repertoire analytics to generate a cutoff for enrollment | Speaker: "binding in PBMCs reflects prevalence of Vβ6/Vβ10 around 6%"

Combine IPN‑1203 with checkpoint inhibitors to further relieve exhaustion; CrisPRO can simulate synergistic effects | Model PD‑L1 blockade plus Vβ‑selective activation to prioritize combination cohorts | Speaker highlighted reduction of exhausted T cells as a key benefit

Baseline KRAS G12C ctDNA positivity strongly predicts response, yet the trial did not require ctDNA screening | CrisPRO can integrate baseline ctDNA allele fraction with clinical outcomes to define a predictive biomarker panel for G12C inhibitor selection | Speaker said: "15 out of 27 patients had ctDNA available at baseline and at cycle two... 87% had >50% clearance"

KRAS amplification emerges as a resistance mechanism; targeting the amplification axis could restore sensitivity | CrisPRO can model amplification‑driven signaling rewiring to identify synthetic lethal partners for combination therapy | Speaker noted: "16% of patients had KRAS amplification, a well‑known resistant mechanism to G12C inhibitor"

Elacrasib demonstrated a favorable safety profile, making it amenable to combination with checkpoint blockade | CrisPRO can predict synergistic immune‑oncology combinations by linking KRAS‑driven immune evasion signatures to checkpoint pathways | Speaker highlighted: "treatment discontinuation due to toxicity was rare" and later suggested a pivotal trial with checkpoint inhibitor

Incorporate mandatory on‑treatment ctDNA and stratify by prior G12C inhibitor wash‑out period to reduce response heterogeneity | CrisPRO can simulate trial arms with ctDNA‑guided enrichment to forecast power gains | Speaker admitted uncertainty whether responses in refractory cohort reflect true circumvention of resistance

Targeting the GTP‑bound KRAS state (on‑inhibitors) could overcome bypass activation that limits off‑inhibitors | CrisPRO can model the dynamic equilibrium between GDP and GTP KRAS states to prioritize on‑state inhibitors for patients with RTK‑driven bypass | Speaker said: "novel KRAS G12C on tri‑complex inhibitors ... may overcome the fundamental limits of off inhibitors"

Safe toxicity profile of elacrasib suggests pairing with checkpoint blockade | CrisPRO can predict synergistic immune signatures in KRAS‑mutant tumors to select optimal ICI partners | Speaker noted: "treatment discontinuation due to toxicity was rare" and later suggested combination trials

PD‑L1 low and STK11/KEAP1 co‑mutations remain poorly stratified for off‑inhibitor benefit | CrisPRO can integrate multi‑omics to define a composite biomarker that predicts which co‑mutated tumors will respond | Speaker highlighted: "activity in difficult‑to‑treat subsets like STK11 and KEAP1 co‑mutated patients" without quantitative data

Baseline KRAS G12D ctDNA detection predicts higher response but was not required for enrollment | CrisPRO can develop a ctDNA‑based enrichment algorithm to select patients most likely to benefit | Speaker reported: "15 out of 27 patients had ctDNA available at baseline... 87% had >50% clearance"

Redevelop GPC2‑only CARs with CRISPR‑mediated up‑regulation of GPC2 to overcome antigen loss | CrisPRO can predict transcriptional regulators of GPC2 and suggest epigenetic drugs to sustain its expression | Speaker reported GPC2 downregulation in all treatment groups

Leverage CrisPRO's subcellular proteomics modeling to predict other mislocalized nuclear envelope proteins as CAR targets | CrisPRO can integrate proteomics and subcellular localization data to prioritize novel surface antigens | Speaker emphasized that conventional pipelines miss nuclear envelope proteins

Develop a diagnostic assay for LBR surface expression to select Group 3 patients | CrisPRO can model expression dynamics and propose a cutoff for patient selection | Speaker showed LBR enrichment at recurrence and post‑therapy

Target N‑CADHERIN signaling pathway to block activity‑driven proliferation | CrisPRO can model downstream signaling networks of N‑CADHERIN and suggest druggable nodes | Speaker showed N‑CADHERIN increased proliferation in G34 cells

Lack of baseline HPV serology or immune correlate data to identify individuals who may need more than one dose | CrisPRO can model serological thresholds and predict responders vs. non‑responders to single‑dose vaccination | Speaker noted: "We couldn't do this in the clinical trials because there are so few breakthrough infections, and there's no immune correlates with breakthroughs."

Leverage VLP structural repeat epitope spacing to design next‑gen vaccines for other STDs | CrisPRO can model epitope spacing effects on B‑cell activation for novel VLP designs | Speaker emphasized: "Structure, structure, structure – dense repetitive display drives potent antibody responses."

Computational pathology biomarker for the Trop‑2 ADC (datupizumab duoxetecane) lacks prospective validation and multiplex integration across indications. | CrisPRO can provide robust multimodal biomarker pipelines that integrate pathology, ctDNA, and proteomics to accelerate validation and enable multiplexed QCS across tumor types. | Speaker said: "we're now in the process of getting prospective validation of that in a phase three trial, and that has the potential to be the world's first computational pathology biomarker"

Paralog‑specific dependencies (e.g., SMARCA2 in SMARCA4‑mutant lung cancer) lack robust predictive biomarkers for patient selection. | CrisPRO can integrate genomic, transcriptomic, and functional screening data to generate paralog‑dependency signatures for trial enrichment. | Speaker said: "certain paralogs, if one member or another is lost, these cancer cells become uniquely dependent on the remaining paralog"

Broad BAF inhibitors have shown toxicity; AI‑guided design of interface‑specific modulators could rescue these programs. | CrisPRO's structure‑aware generative models can design small molecules that target discrete protein‑protein interaction hotspots while sparing global complex activity. | Speaker said: "instead of summarily inhibiting the entire engine across our human cells and tissues, really specialized targeting interfaces that may be more amenable to selective drug discovery efforts"

Need for AI‑driven epitope selection tools that explicitly avoid off‑target binding to homologous proteins. | CrisPRO can embed negative‑selection constraints into the generative pipeline, producing antibodies with built‑in off‑target avoidance. | Speaker said: "we do something where you're prompting with things you don't want the model to bind to"

Partner with companies that provide high‑throughput functional screening to close the loop between design and phenotypic validation. | CrisPRO's modular API can integrate partner assay data to iteratively refine designs. | Speaker said: "we work with over a dozen experimental partners"

Demonstrate that AI‑generated antibodies achieve comparable or superior developability metrics to fully human mAbs. | CrisPRO can benchmark developability scores across large antibody libraries to highlight AI‑generated superiority. | Speaker showed that "humanness actually looks pretty similar to fully human antibodies"

Integrate CRD/CVD multimorbidity risk scores with CrisPRO's molecular risk models to improve lung cancer early detection | CrisPRO can add genomic and transcriptomic layers to the multimorbidity risk, refining high‑risk identification | Speaker said: "Healthy lifestyle was associated with 57% lower risk of progression from CRM to lung cancer"

CrisPRO could model how height‑related genetic risk interacts with androgen signaling pathways to predict aggressive prostate cancer. | CrisPRO can simulate gene‑environment interactions linking polygenic height scores to pathway activity. | Speaker highlighted the androgen response pathway as up‑regulated in taller individuals' tumors.

Spatially distinct tumor cell states (melanocytic vs neural‑crest) correlate with immune niches, offering a spatial biomarker for patient stratification. | CrisPRO can integrate spatial transcriptomics with outcome data to derive predictive spatial signatures. | Speaker said: "Tumor cells in state one are relatively depleted in immune cells in their neighborhood, and then there's a particular enrichment in T cells in tumor cells with state two."

CSF2 signaling from basal cells is a vulnerability; CrisPRO can design combinatorial inhibitors to disrupt this niche. | CrisPRO can predict synergistic targets downstream of CSF2 to mimic basal‑cell ablation without genetic manipulation. | Speaker said: "CSF2 might be doing something here... removing CSF2 just from the basal cells phenocopies collapsing and killing the basal cells."

SEGER outperforms boundary‑based decontamination methods, offering a more accurate spatial transcriptomics pipeline. | CrisPRO can integrate SEGER‑processed data to improve downstream computational modeling of spatial niches. | Speaker said: "We just say forget the boundary, assign transcripts to cells as link assignment, and that's our big difference."

Targeting OSM‑OSMR signaling together with checkpoint blockade could overcome core‑localized EMT–mediated immunosuppression. | CrisPRO can simulate combined OSM inhibition and immunotherapy to predict synergistic effects on tumor microenvironment. | Speaker said: "Oncostatin M... induces many of the partial EMT genes" and "EMT at the core is associated with lower lymphocyte infiltration."

Spatial EMT pattern (edge vs core) can serve as a predictive biomarker for patient stratification in trials. | CrisPRO can integrate spatial transcriptomics with survival data to develop a spatial EMT signature. | Speaker said: "In some samples, EMT enriched at the edge; in others, EMT enriched at the core... suggests two subtypes of tumors."

The ability to detect multi-marker EV surface signatures offers a new dimension for analyzing liquid biopsies and capturing tumor ecosystem complexity that single analyses cannot resolve. | CrisPRO's computational spine can analyze complex multi-marker signatures from EV surface data to identify novel patient stratification biomarkers. | So overall, we've put together a multimarker profiling technique that we think opens new dimensions for analyzing liquid biopsies. It helps to capture the tumor ecosystem complexity in a way that single analyses can't resolve.

The technology is being expanded to other cancer types beyond colorectal cancer, with potential to decode the composition of the tumor microenvironment based on circulating EVs. | CrisPRO can integrate EV surface signature data with other multi-omic data to provide a comprehensive understanding of the tumor microenvironment across various cancer types. | So we've started working with a few different cancer types, not just colorectal cancer. We're also interested in expanding our library of antibodies to look at the broader tumor microenvironment to kind of decode the composition of that microenvironment based on the circulating EVs.

The spatial organization of B cells and their interactions within niches are predictive of immunotherapy response in triple-negative breast cancer, suggesting a gap in current predictive models that primarily focus on T cells or PD-L1. | CrisPRO can leverage spatial multi-omic data to identify and validate B cell-centric biomarkers for immunotherapy response prediction in TNBC. | So taken together, these results from niches, their interactions suggest what drives response to immunotherapy is not just the abundance of B cells but also measures of their spatial organization.

The presence of B cell niches and their interactions, particularly the B activated niche, are associated with immunotherapy response, suggesting that targeting B cell pathways could enhance immunotherapy efficacy. | CrisPRO can analyze the molecular pathways within B cell niches to identify potential combination targets that synergize with immunotherapy. | That specifically the B cell activation signature remains significant across spatial scales, and its interactions are also having predictive capacity for immunotherapy response.

Deep Visual Proteomics can identify early molecular changes in pancreatic precursor lesions and normal ducts associated with cancer development, offering a potential for early detection and stratification. | CrisPRO can integrate DVP-generated proteomic data with genomic and clinical data to build predictive models for PDAC risk stratification and early detection. | And then we had another cohort, which is the cancer-associated cohort, where we isolated cancer-associated normal ducts, low-grade and very rare high-grade PANAs, and the tumor cells.

The ability to combine genotype with phenotype, including KRAS mutations, using DVP, could help in understanding resistance mechanisms to targeted therapies and potentially identify salvage strategies. | CrisPRO can analyze DVP data to identify specific KRAS mutation profiles associated with treatment resistance and suggest combination therapies or alternative treatment strategies. | And just to give you an idea, what we found is that when we look at the ADMs in low-grade, we can see in a number of those hotspot mutations, when we look on the patient level, we can see that some patients have one mutation, others have several different mutations in the different regions of interest.

High stromal CD8 density in ER+ breast cancer is a predictive marker of chemo inferiority and adds prognostic information to clinical variables, suggesting a need for improved patient stratification beyond current genomic assays. | CrisPRO can integrate spatial immune multi-omic data with genomic and clinical data to develop a refined prognostic model for ER+ breast cancer, identifying patients who may not benefit from chemotherapy. | But more crucially is that the inflamed milieu, particularly those with high stromal CD8, at least in alcohol, is a predictive marker of chemo inferiority. It does add significant prognostic information to clinical variables, including menopausal status.

text: The identification of dysfunctional immune states in ER+ breast cancer, including checkpoint upregulation and M2-like macrophage signatures, suggests potential for combination therapies with immunotherapy. | CrisPRO can analyze the molecular pathways within these dysfunctional immune states to identify novel combination targets that could synergize with immunotherapy in ER+ breast cancer. | The inflamed states do appear transcriptomically wired to more dysfunctions, such as the expression of checkpoints, exhaustion transcripts, M2-like macrophage, and remodeling genes, as well as dedifferentiation, potentially from luminal biology.

metadata.speaker: Zach Kinsella
metadata.institution: Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland

text: The platform allows for the identification of novel combination targets by analyzing the phenotypic shifts of CRISPR-edited tumors upon therapeutic intervention, such as identifying a rationale for combining VEGF pathway inhibitors with PD1 blockade. | CrisPRO can leverage the BERTA platform to screen genetic perturbations and therapeutic combinations, identifying synergistic targets and predicting optimal therapeutic strategies. | And so what becomes interesting is that we can look at the trajectories of these different knockouts upon treatment with different drugs. And for example, if you here look at this knockout of VGFR1, the VGFR receptor, when you treat this knockout with PD1, you see a drastic shift towards the right of the space of the phenotype of this tumor. So these tumors under PD1 become tumors that have a very hot TME.

The ability to project human biology onto mouse models allows for the identification of human-specific biomarkers, such as CCAM6, in preclinical settings, which can then be used for patient stratification. | CrisPRO can utilize the humanization capability of the BERTA platform to identify and validate human biomarkers in preclinical models, facilitating their translation to clinical applications. | And what we find that we look at the knockouts, it's a knockout of a transcription factor that essentially is going to induce a switch in histology of the tumor. And the resulting histology resembles the tumor histology in patients that have high CCAM6 expression.

The trial did not use risk‑based biomarkers to prioritize patients for FIT vs FIT‑DNA, creating an opportunity for CrisPRO to develop predictive risk scores to guide test selection. | CrisPRO can generate individualized risk models integrating demographics, insurance status, and prior screening history to assign the optimal stool‑based test, improving yield and cost‑effectiveness. | Speaker noted that "we did not assess cost effectiveness" and that FIT kit brand differences affected positivity rates

Standardize FIT kit brand and incorporate real‑time colonoscopy capacity data to reduce variability across sites. | CrisPRO’s simulation engine can model site‑specific logistics and suggest optimal kit selection and navigation intensity per clinic. | Speaker said "different FIT kit brands with different positivity rates" and "colonoscopies were limited despite navigation"

CrisPRO can incorporate real‑time scan results and comorbidity weighting to improve algorithm precision for minority patients. | CrisPRO’s dynamic data integration layer can ingest EMR imaging feeds instantly, updating eligibility matches on the fly. | Speaker noted that timing of scan results was a major limitation for the algorithm

Provide a unified, AI‑driven trial‑matching platform that reduces manual review by >35% and improves eligibility capture. | CrisPRO’s scalable matching engine can handle larger trial catalogs and patient cohorts with higher accuracy. | Speaker reported that the current algorithm reduced manual review by 35% but still missed many eligible patients

Partner with CrisPRO to embed zip‑code based risk modeling and AI‑driven mobile unit routing to extend screening reach. | CrisPRO can generate geospatial risk maps and optimize mobile unit deployment schedules. | Speaker highlighted need for mobile vans and mentioned zip‑code level disparities

Develop blood‑based NET or inflammatory gene signatures that correlate with epigenetic age acceleration and social stressors | CrisPRO can integrate multi‑omic stress signatures to refine risk stratification beyond socioeconomic indices | Speaker highlighted that tobacco use and BMI were strong drivers of epigenetic age acceleration

Design prospective cohort with repeated epigenetic clock measurements and detailed glucocorticoid exposure to capture temporal dynamics | CrisPRO can model optimal sampling intervals and power calculations for epigenetic aging endpoints | Speaker noted need for larger samples and more repeated measures to assess trajectories

Need for biomarkers to predict which tumors are dependent on KAT2A versus KAT2B, enabling patient selection for selective degraders | CrisPRO can integrate proteomic dependency data with structural predictions to define a KAT2A‑dependency signature | Speaker said: "in paralog screening data ... most of the activity really comes from the A component"

PK challenges of the KAT2A degrader could be addressed by redesign using CrisPRO‑guided scaffold optimization | CrisPRO predicts how small‑molecule modifications affect degrader‑induced ternary complex stability and pharmacokinetic properties | Speaker said: "These compounds still have some PK challenges, so we didn't quite fully cover the target"

Extending the degradomics pipeline to non‑cereblon E3 ligases where CrisPRO can model novel ternary interfaces | CrisPRO’s computational spine can generate predictive models for any E3‑ligase substrate receptor given structural inputs | Speaker said: "we have similar data on other ligases. Not as much, but we're building that"

HR1047R mutation drives helix‑12 swinging; CrisPRO can model how this mutation stabilizes the active conformation for targeted inhibitor design | Predictive modeling of mutant‑specific conformational ensembles to design molecules that re‑stabilize the inactive state | Speaker said: "the histidine 1047 mutation ... allows swinging of the helix and adopting this active conformation"

Differential dependence on RTK versus RAS recruitment suggests a need for mutation‑specific biomarkers | Integrate structural activation states with phosphoproteomic signatures to define patient subsets | Speaker said: "the helical domain mutations retain pretty high dependency on phosphorylated RTKs"

Incorporate membrane‑mimetic nanodisc assays into early‑phase trials to select compounds that achieve full membrane‑engaged activation blockade | CrisPRO can simulate compound effects on membrane‑bound conformations to prioritize candidates before clinical testing | Speaker said: "we used lipid nanodiscs to reconstitute the active complex"

CrisPRO can computationally predict low‑populated kinase conformations, complementing NMR and accelerating hit identification | CrisPRO’s conformational ensemble modeling can generate virtual libraries targeting the same invisible pockets identified by NMR | Speaker said: "we can now design selective inhibitors for this state"

Apply the invisible‑state targeting approach to kinases implicated in resistant cancers where current inhibitors fail | Use CrisPRO to map invisible states across the kinome and match them to disease‑specific mutation profiles | Speaker said: "Gleevec binds very selectively to this low populated state"

Quantitative BAFF‑R expression thresholds could identify patients most likely to benefit from the BAFF‑R CAR | CrisPRO can integrate flow cytometry and transcriptomic data to define a BAFF‑R expression score for patient selection | Speaker noted uncertainty about antigen density and its impact on CAR efficacy

Combine CD19 CAR with BAFF‑R CAR (bispecific) to prevent antigen‑loss relapse in ALL | CrisPRO can model synergistic killing dynamics of dual‑target CARs and predict optimal dosing ratios | Speaker mentioned development of a bispecific CAR expressing both Baff‑CAR and CD19 scFv

Target the TGF‑β–driven transcriptional program (e.g., Aeolus) with CrisPRO‑derived small‑molecule modulators to restore T cell function without inducing apoptosis | CrisPRO can predict transcription factor modulators that selectively dampen TGF‑β‑induced Aeolus activity while preserving survival pathways | Speaker identified a dominant TGF‑β signature and Aeolus as a key regulator of dysfunction

Leverage CrisPRO’s ability to design high‑affinity, methylation‑insensitive TCRs for KRAS G12V, overcoming epitope heterogeneity | CrisPRO can model post‑translational modifications and redesign TCR CDR loops for consistent binding to both methylated and unmethylated peptides | Speaker described methylation of the KRAS G12V epitope causing variable TCR recognition

Combine engineered CD4 helper cells with costimulatory fusion receptors to sustain CD8 TCR function in solid tumors | CrisPRO can predict optimal CD4‑CD8 pairing and fusion receptor designs to maximize synergistic anti‑tumor activity | Speaker showed that CD4 help restored CD8 persistence and that fusion receptors can provide costimulation

Functional HRD assays (e.g., RAD51 foci, STRIDE) could better select patients who will benefit from high‑trap PARP inhibitors. | CrisPRO can integrate functional HRD signatures with genomic data to predict PARP trapping dependency. | RAD51 foci expression indicating reactivation of HR in non‑responders; >90% of resistant models show RAD51 foci.

Combine high‑trap PARP inhibitors with agents that prevent HR re‑activation (e.g., POLQ inhibitors) to overcome resistance. | CrisPRO can model synthetic lethal networks to prioritize POLQ as a partner for PARP inhibition. | Resistant clones lost ability to trap PARP; loss of trapping correlated with resistance.

Use CrisPRO to redesign ARID1B binders to eliminate hook effect and improve degradation kinetics. | Computational protein‑ligand modeling can predict off‑target interactions and guide redesign. | Hook effect observed with cereblon‑based molecule; need for better potency/selectivity.

Identify synergistic partners for SMARCA2 inhibition (e.g., ATR inhibitors) using synthetic lethal network analysis. | CrisPRO can map dependencies in BRG1‑deficient tumors to prioritize rational combos. | SMARCA2 inhibition combined with PD‑1 blockade showed complete responses in mouse model.

PSMA PET intensity alone does not fully predict response; integrating FDG PET or dynamic SUV kinetics could improve patient selection for lutetium‑based RPT. | CrisPRO can model multimodal imaging signatures (PSMA + FDG) to predict therapeutic response and guide eligibility thresholds. | Speaker noted that "30% of patients did not respond or were resistant" and highlighted low PSMA uptake and FDG discordance as possible reasons.
